## 1.5 The Anthology, Part B: Pricing the Default You Might Be Catching (Bohn–Stein; Schmid; Bolder; BlackRock)

The second question about the forced seller: *if the seller is not informed, what is the bond actually worth?* That is the fair-value term, and the shelf offers two families of answers that have been arguing since the 1970s.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.128:* "we need only stipulate that the market is attempting to fairly value a firm, most typically through its equity."
>
> **Annotation.** This is the structural model's entire philosophical cost, and it is cheap. If the equity market is trying to value the firm, then equity is a call option on the assets struck at the debt, $E_t = V_t N(d_1) - F e^{-r(T-t)} N(d_2)$, and the bond is the assets minus that call. Replace the risk-free drift with the physical asset drift $\mu_V$ and you get the distance to default, the number of asset-volatility standard deviations between the firm and its default point:
>
> $$
> \text{DD}_t = \frac{\ln(V_t/F) + (\mu_V - \tfrac12\sigma_V^2)(T-t)}{\sigma_V\sqrt{T-t}}, \qquad \text{PD}^{\mathbb{P}}_{\text{Gauss}} = N(-\text{DD}). \tag{1.4}
> $$
>
> $V_t$ and $\sigma_V$ are not observed; they are backed out of equity value and equity volatility using $\sigma_E E_t = \sigma_V V_t N(d_1)$ (Chapter 6 and Chapter 23 do it properly). The default point $F$ is a convention; the KMV choice commonly reported is short-term liabilities plus half of long-term debt. The desk use is immediate: equity trades every millisecond and the bond trades twice a week, so the equity market gives you a fresh fair-value input for the bid between bond prints.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.138:* "under MKMV's empirical distribution and using the VK model described later in this chapter, a DD of 4 converts into an EDF of almost 1 percent."
>
> **Annotation.** Under the Gaussian map, $N(-4) \approx 0.003\%$. Under the empirical map, it is almost $1\%$: a factor of roughly 300. Kaz, on hearing this: "Let's just assume Gaussian... I regret it already." The lesson for a specifier is that the structural model is excellent at *ranking* firms and terrible at *calibrating* them, so production systems keep the DD and replace $N(\cdot)$ with an empirically fitted, monotone map from DD to default frequency. If ROBO is told to "compute PD from Merton," it will use $N(-\text{DD})$, and every IG name in the book will look immortal.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Schmid_Credit_Risk_Pricing_Models p.128:* "the default time is unpredictable and therefore the behavior of credit spreads for short maturities can be captured more realistically." ... "their main draw-back is the missing link between firm value and corporate default."
>
> **Annotation.** The other family. Intensity (reduced-form) models skip the balance sheet and let default arrive as the first jump of a Poisson process with intensity $\lambda_t$. Their virtue is that a pure diffusion can never default by surprise tomorrow, so structural models imply near-zero short-dated spreads, which the market flatly contradicts. With a constant $\lambda$ under $\mathbb{Q}$, a flat rate $r$, recovery $R$ of par paid at default, and a continuously paid premium $s$, equate the two legs of a CDS:
>
> $$
> s\int_0^T e^{-(r+\lambda)t}\,dt \;=\; (1-R)\int_0^T \lambda\,e^{-(r+\lambda)t}\,dt \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s = \lambda\,(1-R). \tag{1.5}
> $$
>
> The integrals are identical, so they cancel exactly, at every maturity: this is the credit triangle. With quarterly ACT/360 premium accrual it becomes an approximation. Two errors to forbid in every spec: feeding a physical EDF into (1.5), which is a $\mathbb{Q}$ relation (risk-neutral intensities run well above physical ones for IG, which Chapter 6 derives); and treating "40% recovery" as a fact about the bond rather than a CDS quoting convention (Chapter 5).

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *Bolder_Credit_Risk_Modelling p.597:* "If one assumes independence of default, then default risk is entirely idiosyncratic." ... "Relaxing this unrealistic choice, however, is the source of most of the complexity in this field."
>
> **Annotation.** For a desk catching forced flow, correlation is not a portfolio-risk nicety; it is the reason forced sellers arrive in herds. The one-factor threshold model makes it concrete: firm $i$ defaults when $\sqrt{\rho}\,Y + \sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon_i < N^{-1}(p)$, with a common factor $Y$ and idiosyncratic $\varepsilon_i$, both standard normal. Conditional on the factor, defaults are independent with probability
>
> $$
> p(Y) = N\!\left(\frac{N^{-1}(p) - \sqrt{\rho}\,Y}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right),
> $$
>
> so a bad draw of $Y$ moves *every* PD at once, and with it every downgrade, every CCC bucket, and every redemption. Bolder's chapter opens with Richard Feynman's line, "What I cannot create, I do not understand," which belongs on the wall of anyone who specifies models for a coding agent: if you cannot write the simulation, you do not understand the model, and neither will ROBO.

> **[SOURCE EXTRACTION]** *BlackRock_Systematic_High_Yield_Credit p.6:* "Our proprietary probability of default signal that has underpinned all of our credit strategies for over 20 years has successfully identified 77% of the defaulted bonds in the ICE BofA High Yield Index within 24 months of its default since 2010."
>
> **Annotation.** This is the structural lineage in production, reported by the manager about its own signal (treat it as a self-reported hit rate, not an audited one, and note that a hit rate without a false-positive rate is half a confusion matrix). The point for Chapter 1 is what the signal is *for*: in high yield, avoiding the default you might be catching is worth more than any factor tilt, because a 50-point jump to default erases years of carry. Chapter 11 builds the defensive book around it.

```python
from scipy.integrate import trapezoid
from scipy.stats import norm


def distance_to_default(V, F, mu_V, sigma_V, T=1.0):
    """Eq. (1.4): physical distance to default (unitless)."""
    return (np.log(V / F) + (mu_V - 0.5 * sigma_V**2) * T) / (sigma_V * np.sqrt(T))


def credit_triangle_check(lam=0.03, R=0.40, r=0.04, T=5.0, n=200_001):
    """Numerically integrate both CDS legs (measure Q) and return the par spread."""
    t = np.linspace(0.0, T, n)
    disc_surv = np.exp(-(r + lam) * t)
    prem_annuity = trapezoid(disc_surv, t)
    protection = (1.0 - R) * trapezoid(lam * disc_surv, t)
    return protection / prem_annuity


dd = distance_to_default(V=150.0, F=100.0, mu_V=0.06, sigma_V=0.10)   # illustrative IG-like firm
assert dd > 4.0 and norm.cdf(-dd) < 1e-4                               # Gaussian: 'immortal'
assert abs(credit_triangle_check() - 0.03 * 0.60) < 1e-10              # s = lambda (1 - R)

# One-factor threshold model: Monte Carlo default rate matches p; tails fatten with rho
rng = np.random.default_rng(RNG_SEED + 1)
p, rho, n_sims, n_firms = 0.02, 0.20, 20_000, 500
Y = rng.standard_normal(n_sims)
p_cond = norm.cdf((norm.ppf(p) - np.sqrt(rho) * Y) / np.sqrt(1.0 - rho))
loss_frac = rng.binomial(n_firms, p_cond) / n_firms
assert abs(loss_frac.mean() - p) < 4 * loss_frac.std() / np.sqrt(n_sims)
assert np.quantile(loss_frac, 0.99) > 5 * p                            # herds, not coin flips

1.6 The Anthology, Part C: Which Flows Are Harvestable (Dynkin; Man; Paleologo)

The third question: is there a systematic way to be on the other side of forced flow, often enough, at a price that pays? Dynkin, Ben Dor and the Barclays QPS team answer yes, and the cleanest example is the fallen angel.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.349: “The primary driver of this phenomenon does not seem to be overreaction to information, but rather the structural inefficiency stemming from the segmentation between the investment and non-investment-grade markets.”

Annotation. Read “segmentation” as “a graph edge with a capacity limit.” When a bond crosses from BBB- to BB+, the holders whose mandates end at the IG line must sell, and the holders whose mandates begin there are fewer, smaller, and not in a hurry. The price falls below its equilibrium level and then reverses as the bond finds its new owners. That reversal is a liquidity provision premium, not a forecast of fundamentals, which is why it survives: you cannot arbitrage it away by being smarter, only by having a balance sheet that does not care about ratings. Dynkin adds the conditional version: forced selling “should not uniformly affect all issuers. Poor performers during the formation period were more likely to be subject to forced selling and, therefore, to experience a subsequent reversal, unlike top performers” (Dynkin_Systematic_Investing_in_Credit p.158). The reversal is concentrated where the forced supply is.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Dynkin_Systematic_Investing_in_Credit p.361: “For Baa‐rated debt, the probability that a forced sale will occur at some time over the five‐year horizon is 23.7% if forced to sell upon any downgrade to Ba or lower, and 7.2% under the less aggressive policy of selling upon a downgrade to B or lower.”

Annotation. This is the RSSG banker’s favorite kind of number: a contractual trigger, converted into a probability over a horizon. It is also the forced-supply function of §1.8 for one holder type, one trigger, and one cohort. A 23.7% five-year chance of being a forced seller is a cost the IG-only investor pays every year in the form of selling at the bottom. Dynkin’s broader point (p.135) is that “the long‐term risk/return performance of a given asset class is determined in part by the sell discipline that is in place for the portfolio.” The sell rule is part of the asset class, which means somebody else’s sell rule is part of your opportunity set.

Equity momentum: the flow you can see coming. The second harvestable flow is slower. Equity markets digest bad news faster than bond markets (more trading, more short sellers, more analysts), so bond prices lag equity prices. Dynkin’s decile sorts show it plainly: the bottom equity-momentum decile of US HY “delivered negative average excess return of –4.7% per year between 1993 and 2017. In contrast, the average excess return of the top decile portfolio (D10), with the strongest equity momentum, was +4.01% per year” (Dynkin_Systematic_Investing_in_Credit p.606). Man’s own factor research finds the same: “the only spill-over to achieve meaningful statistical significance is equity Momentum, which generates a higher alpha than corporate bond Momentum itself” (Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.31). In the language of the bid equation, equity momentum is a public feature that updates the fair-value term before the bond trades. Man’s backtested factor ladder (p.28) reports information ratios of 2.15 for value, 1.69 for momentum, 1.55 for quality, and 0.79 for its “informed investor” signal, combining to 2.35; those are model returns from the manager’s own backtest, and the Trend Watch below explains why a 2026 reader should haircut them.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Man_Revolutions_in_Credit_Trading_2023 p.2: “The greatest barriers to systematic approaches breaking through in credit have traditionally been execution and the ability to model transaction costs and liquidity within decades-old manual processes.”

Annotation. Every premium above is a premium before costs, and in 2015 the costs ate most of them. What changed is plumbing. Once a manager can send a 400-line list to a portfolio-trading desk and get a single price in minutes, the cost term \(c(\Delta q)\) of the bid equation falls for the buyer of liquidity, and the systematic investor can finally harvest premia that were always there on paper. The same paper puts it as an aphorism: “an optimised portfolio is not optimal if you can’t trade it” (p.4). It also notes that Man Numeric moved from roughly 30% of its HY and 60% of its IG order flow on electronic venues to over 90% (p.3).

Trend Watch: The execution revolution, 2018–2026. What changed: US corporate bonds went from phone-and-chat to a market where half of IG volume trades electronically and portfolio trades are a standard protocol. How big: Coalition Greenwich put IG e-trading at 37% and HY at 27% in 2021 (via IFR); at 48% and 33% in 2024, with average daily notional volume (ADNV) of $46bn, up 21%, and daily turnover rising from 0.33% of outstanding (2021) to 0.44% (2024) (The DESK, 21 Jan 2025). In 2025 ADNV passed $50bn for the first time, IG e-trading sat just under 50% and HY at 32%, and disclosed RFQ fell to 38.6% of electronic volume (Coalition Greenwich via The DESK, 30 Jan 2026). The single-day record of $84.7bn on 30 Sep 2025 was 18% portfolio trades (Coalition Greenwich, 27 Jan 2026). Portfolio trading rose from 11% of US corporate bond volume in 2024 to 15% in 2025, peaking at 17% in July 2025 (Morgan Stanley via The DESK, 19 Feb 2026); Barclays counted a portfolio trade every six minutes in H1 2025, against one every 41 minutes in 2020 (IFR, 2025). January 2026 then set a new record, ADNV up 22% year on year to $61bn (Coalition Greenwich, 17 Feb 2026). What it means for the desk: the cost term fell, so premia that were paper alpha in 2015 became tradable; and the RFQ in the cold open is now one of tens of thousands per day, which makes toxicity screening an automated, statistical job rather than a trader’s hunch. Mags: “Back in my day a portfolio trade was a fax with forty CUSIPs and a prayer. Now it’s four thousand line items and no prayer. The pricing is better. I hate it.” (Tradeweb reported a single portfolio trade with more than 4,000 line items; IFR, 2025.)

Trend Watch: The corporate bond factor replication crisis, 2019–2026. What changed: the academic foundation under credit factors is being re-audited with cleaned TRACE data. Dickerson, Mueller and Robotti (2023, Journal of Financial Economics) found that previously proposed corporate bond factors add little beyond the bond market factor; the 2019 JFE factor paper by Bai, Bali and Wen was retracted in 2023 after a data-timing error surfaced in replication. On 9 April 2026, Dickerson, Robotti and Rossetti posted The Corporate Bond Factor Replication Crisis (arXiv:2604.07880), which tests 108 signals and finds that most previously documented factors lose statistical significance in bond-CAPM alphas once transaction-price measurement error and asymmetric ex-post return filtering are corrected. What it means for the desk: every backtested IR in this section, Man’s included, should be re-estimated on error-corrected data before it earns capital (the Open Source Bond Asset Pricing project publishes such data). The flows in this chapter, fallen angels and forced sales, are more robust than the factor zoo for a structural reason: they are paid for by someone’s mandate, not discovered in a regression. Chapter 9 runs the audit.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Paleologo_Advanced_Portfolio_Management p.111: “Performance can be decomposed into systematic and idiosyncratic components. Most importantly, these components are investable.” … “your investors are not paying you to replicate the market, ride momentum, or short already shorted stocks.”

Annotation. Paleologo writes about equities; the logic transfers whole. Theo, proudly: “Fallen angels beat high yield by three percent a year.” Kaz: “Strip the HY beta, the DTS, and the index-inclusion bid, then tell me.” IDO or it didn’t happen. Part of the fallen-angel premium is plain spread beta (fallen angels are long-duration BBs), part is the liquidity premium you are paid for being there on the rebalance date, and only the residual is skill. Paleologo’s sharper version (p.139) is the desk motto’s parent: “factors can find infinite ways to mar your performance, but cannot tell you how to be profitable.” The bid equation’s \(\sigma_{\text{IDO}}\) is that decomposition applied to a single trade.

1.7 The Anthology, Part D: Where the Flows End Up (Moyer; Houlihan Lokey)

The last question: when the company breaks, who is left holding what, and who has to sell it? This is home turf for the reader, and Moyer’s distressed-debt classic is honest about how far the quants had come when it was written.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Moyer_Distressed_Debt_Analysis p.275: “As much as the quantitative approach of financial econometricians would suggest that investing is fundamentally a science, in distressed investing it is more of an art.” … “This is why knowledge of the process, experience, and judgment are often more critical to investment success than tedious hours of financial modeling.”

Annotation. This book agrees with every word and draws the opposite conclusion. “Knowledge of the process” is exactly what can be written down: exclusivity periods, voting thresholds, DIP roll-ups, plan classes, and which creditor has the hold-up value. Once written down, process knowledge becomes features, transition probabilities, and a prior over \(J\) in the bid equation. What stays an art is the judgment about which features matter in this case, and that is the job description for the human in Man’s quote from §1.1. Moyer also tells us where to look for mispricing: “when the news is very bad, the market often will trade down to the worst-case scenario valuations” (p.257), because sellers who need out meet buyers who demand a discount for uncertainty. That is a forced-seller edge with a docket number.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Moyer_Distressed_Debt_Analysis p.370: “Banks and collateralized debt obligations (CDOs) are not natural holders of equity securities.” … “when such entities are known to be large holders of the postreorganization equity, other market participants will certainly consider their net sell disposition.”

Annotation. The forced-seller graph does not end at default; it rewires. Loans convert into post-reorganization equity, and the holders of those loans (CLOs, banks) are often barred from, or penalized for, holding equity. So the most predictable seller of a newly reorganized stock is its largest holder, and everybody knows it. Moyer’s other forced seller is smaller and sadder: the trade creditor who “may not have the financial wherewithal to wait until the completion of a bankruptcy case to realize full value of the claim and thus is a forced seller” (p.310). Claims trading is that edge in pure form (Chapter 16).

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Houlihan_Lokey_Distressed_MA p.35: “Under Section 363, for example, a debtor with Court approval may sell assets free and clear of all liens, claims and encumbrances (which attach only to the proceeds of such sales).”

Annotation. One clause, and it converts the assets of a broken firm into a clean asset sale while the claims follow the cash. For the flow graph, a 363 sale is a node where the holder set changes completely: the buyer gets the assets with no legacy creditors, and the old creditors get a claim on a pot whose size the auction sets. Pricing the claim means pricing the auction.

Kaz, reading over Theo’s shoulder: “A fulcrum is where a lever balances. So the fulcrum security is the tranche with zero duration?” Mags: “It’s the tranche that gets the equity and the lawsuits.” (The fulcrum is the class whose recovery straddles the enterprise value: everything senior is covered, everything junior is out of the money, and the fulcrum becomes the new owner. It has more duration than anything, measured in years of litigation.)

1.8 The Ecosystem as a Forced-Seller Flow Graph

Put the four parts of the anthology together and the market stops looking like a crowd and starts looking like plumbing. Each holder type is a node. Each trigger (a downgrade to HY, a downgrade to CCC, a default, a redemption wave) opens a set of edges with a known direction, an estimable size, and a response window. Blackstone’s systematic credit paper describes the machine built to sit at the end of those edges, in the vendor’s own words: “The systematic optimizer naturally acts as a contrarian liquidity provider. When credit spreads widen aggressively (often due to market panic rather than fundamental deterioration), the model algorithmically increases credit exposure” (Blackstone_Systematic_Credit p.1). The parenthesis is the whole bet: that the seller is forced, not informed.

1.8.1 The model (measure: \(\mathbb{P}\))

Let holder types be \(i = 1,\dots,n\), bond segments \(k\), and triggers \(\tau\). Holdings \(H_{k,i}\) are in $bn of par; \(f_i(\tau)\in[0,1]\) is the fraction holder \(i\) must sell after trigger \(\tau\), over a window \(w_i(\tau)\) (insurers: quarters; index funds: the month-end rebalance; CLOs: the next test date; open-end funds: days). Natural absorbers \(j\) have capacity \(A_{k,j}(\tau)\): HY index funds that must buy at inclusion (Moyer p.35’s “forced” buyers), fallen-angel programs, crossover and distressed funds, and dealers’ balance sheets. Then

\[ Q^{\text{sell}}_k(\tau) = \sum_i H_{k,i}\,f_i(\tau), \qquad I_k(\tau) = Q^{\text{sell}}_k(\tau) - \sum_j A_{k,j}(\tau). \tag{1.6} \]

The positive part of the imbalance \(I_k\) must be absorbed at a price concession. Model the price as a fundamental value \(p^*\) minus a temporary pressure term that decays at rate \(\theta\) (per day) after the trigger date \(t_0\):

\[ p_t = p^* - \kappa\,\frac{\max(I_k,0)}{\text{ADV}_k}\,e^{-\theta(t-t_0)}, \qquad t \ge t_0, \tag{1.7} \]

where \(\text{ADV}_k\) is the segment’s average daily volume and \(\kappa\) is price impact in points per day of volume. The absorber who buys at \(t_0\) and holds for \(T\) days earns the recovered pressure, \(\kappa\,(I_k^+/\text{ADV}_k)(1-e^{-\theta T})\). That is the drop-and-reversal that Ben Dor (p.349) and Dynkin (p.158) document for fallen angels, and that Ellul, Jotikasthira and Lundblad (2011) tie to insurers’ regulatory constraints. Note what (1.7) leaves out: a permanent component. If the seller is informed, part of the drop never reverses, and that is the toxicity term \(\pi J\) from (1.2). The forced-seller graph prices the temporary component; the RFQ model prices the permanent one. A desk needs both.

Where this blows up. Holders get double-counted (a loan inside a CLO is not also on the bank’s books). Windows get misaligned (insurer selling is slow; index selling is a date). \(\kappa\) is not stable across regimes. Above all, absorption capacity is state-dependent: it collapses exactly when supply peaks, because the absorbers are also being redeemed. A model with constant \(A\) is a fair-weather model. Moyer (p.55) gives the CLO version of the trigger: “When an investment in the portfolio is downgraded to B– or CCC, the manager may be forced to sell something (again without regard to the portfolio manager’s view of fair value) to remain in compliance with the CDO-ORs.” A CLO is a buy-and-hold investor with a 7.5% allergy. It does not sell because it wants to; it sells because the indenture sneezes.

Trend Watch: Who holds credit now, 1993–2026. What changed: the holder graph got more mechanical. CDOs and CLOs held about 3% of low-rated loans and bonds in 1993 and more than 20% by the early 2000s (Moyer_Distressed_Debt_Analysis p.55, Figure 2-18); by 2026 US CLOs held roughly $1tn, about 65% of a roughly $1.5tn institutional leveraged loan market (Maples/Nuveen Q&A, 13 Apr 2026). CLO ETFs went from $2.25bn in 2023 to more than $20bn at end-2024 (Deutsche Bank flow, 11 Feb 2025). US fixed income ETF assets reached about $2tn in June 2025 (The Daily Upside, 2 Jul 2025). Life insurers’ private placements rose from 14% (2016) to 22% (2024) of their corporate bond holdings (Chicago Fed Insights, May 2026), and privately placed bonds reached 48.4% of life-industry bonds at YE2025 against 37.4% five years earlier (S&P Global Market Intelligence via Insurance Business, 10 Aug 2026). Dealers, meanwhile, set a record net short position in corporate bonds in early 2026 (Coalition Greenwich, 17 Feb 2026). And the fallen-angel pipeline reopened: about $30bn entered fallen-angel indices in 2026 through mid-year, the most since 2020 (Insight Investment/BNY, Aug 2026). What it means for the desk: more of the market sits with holders whose sales are triggered by rules (CLO tests, ETF flows, NAIC capital), and less with dealers whose balance sheet used to absorb them. More predictable forced supply, less natural absorption: that is a bigger \(I_k\) for the same shock, and a bigger premium for whoever has the capacity.

Specification for AI Implementation

What ROBO built from the vague version. Spec: “map the forced sellers.” ROBO returned a graph with one node, labeled “Everyone, March 2020,” and a self-loop.

The Spec You Hand the Robot. Build ForcedSellerGraph(holdings, rules, capacity). holdings: a DataFrame, index = segment, columns = holder, values in $bn par, all \(\ge 0\). rules: {holder: {trigger: (fraction, window_days)}} with 0 <= fraction <= 1 and window_days > 0; a holder with no rule for a trigger sells nothing. capacity: {trigger: DataFrame(index = segment, columns = absorber)} in $bn, all \(\ge 0\). run(trigger, segment, stress=False) returns sells by holder, buys by absorber, dealer_residual (the positive imbalance), and a list of (seller, buyer, size) edges, allocating supply to absorbers pro rata to capacity and the remainder to dealer_residual. Assertions that must hold on every call: (a) conservation, total sells equal total buys plus dealer_residual to \(10^{-9}\), and the edge sizes sum to total sells; (b) no holder sells more than it holds; (c) price_path per (1.7) returns to within 0.01 points of \(p^*\) by 10/theta days; (d) stress=True zeroes all capacity, and then dealer_residual equals forced supply exactly. All numbers in the demo are illustrative.

class ForcedSellerGraph:
    """Holder x trigger forced-supply engine: eqs. (1.6)-(1.7). Units: $bn par, days, points."""

    def __init__(self, holdings, rules, capacity):
        self.H = holdings.astype(float)
        if (self.H.values < 0).any():
            raise ValueError("holdings must be non-negative")
        for holder, by_trigger in rules.items():
            for trig, (frac, window) in by_trigger.items():
                if not 0.0 <= frac <= 1.0:
                    raise ValueError(f"{holder}/{trig}: fraction must lie in [0, 1]")
                if window <= 0:
                    raise ValueError(f"{holder}/{trig}: window_days must be > 0")
        for trig, cap in capacity.items():
            if (cap.values < 0).any():
                raise ValueError(f"{trig}: capacity must be non-negative")
        self.rules, self.capacity = rules, capacity

    def forced_supply(self, trigger, segment):
        """Q^sell_k(tau) by holder, eq. (1.6)."""
        frac = {h: self.rules.get(h, {}).get(trigger, (0.0, 1))[0] for h in self.H.columns}
        return self.H.loc[segment] * pd.Series(frac)

    def run(self, trigger, segment, stress=False):
        sells = self.forced_supply(trigger, segment)
        assert (sells <= self.H.loc[segment] + 1e-12).all()             # (b)
        Q = float(sells.sum())
        cap = self.capacity.get(trigger)
        caps = cap.loc[segment].astype(float) if cap is not None else pd.Series(dtype=float)
        if stress:
            caps = caps * 0.0                                            # March 2020 toggle
        total_cap = float(caps.sum())
        absorbed = min(Q, total_cap)
        buys = caps * (absorbed / total_cap) if total_cap > 0 else caps * 0.0
        residual = Q - float(buys.sum())
        edges = []
        if Q > 0:
            for s, sz in sells[sells > 0].items():
                edges += [(s, b, sz * bz / Q) for b, bz in buys[buys > 0].items()]
                if residual > 0:
                    edges.append((s, "dealer_residual", sz * residual / Q))
        assert abs(Q - (buys.sum() + residual)) < 1e-9                   # (a) conservation
        assert abs(sum(e[2] for e in edges) - Q) < 1e-9
        return {"sells": sells, "buys": buys, "dealer_residual": residual, "edges": edges}

    @staticmethod
    def price_path(imbalance, adv, kappa, theta, days, p_star=100.0):
        """Eq. (1.7): temporary price pressure decaying at rate theta per day."""
        if adv <= 0 or theta <= 0:
            raise ValueError("adv and theta must be > 0")
        t = np.arange(days + 1, dtype=float)
        return p_star - kappa * max(imbalance, 0.0) / adv * np.exp(-theta * t)


# --- a Ford-sized fallen angel, March 2020 style (all numbers illustrative) ---
seg = "BBB- auto issuer, $36bn"
holdings = pd.DataFrame({"insurers": [12.0], "ig_active_funds": [8.0], "ig_index_funds_etfs": [5.0],
                         "banks_foreign_other": [9.0], "hy_funds": [2.0]}, index=[seg])
rules = {"insurers": {"IG_to_HY": (0.25, 90)}, "ig_active_funds": {"IG_to_HY": (0.50, 30)},
         "ig_index_funds_etfs": {"IG_to_HY": (1.00, 5)}, "banks_foreign_other": {"IG_to_HY": (0.10, 60)}}
capacity = {"IG_to_HY": pd.DataFrame({"hy_index_inclusion": [3.0], "fallen_angel_programs": [1.5],
                                      "crossover_distressed": [2.0]}, index=[seg])}
g = ForcedSellerGraph(holdings, rules, capacity)
base_run, stress_run = g.run("IG_to_HY", seg), g.run("IG_to_HY", seg, stress=True)
Q = float(g.forced_supply("IG_to_HY", seg).sum())
assert abs(Q - 12.9) < 1e-12 and abs(base_run["dealer_residual"] - 6.4) < 1e-9
assert abs(stress_run["dealer_residual"] - Q) < 1e-12                    # (d)

theta = 1 / 20                                                           # ~14-day half-life
path = ForcedSellerGraph.price_path(base_run["dealer_residual"], adv=0.5, kappa=0.4, theta=theta,
                                    days=int(10 / theta))
assert abs(path[-1] - 100.0) < 0.01                                      # (c) reversal
drop, recovered_60d = 100.0 - path[0], path[60] - path[0]
assert abs(recovered_60d - drop * (1 - np.exp(-theta * 60))) < 1e-9     # absorber's expected gain
assert reservation_bid(**base, pi=0.5, J=13.0) < reservation_bid(**base, pi=0.4, J=13.0)
print(f"forced supply {Q:.1f}bn | dealer residual {base_run['dealer_residual']:.1f}bn "
      f"(stress {stress_run['dealer_residual']:.1f}bn) | drop {drop:.2f}pt | 60d reversal {recovered_60d:.2f}pt")

1.8.2 Case Study A: Ford and the March 2020 Fallen-Angel Wave

March 2020 is the flow graph with every edge lit. More than $90bn of debt fell from investment grade in that one month, nearly twice the prior monthly record of $48bn set in 2005, and the first half of 2020 reached $197bn, the largest on record (J.P. Morgan data via T. Rowe Price, Nov 2020). The headline was Ford: S&P cut it to BB+ on 25 March 2020 (as reported by Bloomberg), and with two high-yield ratings roughly $36bn of Ford debt left the IG index at the month-end rebalance (T. Rowe Price). Man’s paper describes the mechanism exactly: “When a company is downgraded to below investment grade status by the ratings agencies, it drops out of the index at the next monthly rebalancing and there is a significant wave of forced selling around the event” (Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.38).

Walk the graph. Who sells, and when: IG index funds and ETFs on the rebalance date (a date anyone could read off a calendar); IG active funds over weeks; insurers over quarters, because higher capital charges make holding costly but not impossible. Who buys: HY index funds, forced to add the bond at inclusion, which made Ford one of the largest issuers in HY indices overnight; fallen-angel programs; crossover funds. What broke: absorption capacity, because HY funds were themselves facing record outflows. What changed it: the Federal Reserve. The Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facility was established on 23 March 2020, and in April the Fed extended its corporate facilities to issuers that had been investment grade as of 22 March, which covered Ford. A forced-seller event became a forced-buyer event by announcement. In (1.6), a new absorber with very large \(A\) appeared, and \(I_k\) went from huge to manageable before most of the selling had happened.

How a systematic desk would have flagged it: distance to default collapsing through February and March as equity fell and equity volatility rose (§1.5); Ford’s equity in the bottom momentum decile (§1.6); the rating-agency watch list giving the trigger date, and the index calendar giving the window. How it would have traded it: estimate \(Q^{\text{sell}}\) by holder, stand ready to absorb at the rebalance with a bid that charged for inventory and cost but put \(\pi\) near zero (index funds are the textbook uninformed seller), and size it with DTS rather than duration. IDO or it didn’t happen: the profit that followed was mostly the Fed and spread beta, and a desk that booked it as alpha learned nothing.

1.8.3 Case Study B: 12 March 2020, LQD at a 5% Discount

On 12 March 2020, the iShares iBoxx $ Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF (LQD) closed at a 5.0% discount to its net asset value; the next day the discount was 0.19%, while VCIT and SPIB had shown discounts of 3.2% and 3.1% (WealthManagement.com, 16 Mar 2020). Kaz’s first instinct was arbitrage: buy the ETF, short the basket, collect five points. The problem was the basket. The NAV was computed from evaluated bond prices that had not traded, so it was stale, and the ETF price was the only live price in the market. Authorized participants stopped closing the gap because they could not sell the underlying bonds at NAV either. The ETF was not mispriced; the NAV was.

In the bid equation, both the inventory term and the cost term exploded at once: \(\sigma_{\text{IDO}}\) jumped because DTS-scaled volatility jumps in a crisis (Ben Dor p.26), and \(c(\Delta q)\) jumped because the exit was the same crowded door. In the flow graph, open-end funds and ETFs became sellers of whatever was liquid, and the absorber of last resort arrived only by announcement: the SMCCF was established on 23 March 2020, began buying ETFs on 12 May 2020 (New York Fed, 11 May 2020) and corporate bonds in June, and ceased purchases on 31 December 2020 (Federal Reserve). Chapter 20 rebuilds the creation–redemption arbitrage band and shows why it widens exactly when you want to use it.

1.9 Toxic Flow: When the Seller Knows

The forced-seller graph is the good news: flows you can see coming, from sellers who know nothing. The cold open was the bad news: a seller who knew everything. The difference between them is the permanent component that (1.7) leaves out and (1.2) charges for.

1.9.1 Case Study C: Serta Simmons, 2016–2026 (the Counterparty Who Knew)

Docket Diary. November 2016: Serta Simmons Bedding borrows under a $1.95bn first-lien term loan. June 2020: a majority group holding about 52.6% of the roughly $1.887bn first-lien loans exchanges about $992mm of them into about $734mm of new super-priority “first lien second out” debt, alongside $200mm of new money; the excluded lenders, about 47.4% (roughly $895mm), are primed. 31 December 2024: the Fifth Circuit holds that the exchange was not an “open market purchase” and that the excluded lenders’ sacred right to pro rata sharing was breached. 7 July 2026: on remand, the participating lenders are held liable for $261.13mm of damages as of 22 June 2020, plus 9% New York prejudgment interest, with the cashless exchange treated as a “payment” (Mayer Brown, July 2026). The Ad Hoc Group, in unison: “We were represented by counsel. We were not, the Fifth Circuit has now clarified, represented in an open market.”

The same day the Fifth Circuit ruled on Serta, New York’s Appellate Division upheld Mitel’s uptier, because Mitel’s agreement let it “purchase” loans with no “open market” qualifier at all (Mayer Brown, May 2025); and in December 2025 a federal district court reversed the bankruptcy court and blessed the multi-step Wesco/Incora uptier (Mayer Brown, January 2026). Three courts, three documents, three outcomes. “Open market purchase” has become the most expensive three words in finance: on the Serta remand they were priced at $261.13mm plus nine percent a year since June 2020, for a phrase nobody had defined.

The market maker’s version. Forget the litigation and replay the RFQs. In the weeks before 22 June 2020, a sell RFQ on Serta first-lien paper could come from two kinds of account: a lender outside the negotiating group (uninformed, perhaps a CLO trimming a CCC name), or a lender inside it, offloading exposure it was about to prime, or that it knew would be left behind. The second is the purest toxic flow in credit: the jump \(J\) is the priming loss, and the seller knows its sign and roughly its size. Equation (1.2) says the right bid depends on \(\pi(\mathbf{x})\), and the Bayes step of §1.3.3 says \(\pi\) is a function of who is on the call: membership in the group, Rule 2019 disclosures once a case is filed, the timing relative to lender meetings, the account’s markout history. None of that is in the bond’s price history. All of it is in the documents and the docket, which is where Theo comes in. Ines’s hand history closes the loop: bucket every RFQ by those features, compute five-day markouts, and the average markout per bucket is your estimate of \(-\pi J\). Chapter 3 builds the toxicity model; Chapter 13 builds the Priming Risk Score that feeds it.

Trend Watch: Liability management takes over the default statistics, 2024–2026. What changed: most “defaults” are now negotiated. Distressed exchanges were more than 60% of default volume in 2024 through mid-December, the highest share since at least 2000; the 2024 HY default rate was 1.4% including distressed exchanges against 0.3% excluding them, and for loans 4.0% against 1.5% (Marquette Associates, 18 Dec 2024). Moody’s (18 May 2026) put distressed restructurings at about 65% of 2025 corporate defaults, and in its 1,173-event history of soft credit events since 1979, about one in four ended in a hard default, with more than 70% of eventual hard defaults arriving within two years. What it means for the desk: the jump \(J\) in the bid equation is increasingly a negotiated jump, timed by lender calls and documents rather than by a missed coupon, which makes counterparty state the dominant feature in \(\pi(\mathbf{x})\) and makes “default” a poor label for anything you train on. Chapter 14 models the regime shift.

1.10 Desk Debrief

  • Every bid is three bets. Fair value, inventory, toxicity: \(B^* = S_t - \pi J - \tfrac12\gamma\sigma^2_{\text{IDO}}h(2q+\Delta q) - c\). Kaz’s engine got two of them right; the third cost $2mm.
  • A forced sale is information-free about the bond and information-rich about the seller. Price the seller, not just the CUSIP.
  • \(\pi\) is a function of who is on the call. The Bayes step turns counterparty state into a logistic regression; markouts by feature bucket are how you estimate it.
  • Risk scales with spread. Use DTS, not spread duration, and remember that the slope steepens in a crisis. Below about 70, stop quoting spreads and start modeling recoveries.
  • Calibrate, don’t just rank. A Gaussian DD of 4 says 0.003%; an empirical map says almost 1%. Feed only \(\mathbb{Q}\) quantities into the credit triangle.
  • The holder graph is getting more mechanical. CLOs (about 65% of loans), ETFs (about $2tn), insurers’ private placements (48% of life-industry bonds) and record dealer net shorts mean more rule-driven supply and less natural absorption.
  • Execution made it possible; replication will decide what survives. Half of IG trades electronically and PT is 15% of volume, but most published bond factors fail on clean data. Flows paid for by someone’s mandate are sturdier than factors found in a regression.
  • IDO or it didn’t happen.

The Spec You Hand the Robot

Build a Python module desk_core (numpy, pandas, scipy; seeded; no I/O). (1) reservation_bid(S, q, dq, gamma, sigma_ido, h_years, pi, J, c) per eq. (1.2), measure \(\mathbb{P}\); units: points per 100 par, $mm par (long positive; dq > 0 = client sells), \(1/(\$\text{mm}\cdot\text{pt})\), years; raise on dq <= 0, pi outside \([0,1]\), h_years <= 0, negative scale inputs; never clip a short desk’s bid. (2) posterior_informed(mu, log_lr) in logit form; reject mu in \(\{0,1\}\). (3) dts_vol(D_spr, s_bp, sigma_rel) per eq. (1.3), result in bp per period; lcs() with spread-quoted and price-quoted branches. (4) ForcedSellerGraph(holdings, rules, capacity) per eqs. (1.6)–(1.7) with pro rata absorption, a dealer_residual node, edges, and price_path. Mandatory assertions: comparative statics of the bid (\(\partial B/\partial q<0\), \(\partial B/\partial\pi<0\), \(\partial B/\partial\Delta q<0\)); simulated markout equals \(-\pi J\) within 3 s.e.; lognormal Monte Carlo reproduces DTS·\(\sigma_{\text{rel}}\) within 2%; conservation of flow to \(10^{-9}\); stress toggle sends all supply to dealer_residual; price path reverts to within 0.01 points by 10/theta days. Do not condition on the RFQ twice. Label every demo number illustrative.

Exercises

  1. (Derivation.) Derive the dealer’s ask for a client buying \(\Delta q\), and show that the bid–ask midpoint for a two-sided quote of size \(\Delta q\) equals the reservation mid \(r^{\text{res}} = m - \gamma\sigma^2_{\text{IDO}}h\,q\) when both sides carry the same \(m\). What happens to the midpoint when the buy-side RFQ carries a different toxicity \(\pi'\)?
  2. (Bayes, with a poker face.) The prior share of informed sellers is 3%. An account in a known ad hoc group sells 58 minutes after a lender call, which you estimate multiplies the likelihood ratio by 12, and shows the bond to five dealers, which multiplies it by 1.5. Compute \(\pi\). At \(J = 13\) points, how many points does toxicity take off the bid? Would you rather know the jump size or the counterparty?
  3. (DTS.) A portfolio holds equal market values of a 10-year BBB at 140 bp and a 3-year CCC quoted at 68. Explain why DTS is meaningful for the first and not the second, and propose a single risk measure that covers both (hint: Ben Dor’s two-branch LCS is a clue).
  4. (Flow graph.) Re-run the Ford-sized example with the Fed added as an absorber with $5bn of capacity from day 10. Modify run so capacity can arrive on a date, and show how the drop and the 60-day reversal change. Who earned the reversal: the desk, or the central bank?
  5. (ROBO literalism.) Write the one-sentence vague spec that would make ROBO fit a toxicity model with a perfect in-sample markout and zero out-of-sample value. Then write the two clauses that prevent it (one concerns issuer-grouped cross-validation, Chapter 7; the other concerns the label window).
  6. (Courtroom quant.) Using the Serta and Mitel facts, write a binary feature “credit agreement permits non-pro-rata purchases without an open-market qualifier,” and argue whether it belongs in \(\pi(\mathbf{x})\), in \(J\), or in both.

Chapter 2: The Revolutions in Credit Trading

Tuesday, 3:41 p.m. Nineteen minutes to the index mark. The desk smells like burnt espresso and somebody else’s DV01.

The ticket on Theo Marsh’s screen is the first one that is entirely his: buy $4mm, Halvorsen Freight 7.125% senior notes due 2030, B2, sent all-to-all. (Halvorsen is fictional. The chime is not.) Responders get two minutes. In the old world Theo would have called three dealers, waited for two of them to call back, and spent the wait rereading the restricted payments covenant. In this world eleven responses arrive before he has found the covenant: four banks, two non-bank market makers, three asset managers, a hedge fund, and something whose name is a string of capital letters.

He lifts the best offer. The cover, the second-best response, is three-eighths of a point behind. Done in forty seconds.

“Back in my day,” says Marguerite “Mags” Dunleavy, without looking up, “I priced these by phone and by grudge. You called Steve, Steve gave you a number that punished you for something you did in 1997, and the print showed up on TRACE seventy-five minutes later, if it showed up at all.”

“Seventy-five minutes?”

“July 2002. The regulator gave us transparency the way a casino gives you a free drink: about five hundred bonds, seventy-five minutes late.”

Ines Okafor rolls her chair over and studies the eleven rows the way she once studied a final table. “Eleven players. Nice pot, tight cover. Now tell me which one of them just got off a lender call.”

Theo knows exactly what a lender call does to an offer, and he reaches for the indenture out of habit. “But what does the credit agreement say about electronic trading?”

“Nothing, Theo.” Dr. Kasimir “Kaz” Lind keeps typing. “The bond doesn’t know how it was traded. The dataset does.”

That exchange is the whole chapter. A bond’s value lives in its documents. Its tradability lives in its data exhaust: how many prints it gets per day, how many dealers answer an RFQ for it, how far the cover sits from the winner, whether it sits in an ETF redemption basket, and which of its trades the public tape refuses to show you. The question this chapter answers: what changed in the plumbing of credit trading between 2002 and 2026, how big was each change, and why did those changes, rather than any new factor, make systematic credit possible?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to: date seven changes in market structure (TRACE plus six “revolutions”) and size each with sourced 2018–2026 numbers; read TRACE’s size caps as a censoring problem and back out the tail index of hidden block sizes; fit an electronic-adoption S-curve with an honest ceiling; price an RFQ as an order-statistics problem, and show why eleven responders anchored to one composite are worth less than two independent ones; compute Barclays LCS and Man’s transaction-cost decomposition with the units right; treat protocol choice (RFQ, all-to-all, portfolio trade, ETF) as cost minimization; and show why a fall in cost per ticket raises the breadth, and so the information ratio, a quant strategy can harvest.

A housekeeping note for Kaz: every expectation in this chapter is under the physical measure \(\mathbb{P}\). Market-structure statistics record what traders actually did. A count of RFQ responses has no pricing measure.

2.1 The Desk View: Execution Certainty and a Modelable Cost

Start with how a market maker sees a systematic credit book. A quant credit strategy is a function from data to target weights. Every day, or every hour, it says “own more of these 400 bonds and less of those 300.” The optimizer behind those targets makes an assumption it never states: that the bonds can actually be traded, at a cost it can predict.

For most of its history, credit broke that assumption. Man Group’s systematic team put the barrier plainly:

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Man_Revolutions_in_Credit_Trading_2023 p.2: “The greatest barriers to systematic approaches breaking through in credit have traditionally been execution and the ability to model transaction costs and liquidity within decades-old manual processes.”

Annotation. Notice what is not on the list: signals. By 2023, credit factors (value, momentum, quality, low risk) had more than a decade of published evidence behind them (Chapters 9–12). What was missing was a way to turn a target weight into a fill. The sentence recasts the history of quant credit as a history of plumbing, and that is this chapter’s frame. Where the 2026 desk departs: in liquid IG, “manual processes” no longer bind, because most small tickets are electronic and many are auto-executed. They still bind for high-yield blocks, stressed names and anything near a liability-management transaction (Chapters 13–14). The barrier did not disappear. It moved down the credit curve, into Theo’s old neighborhood.

On the next page of the same paper, Man named the two conditions a systematic strategy needs:

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Man_Revolutions_in_Credit_Trading_2023 p.4: “Two of the key challenges for such systematic techniques are having a high certainty of execution and having a relatively good sense of the likely transaction costs, as quantitative approaches depend on being able to model accurately which securities can be traded and at what cost.”

Annotation. These are the two inputs a portfolio optimizer cannot do without. One is a feasible set: which bonds can be traded. The other is a cost function: at what price. Write them as \(\Pr(\text{fill}\mid x)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[c \mid \text{fill}, x]\), where \(x\) is a vector of ticket features such as size, rating, age, recent prints, and the number of dealers who answered the last RFQ. Every revolution in this chapter improves one or both. TRACE made \(\mathbb{E}[c]\) estimable after the fact. RFQ platforms made it measurable at the moment of trade. All-to-all and automation raised \(\Pr(\text{fill})\) for small tickets. Portfolio trading and ETFs created fills for baskets that no single-bond RFQ could absorb. The modern departure is that by 2026 both quantities are forecast, not just measured, and §2.5 shows them feeding a router rather than a spreadsheet.

Man’s earlier paper explains why this matters to an optimizer. The subject of the sentence is the optimizer’s solution:

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.19: “is no longer really optimal if that bond is not available for purchase. In addition, unfilled orders can lead to unintended and potentially unmodelled risk exposures.”

Annotation. An optimal portfolio you cannot buy is not optimal, and an unfilled order is not a zero. It is an unintended position. If you sold the bond you meant to swap out of but failed to buy its replacement, you are now short beta you never chose. A modern desk logs every unfilled order, and the realized fill rate becomes a training label (§2.5). The desk motto applies to execution as much as to alpha: IDO or it didn’t happen. A backtest that assumes every target fills is reporting the alpha of a market that does not exist.

Here is the RSSG translation, because Theo needs one. At PJT the unit of analysis was a document and a process. Prices arrived by phone, late, from a dealer who was also your counterparty. That world had one kind of liquidity information, which was whatever Steve said. A systematic desk needs liquidity to be a variable: measured for every bond every day, forecastable, and comparable across 10,000 CUSIPs. Electronification is the process that turned liquidity from a relationship into a variable. The rest of this chapter dates that process, sizes it, and shows where it has still not reached.

2.2 Revolution 0: TRACE, or the Dataset Appears

Before you can trade a bond on a model, the model needs training data. For US corporates that data is TRACE, FINRA’s Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine. It underlies everything that follows, so we call it Revolution 0. It did not change how bonds traded. It changed what anyone could know about how they traded.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.91: “In the past, credit markets have been hampered by lack of transparency in pricing, making it difficult to mark a portfolio to market let alone hedge or trade a particular exposure.”

Annotation. Bohn and Stein wrote when TRACE was a few years old, and their footnote 6 on the same page dates its origin: in September 1998 the SEC asked the NASD (now FINRA) to provide more transparency in corporate debt. The sentence lists three uses in rising order of difficulty: mark, hedge, trade. A systematic desk needs all three every day for every bond in its universe. Where the 2026 desk departs: transparency is no longer the scarce input for the liquid half of the market. The scarce input is clean transparency, meaning duplicate prints, processed voice trades and capped sizes have all been dealt with. That is the subject of the rest of this section.

2.2.1 The dissemination timeline

TRACE did not arrive all at once. FINRA phased it in by issue size and rating and cut the reporting clock in steps. The dates below come from the FINRA TRACE Fact Book (2025 edition) and FINRA’s reporting-timeframes page. The one-minute saga comes from SEC and FINRA releases.

Trend Watch. The reporting clock, 2002–2026: a twenty-four-year countdown that stopped at fifteen minutes.

Date Change Source
Sept 1998 SEC asks NASD for corporate-debt transparency Bohn_Stein p.91, fn. 6
July 1, 2002 TRACE launches with 75-minute reporting. Phase I disseminates IG issues of $1bn or more plus the “FIPS 50” HY names: about 520 securities by end-2002 FINRA TRACE Fact Book 2025
Mar 3 and Apr 14, 2003 Phase IIa (AAA/AA/A issues of $100mm or more) and Phase IIb (120 BBB plus 50 HY names): about 4,650 bonds Fact Book
Oct 1, 2003 Clock cut to 45 minutes Fact Book
Oct 1, 2004 Phase IIIa; clock cut to 30 minutes Fact Book
Feb 7, 2005 Phase IIIb: about 99% of public transactions and 95% of par value disseminated immediately Fact Book
July 1, 2005 Clock cut to 15 minutes Fact Book
Jan 9, 2006 Immediate dissemination of all public TRACE-eligible corporates Fact Book
June 30, 2014 Rule 144A corporate trades disseminated Fact Book
May 15, 2023 Portfolio-trade modifier required on corporate bond reports Fact Book; FINRA RN 22-12
Jan 11, 2024 FINRA files SR-FINRA-2024-004 to cut the 15-minute outer limit to one minute SEC Rel. 34-101121
Sept 20, 2024 SEC approves the one-minute rule SEC Rel. 34-101121
Feb 5, 2025 FINRA says it will not set an effective date Mayer Brown, Free Writings, Feb 10, 2025
Dec 4, 2025 FINRA “is not moving forward”; the 15-minute standard stays FINRA RN 25-17
June 8, 2026 Optional aggregate allocation reporting begins FINRA RN 25-17
Aug 31, 2026 Expanded affiliate-principal indicator becomes available on a voluntary basis (mandatory Aug 2, 2027) FINRA RN 26-16

What it means for the desk. The headline clock (75, then 45, 30 and 15 minutes) understates how fast the market actually is. FINRA’s own statistics, summarized in the SEC’s 2024 approval order, show that in 2022, 82.9% of trades executed between 8:00 a.m. and 6:15 p.m. ET were already reported within one minute, and 90.6% within three. The rule would have accelerated “up to 16.4% of current annual trading volume, or up to 6.1 million trades and 20 trillion dollars in par value” (SEC Rel. 34-101121). So FINRA spent 2022 to 2025 trying to make the market report in one minute, found that 83% of it already did, and dropped the rule. It was the most TRACE-like thing TRACE has ever done: the information arrived, late, and changed nothing. For a quant, the interesting number is the remaining 17%. The trades that still report slowly are the manual ones, and manual trades are where blocks and distressed names live.

Model the print delay \(\ell\) as a two-component mixture:

\[ \Pr(\ell \le u) = \pi\,F_{\text{fast}}(u) + (1-\pi)\,F_{\text{slow}}(u), \qquad 0 \le u \le 15 \text{ min}. \]

Here \(F_{\text{fast}}\) is the delay distribution of straight-through electronic reports (seconds), \(F_{\text{slow}}\) is the delay distribution of manually booked voice trades (minutes), and \(\pi\) is the weight on the electronic component. FINRA’s 2022 statistic pins down one point of the mixture: \(\Pr(\ell \le 1\text{ min}) = 0.829\). What matters for feature design is that \(\pi\) is not constant across bonds. It is lowest exactly where the information is richest: large, stressed, voice-traded tickets. So a feature like “minutes since last print” means different things in different bonds. In an IG bond a stale print means nobody traded. In a CCC bond it may mean somebody traded big and the ticket is still being booked.

2.2.2 The caps: censoring as a data problem

Two strings in the TRACE feed matter more to a credit quant than any others: 5MM+ and 1MM+. FINRA disseminates the exact size of an IG trade only up to $5mm and of an HY trade only up to $1mm, and anything larger prints as the capped string. The cap is the bond market’s version of “a source familiar with the matter”: you know something big happened, but not how big.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.162 (note 3): “disseminates trade-by-trade corporate bond execution information within 15 minutes to all market participants. At this time, TRACE data are censored at $5 million for investment grade and $1 million for high-yield securities.”

Annotation. The Barclays authors use the right word: censored. A censored observation is not missing data. It tells you the true value is at least the cap, which is information, so you should neither drop it nor treat it as equal to the cap. The caps have not moved since this was written. FINRA still disseminates 5MM+ for IG and 1MM+ for HY, and RN 25-17 applies the same caps to the new allocation reports. The ticket has moved: average trade size fell from about $560k to about $360k over the four years to 2024 (IFR, citing MarketAxess data), so a larger share of trades now prints uncapped. The capped minority is the part of the market an RSSG veteran knows best.

Every TRACE-based turnover model needs the following derivation. Let \(X\) be the true size of a trade, with CDF \(G\), and let the cap be \(c\). TRACE shows \(\tilde X = \min(X, c)\). For any nonnegative random variable, \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^\infty \Pr(X > x)\,dx\), so

\[ \mathbb{E}[\tilde X] = \int_0^{c} \big(1 - G(x)\big)\,dx, \qquad \mathbb{E}[X] - \mathbb{E}[\tilde X] = \int_c^{\infty} \big(1 - G(x)\big)\,dx \;\ge\; 0 . \]

Volume summed from capped prints therefore biases turnover down, by the area under the size distribution’s tail beyond the cap. Ben Dor and coauthors flag exactly this:

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.364 (note 8): “TRACE truncates the sizes of large transactions at $1 million and $5 million for high-yield and investment-grade bonds, respectively, which may cause our estimates of turnover to be downward biased.”

Annotation. The same note then gives the fix. Capped trades are assigned larger sizes, chosen so that the sum of individual trades matches TRACE’s aggregate volume figures, which “yields higher transaction limits of $4 million and $12.5 million for high-yield and investment-grade bonds, respectively.” That is a moment-matching estimator, and below we use it to extract a structural fact about block sizes. Where the modern desk departs: academic and enhanced TRACE files with uncapped sizes are released with a lag (Appendix B), so a backtest can use true sizes, but a live model sees only the capped feed. Train on what you will see at decision time. Otherwise your turnover feature is look-ahead bias in a lab coat.

Now make the imputation tell us something. Suppose block sizes above the cap follow a Pareto tail, the standard model for heavy-tailed sizes:

\[ \Pr(X > x \mid X > c) = \left(\frac{x}{c}\right)^{-\alpha}, \qquad x \ge c,\quad \alpha > 1 . \]

Then the mean size of a capped trade is

\[ \mathbb{E}[X \mid X > c] = c + \int_c^\infty \left(\frac{x}{c}\right)^{-\alpha} dx = c + \frac{c}{\alpha - 1} = \frac{c\,\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \]

Ben Dor’s imputed limit \(m\) is this conditional mean. Set \(m = c\alpha/(\alpha-1)\) and solve for the tail index:

\[ \hat\alpha = \frac{m}{m - c}. \]

For IG, \(c = 5\) and \(m = 12.5\), so \(\hat\alpha = 12.5/7.5 = 5/3 \approx 1.67\). For HY, \(c = 1\) and \(m = 4\), so \(\hat\alpha = 4/3 \approx 1.33\).

Read that slowly, because it is the book’s first quant “aha” for an RSSG reader. Both tail indices are below 2, so the implied block-size distribution has infinite variance. (Kaz, who was going to assume Gaussian, now regrets it.) The HY tail is also fatter. Relative to its cap, the average hidden HY block is four times the cap, against two and a half times in IG, so 1MM+ hides proportionally more of HY than 5MM+ hides of IG. The trades the tape conceals most completely are large HY and stressed trades, the ones where knowing who sold, and how much, is worth the most. The RSSG skill set is most valuable exactly where the data exhaust is thinnest.

(A caveat for the exercises: a Pareto tail fitted from one moment is a sketch, not an estimate. Chapter 22 fits the tail directly from the uncapped academic file.)

Ways This Blows Up. The riskless-principal echo. Kaz once asked whether a “riskless principal” trade involved a principal with no risk, “like a tenured professor.” Close. It is a dealer who buys from one customer and sells to another at nearly the same moment. The dealer carries no inventory risk, and one economic trade can generate two TRACE reports. Affiliated desks reporting to each other add more echoes. MarketAxess reported that duplicate trade reports inflated US high-grade TRACE volume by up to 8% in June 2026. FINRA’s expanded affiliate-principal indicator exists to suppress them (voluntary from Aug 31, 2026, mandatory Aug 2, 2027; RN 26-16). A volume-based liquidity score fitted on 2020–2026 data therefore has a structural break built in. Tag the regime and deduplicate before you fit anything.

Last, a period piece from the shelf, included because it explains why some of Mags’s habits survive:

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Moyer_Distressed_Debt_Analysis p.416 (note 62): “However, most of the securities required to be posted do not constitute distressed securities.”

Annotation. Moyer was writing in TRACE’s phased-in early years, when dissemination mostly covered larger issues, and the same note expands the acronym as “Trade Reporting and Comparison Entry Source,” an artifact of its vintage. For the distressed investor of that era, the new tape was something that happened to other people. Today every public TRACE-eligible corporate is disseminated, stressed ones included. But the caps and the slow manual component from §2.2.1 still make distressed trading the least transparent corner of a transparent market. That is why Mags still prices some things by grudge, and why she is still, irritatingly, right about some of them.

2.3 Revolution 1: From Phone to RFQ

Mags has a war story for every protocol, and this one begins with a run. “A run,” she tells Theo, who has received several hundred and never been told what one is, “is a dealer’s list of bonds and levels. It goes out at 8 a.m., is stale by 8:05, and binds nobody. It’s a menu where every price says ‘market.’”

Man’s 2022 paper describes the market the electronic RFQ was built to replace:

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.19: “the bond market is structured around a Request for Quotation (RFQ) process that has hardly changed for decades. Corporate bond bid/ask prices are indicated by dealer runs that are not firm and actionable”

Annotation. Two phrases carry the weight. “Hardly changed for decades” means the protocol still runs request, quote, accept. Electronification did not abolish the RFQ. It put it on a wire, sent it to many dealers at once and timestamped every answer. “Not firm and actionable” separates an indication from a price. A run is an indication. A TRACE print is a fact about a trade somebody else already did. Neither is a firm price for the trade you want now. An electronic RFQ is: \(n\) dealers answer the same question at the same moment, each answer is binding for the response window, and the client can execute against the best one or walk away. Each RFQ therefore leaves a labeled record behind it: how many dealers were invited, how many answered, every quote, the winner, the cover, the timestamps, and whether it traded. Where the 2026 desk departs: the RFQ is now being split into variants (request-for-market, session-based auctions, streaming, one-click). Buy-side panelists at FILS Europe in 2026 predicted that the RFQ “in its current form” would become obsolete (The DESK, Oct 2026). If that happens, the request-quote-accept structure will have lasted most of a century. It would be the most durable thing in this chapter.

Here is why a pre-RFQ quant could not build the obvious cost model directly from TRACE:

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.120: “Although it is possible to capture transaction spread data via TRACE, for most bonds the time between a broker-dealer buy and sell transaction for a given CUSIP can be very long, so it is difficult to calculate an accurate bid-ask spread using TRACE.”

Annotation. A bid-ask spread is a statement about two prices at the same moment. TRACE gives you two prices at different moments, a dealer buy on Tuesday and a dealer sell on Friday, with three days of spread moves mixed into the difference. Measured that way, a bond’s “spread” is mostly volatility. This is why Barclays built its Liquidity Cost Score from trader quotes (§2.10), and why RFQ data is the better cost instrument: an RFQ records competing quotes for the same bond within the same two-minute window. Where the 2026 desk departs: composites such as MarketAxess CP+ and Tradeweb Ai-Price (which covers about 30,000 US corporates, per Tradeweb’s FY2025 10-K) now provide a continuous estimated mid. The remaining problem is not getting a mid. It is checking whether the composite deserves your trust (§2.3.2).

The first large academic look at the new protocol is Hendershott and Madhavan (2015), Click or Call? Auction versus Search in the Over-the-Counter Market (Journal of Finance). They study every US corporate bond transaction from January 2010 to April 2011, about 4.6 million trades. Electronic auctions account for 467,614 trades in 5,528 bonds and voice for 4,153,611 trades in 11,122 bonds, so about one trade in ten was electronic. Auctions lasted 5 to 20 minutes, and they turned out to be a workable source of liquidity even in bonds that rarely trade. The paper also carries a warning this book repeats often: traders choose the venue. Easy tickets go electronic and hard tickets go to the phone, so a raw comparison of “electronic cost” with “voice cost” flatters the wire. Every venue-choice model in Chapter 19 has to deal with that selection.

Trend Watch. Electronic share of US corporate bond trading, 2015–2026: IG crossed the halfway line, HY parked at a third.
