drift += rng.normal(0.0, 0.3, (1, P["NB"], F))
X = z_parent[L["issuer"].values] + drift[L["t0"].values, L["bond"].values]   # PURE NOISE features
y = (L["label"].values > 0).astype(int)
auc_naive = cv_auc(X, y, shuffled_kfold(len(y)))
auc_purged = cv_auc(X, y, purged_group_kfold(L["t0"], L["t1"], L["issuer"]))
print(f"pure-noise AUC: shuffled K-fold {auc_naive:.3f}   purged + grouped {auc_purged:.3f}")
assert auc_naive > auc_purged + 0.03          # overlapping labels leak through shuffled folds
assert abs(auc_purged - 0.5) < 0.06           # the honest splitter finds nothing, correctly
# ---------- 6. Meta-label bet sizing, deflated Sharpe, MinTRL, PBO (Sections 7.5, 7.8) ----------
def bet_size(p, side):
    """Secondary-model probability -> size in [0, 1), times the primary model's side."""
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6)
    z = (p - 0.5) / np.sqrt(p * (1 - p))
    return np.maximum(2 * stats.norm.cdf(z) - 1, 0.0) * side

assert abs(bet_size(0.75, 1) - 0.4364) < 1e-3 and abs(bet_size(0.9, -1) + 0.8176) < 1e-3
assert bet_size(0.4, 1) == 0.0                # the meta-model may veto, never reverse

EULER_GAMMA = 0.5772156649015329

def sharpe(R):
    return R.mean(0) / R.std(0, ddof=1)

def psr(sr, T, skew, kurt, sr0=0.0):
    return stats.norm.cdf((sr - sr0) * np.sqrt(T - 1) / np.sqrt(1 - skew * sr + (kurt - 1) / 4 * sr ** 2))

def expected_max_sr(n_trials, var_sr):
    g = EULER_GAMMA
    return np.sqrt(var_sr) * ((1 - g) * stats.norm.ppf(1 - 1 / n_trials)
                              + g * stats.norm.ppf(1 - 1 / (n_trials * np.e)))

def deflated_sharpe(R):
    """R: (T, N) returns of EVERY trial evaluated; reports the best trial, deflated."""
    T, N = R.shape
    srs = sharpe(R)
    b = int(np.argmax(srs))
    sk, ku = stats.skew(R[:, b]), stats.kurtosis(R[:, b], fisher=False)
    sr_star = expected_max_sr(N, srs.var(ddof=1))
    return dict(sr=srs[b], sr_star=sr_star, psr0=psr(srs[b], T, sk, ku), dsr=psr(srs[b], T, sk, ku, sr_star))

def min_trl(sr, sr0, skew, kurt, alpha=0.05):
    return 1 + (1 - skew * sr + (kurt - 1) / 4 * sr ** 2) * (stats.norm.ppf(1 - alpha) / (sr - sr0)) ** 2

def pbo_cscv(R, S=10):
    T, N = R.shape
    blocks = np.array_split(np.arange(T), S)
    logits = []
    for ins in combinations(range(S), S // 2):
        tr = np.concatenate([blocks[i] for i in ins])
        te = np.concatenate([blocks[i] for i in range(S) if i not in ins])
        n_star = np.argmax(sharpe(R[tr]))
        omega = stats.rankdata(sharpe(R[te]))[n_star] / (N + 1)
        logits.append(np.log(omega / (1 - omega)))
    return float(np.mean(np.array(logits) <= 0))

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
T_m, N_tr = 120, 1000                                         # 10 years of months, 1,000 trials
maxes = [sharpe(rng.normal(0, 0.02, (T_m, N_tr))).max() for _ in range(40)]
assert abs(np.mean(maxes) / expected_max_sr(N_tr, 1 / T_m) - 1) < 0.10    # extreme-value formula holds
noise = rng.normal(0, 0.02, (T_m, N_tr))
rep = deflated_sharpe(noise)
assert rep["psr0"] > 0.95 and rep["dsr"] < 0.95               # 'significant' naively; a coin flip deflated
print({key: round(float(val), 3) for key, val in rep.items()})
pbo_noise = pbo_cscv(noise[:, :200])
skilled = np.column_stack([noise[:, :200], rng.normal(0.012, 0.02, T_m)])   # one real edge, SR 0.6/month
pbo_skill = pbo_cscv(skilled)
assert 0.10 < pbo_noise < 0.90 and pbo_skill < 0.25
print(f"PBO noise {pbo_noise:.2f}   PBO with one real strategy {pbo_skill:.2f}   "
      f"MinTRL(SR 0.3 vs 0.1, skew -0.5, kurt 5) {min_trl(0.3, 0.1, -0.5, 5):.0f} months")

What the blocks demonstrate, in desk language. Block 2 shows that smoothed marks cut measured volatility and manufacture autocorrelation, which is Defect 1 in code. Block 4 prints a hat count roughly an order of magnitude below the label count. Block 5 is the chapter’s central experiment: with features that are pure noise by construction, shuffled K-fold reports an AUC well above 0.5 because each test label’s nearest neighbors are its own overlapping siblings in time, while the purged, embargoed, parent-grouped splitter reports about 0.5, which is the truth. Block 6 shows the best of 1,000 noise strategies looking significant at a naive 95% and looking like a coin flip once deflated. Port the same functions to the real panel by replacing simulate_panel with the point-in-time TRACE and pricing-composite feed (Appendix B) and keeping every assert as a production test.

7.13 Desk Debrief

Two weeks after the cold open, Kaz reran the gradient-boosted model through the lab. The screen was much less exciting, which on this desk is how you know a number has been near the truth.

The row count was unchanged: 212,000 bond-months. Above it, in a font Kaz had made deliberately large, sat the hat count, \(N_{\text{eff}} \approx 24{,}000\). Below it: shuffled K-fold AUC 0.61, purged and parent-grouped AUC 0.52; 3,000 trials; an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 0.30 per month across the purged folds; deflated Sharpe ratio 0.84; PBO 0.41 (all illustrative). The top decile still held nine issuers. It no longer had a reason to.

“It isn’t a strategy,” Kaz said. “It isn’t nothing, either. It’s mostly carry and one company.”

“Strip the carry,” Theo said, “and then show me the one company.” IDO or it didn’t happen.

Theo had run something smaller. His primary model was the credit-agreement read turned into flags: drop-down capacity through unrestricted subsidiaries, non-pro-rata uptier risk, and a liquidity runway from the 13-week model shorter than two quarters. That came to about forty flags a year across the high-yield universe. The secondary model, trained on purged, parent-grouped folds, learned only when those flags were right and sized them. He had tried four sizing models, and he wrote the number four at the top of the report as if it were a defined term. Out of sample, the result was a Sharpe ratio of 0.20 per month over 96 months, with skew −1.5 and kurtosis 8. Against the four-trial benchmark (\(SR^\ast \approx 0.02\)), the deflated Sharpe ratio was 0.93, and the minimum track record length was about 115 months, so he needs roughly a year and a half more of live trading before the number means what he wants it to mean (illustrative).

“Now,” Ines said, “you’re showing me a hand and the number of hands you folded. Sit down.”

Mags looked at the four. “Back in my day we had one sizing model. It was called the PM’s mood, and it had an excellent track record, because the PM was the one who kept it.”

At the bottom of the monitor Kaz had taped the epigraph that Dickerson, Robotti, and Rossetti chose for their 2026 audit, Ronald Coase’s line: “if you torture the data enough, nature will always confess.” By lunch a sticky note had appeared beneath it in the unmistakable register of the Ad Hoc Group: The data, represented by counsel, will not confess to anything absent a cooperation agreement. None was signed, so the counter waits for Part IV.

Theo put the USB stick back in his pocket. It had been a 13-week cash flow model when he arrived. It was now a vertical barrier, a primary model, and a reason to distrust anything labeled “adjusted,” which Mags said was the first sign he might last.

Tape these to the monitor.

  • Count hats, not rows. The issuer is the observation: the ultimate parent, not the ticker. Print \(N_{\text{eff}} = \sum_i \bar u_i\) next to every result. In Kaz’s panel, 212,000 bond-months come to about 24,000 hats. A model that times the whole high-yield market has roughly one observation per non-overlapping 13-week window, which is about 79 in twenty years.
  • A mark is not a price. Stale and smoothed marks lower measured volatility, manufacture autocorrelation, and inflate the Sharpe ratio before any deflation. Treat staleness as a feature and as a filter. It is worst in single-B and CCC bonds, exactly where the alpha is supposed to live.
  • Keep the memory, lose the trend. Fractionally difference log spreads to the smallest \(d\) that passes a unit-root test. Taking \(d = 1\) throws away the level information that makes a spread a spread. Warm-up rows are NaN, never zero, and the FFD window counts toward the embargo.
  • Label the trade you would actually make. Use triple barriers scaled by DTS, set on IDO returns (strip the carry, or the label learns the coupon), with a 13-week vertical barrier. Censor exits at the exit value rather than imputing them from peers. A distressed exchange is not an average outcome, however politely the press release calls it an “open market purchase.”
  • The credit agreement picks the side; the model picks the size. Meta-labeling is what RSSG already did by hand. The secondary model may veto a trade. It may never reverse one.
  • Cross-validate as if the bonds were watching. Purge overlapping labels, embargo past the longest lookback, and group by ultimate parent. Shuffled K-fold finds signal in pure noise, and block 5 of §7.12 will demonstrate it on demand.
  • Report the folded hands. Every Sharpe ratio travels with \(N\), \(V[\widehat{SR}_n]\), the DSR, the PBO, and the MinTRL, and a new factor should clear roughly \(t > 3\). ROBO refuses to print a Sharpe ratio without them, and so should you.
  • Timestamps are covenants. Measure returns from the first feasible price after formation (the gap), filter ex-ante and symmetrically, keep the defaults, and join only on availability time. Between a retraction, a corrigendum, and 26 surviving specifications out of 432, the 2019–2026 record says credit ML is a data-integrity discipline first and a modeling discipline second.

The Spec You Hand the Robot

Paste the block below into ROBO’s prompt. It compresses §7.3–7.12 into one engine. The six Python blocks in §7.12 are the executable reference, and their asserts are the acceptance tests.

ROBO: build credit_ml_lab, a leakage-proof research harness for bond-level ML.
Implement exactly this. Where something is unspecified, stop and ask; do not guess.

INPUTS (point-in-time; every field carries available_at; join on nothing else)
  xs[T,NB]       daily excess return vs duration-matched Treasuries, decimal, from marks
  s[T,NB]        spread, decimal;  D_spr[T,NB] in years;  DTS = D_spr * s
  stale[T,NB]    trading days since the last institutional-size TRACE print
  parent[NB]     ULTIMATE-PARENT id (not ticker; unrestricted subs map to their parent)
  exit_day[NB]   call/tender/maturity/exchange/default day, T+1 if none; exit_type[NB]
  primary[T,NB]  side in {-1, 0, +1} from the analyst/covenant model (Chapter 13 flags)

PIPELINE
  1 FFD features on log s: d* = smallest d on 0.00:0.05:1.00 with DF t < -2.86
    (approximate 5%); tau = 1e-4, or 1e-3 if the warm-up exceeds the embargo budget.
    Warm-up rows are NaN and are dropped.
  2 Labels: triple barrier on IDO returns (carry and factor beta stripped, Chapter 8);
    half-width = m * 0.09 * sqrt(h/21) * DTS[t0], m = 1, h = 63 trading days.
    An exit before t0+h closes the label at the exit value: touch="exit", censored=True.
    Never form a label whose vertical barrier lies past the last date.
  3 Weights: parent-level average uniqueness u in (0,1]; N_eff = sum(u); Kish size;
    weights normalized to sum to n_labels.
  4 CV: purged, embargoed, parent-grouped K-fold x time blocks, plus annual walk-forward.
    embargo >= max(h, longest feature lookback including the FFD window).
    A fold with no positive labels is skipped and reported.
  5 Meta-label: secondary model -> p, clipped to [1e-6, 1-1e-6];
    size = max(2*Phi((p-0.5)/sqrt(p*(1-p))) - 1, 0) * primary.  Veto yes, reversal never.
  6 Evaluation returns start at the first feasible price AFTER signal formation (gap).
    Return filters are ex-ante and symmetric; returns around defaults are kept.

OUTPUT (one JSON record per experiment, appended to an immutable trial log)
  n_trials_raw, n_trials_clustered, var_sr, sr, psr0, dsr, min_trl, pbo (CSCV, S=10),
  n_labels, n_eff, kish, auc_shuffled, auc_purged, share_censored, share_stale_gt5d

REFUSE
  - to print any Sharpe ratio without n_trials, var_sr, dsr, pbo and n_eff beside it
  - to estimate kurtosis or the DSR from fewer than 30 returns (report "unavailable")
  - to delete a trial from the log, ever

ACCEPTANCE TESTS (keep in CI)
  - pure-noise features: auc_shuffled > auc_purged + 0.03 and |auc_purged - 0.5| < 0.06
  - 1,000 noise strategies x 120 months: mean max SR within 10% of the formula;
    the best has psr0 > 0.95 and dsr < 0.95
  - FFD weights equal (-1)^k binom(d, k) to 1e-12; d = 1 reproduces np.diff
  - two sibling bonds on identical windows get u = 0.5 each; a lone bond gets u = 1.0

The refusal to delete a trial is the line that matters most. A deflated Sharpe ratio is only as honest as the trial count fed into it, and the cheapest way to raise a DSR is to forget the 2,999 configurations that never made the slide. ROBO does not forget, which is the one respect in which it is a better researcher than any of us.

Exercises

  1. Count Kaz’s hats. One issuer has 11 bonds. Each bond produces a daily triple-barrier label with \(h = 63\) trading days over \(T = 1{,}260\) days, and every label runs to its vertical barrier. (a) Show that an interior label has \(\bar u_i \approx 1/(11 \times 63)\) and that the issuer contributes \(N_{\text{eff}} \approx T/h \approx 20\), whatever the number of bonds. (b) Seven of the 11 bonds are guaranteed OpCo notes. Four are HoldCo notes that were primed last quarter by a drop-down into an unrestricted subsidiary. Do they remain one group for cross-validation? What new label does the drop-down create, and how would you validate a model of it? (c) Compute the Kish effective size of the weights \(w = (1, 1, 1, 1, 6)\). Check: (a) Concurrency is about \(11 \times 63 = 693\) in the interior, and roughly \(11 \times 1{,}197\) labels divided by 693 gives about 19. (b) They remain one group. The ultimate parent is the information unit, and splitting it lets the model read the OpCo bonds’ answers off the HoldCo bonds. The drop-down does create a legitimate within-parent target, the OpCo–HoldCo basis, but it can only be validated across time blocks, because there is no other parent to hold out. (c) \((\sum w)^2 / \sum w^2 = 100/40 = 2.5\): five rows, two and a half opinions.

  2. Memory after a closing night. (a) Compute the first five FFD weights for \(d = 0.4\) from \(w_k = -w_{k-1}(d-k+1)/k\). (b) Prove that \(\sum_{k=0}^{K} w_k = (-1)^K \binom{d-1}{K}\), that this partial sum is strictly positive for every finite \(K\) when \(d \in (0,1)\), and that it tends to zero as \(K \to \infty\). (c) Block 5 of §7.12 uses a 21-day embargo because its features have no lookback. Suppose you add FFD features with \(d = 0.4\) and \(\tau = 10^{-4}\), whose warm-up is about 280 days (block 1). What embargo does the edge-case rule require, and how much of a 1,260-day sample split into four time blocks does it remove after each test block? What does raising \(\tau\) to \(10^{-3}\) buy, and what does it cost? Check: (a) \((1, -0.4, -0.12, -0.064, -0.0416)\). (b) Since \(w_k = (-1)^k \binom{d}{k}\), Pascal’s rule \(\binom{d}{k} = \binom{d-1}{k} + \binom{d-1}{k-1}\) makes the alternating sum telescope to \((-1)^K \binom{d-1}{K} = \prod_{j=1}^{K} (j-d)/j\). Every factor is positive for \(d \in (0,1)\), and the product behaves like \(K^{-d}/\Gamma(1-d) \to 0\). (c) The embargo must be at least 280 days. That is close to 90% of a 315-day block, and more than a fifth of the sample, removed after every test block. At \(\tau = 10^{-3}\) the window falls to about 54 days, and the horizon \(h = 63\) sets the embargo again. The cost is a larger leftover weight sum, so the filtered series carries more of the trending level, and the smallest \(d\) that passes the unit-root test usually rises. You pay for the extra training data in memory.

  3. Size Theo’s hand. Theo’s primary model raises 40 flags a year with a precision of 35%. A winning flag earns +4% and a losing one −2% in IDO return, at unit size (illustrative). The meta-model keeps 60% of the winners and lifts precision to 55%. (a) Compute the expected IDO return per trade, and per year summed over trades at unit size, with and without the meta-model. (b) Compute the bet size for \(p = 0.75\) and for \(p = 0.55\). In Ines’s terms, explain why a 55% read earns a small position rather than a slightly-better-than-half one. (c) The meta-model’s training set contains every flag Theo has ever raised, including flags on issuers that later did a drop-down. Which splitter must you use, and what goes wrong with the obvious one? Check: (a) Without it: \(0.35 \times 4 - 0.65 \times 2 = +0.10\%\) per trade, or \(+4\%\) a year. With it: 8.4 winners at 55% precision means about 15.3 trades, and \(0.55 \times 4 - 0.45 \times 2 = +1.30\%\) per trade, or about \(+20\%\) a year from fewer than half the trades. (b) For \(p = 0.75\), \(z = 0.25/\sqrt{0.1875} \approx 0.577\) and \(2\Phi(z) - 1 \approx 0.44\). For \(p = 0.55\), \(z = 0.05/\sqrt{0.2475} \approx 0.10\), giving about 0.08. The sizing rule converts the edge into a test statistic and bets the confidence that the edge exists. A 55% read is barely distinguishable from a coin flip, so it gets a chip, not a stack: bet your confidence, not your opinion. (c) Use purged, parent-grouped folds. Flags on one parent cluster in time around the same corporate event, so a shuffled split trains on the answer to the test flag.

  4. Deflate the honest number. Section 7.8 deflated Kaz’s in-sample winner. Now deflate the number on his new report: a purged out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 0.30 per month over \(T = 240\) months, with skew \(-0.5\) and kurtosis 5, selected from \(N = 3{,}000\) trials with \(V \approx 1/T\). (a) Show that the DSR is about 0.84. (b) Clustering the trial-return correlations finds about 400 effectively distinct trials. Holding \(V\) fixed, recompute \(SR^\ast\) and the DSR. (c) Compute the MinTRL at 95% confidence against the clustered \(SR^\ast\), and compare it with the history TRACE has. (d) Explain why feeding the in-sample Sharpe ratio of 2.9 into the DSR is a category error. Check: (a) \(SR^\ast \approx 0.23\), the denominator is \(\sqrt{1 + 0.15 + 0.09} \approx 1.11\), and \(\Phi(0.07 \times 15.46 / 1.11) = \Phi(0.98) \approx 0.84\). (b) \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - 1/400) \approx 2.81\) and \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - 1/(400e)) \approx 3.12\), so \(SR^\ast \approx 0.065 \times (0.423 \times 2.81 + 0.577 \times 3.12) \approx 0.065 \times 2.99 \approx 0.19\), and the DSR is \(\Phi(0.11 \times 15.46 / 1.11) = \Phi(1.5) \approx 0.93\). It is better, and still short of 95%. (c) \(T^\ast = 1 + 1.24 \times (1.645/0.11)^2 \approx 280\) months, roughly 23 years. That is about the entire life of TRACE (dissemination began in July 2002), and more than three years longer than Kaz’s sample. (d) The DSR corrects for selection across trials. An in-sample Sharpe ratio also contains overfitting within the trial (the trees memorized the 47 hats), so each trial’s return series must already be out of sample before it is deflated. Deflating an in-sample number is like haircutting a pro forma EBITDA that already includes the synergies.

  5. The composite is not a clean gap. In §7.9 the gap return used a month-begin price whose noise \(\delta'_{t^+}\) was uncorrelated with the month-end noise \(\delta_t\). Suppose instead that the month-begin price is an AI composite anchored partly on the last print, so that \(\operatorname{Corr}(\delta'_{t^+}, \delta_t) = \rho > 0\), with standard deviations \(\sigma_{\delta'}\) and \(\sigma_\delta\). (a) Show that \(\operatorname{Cov}(\tilde r_t, \tilde r^{\text{gap}}_{t+1}) = \operatorname{Cov}(r_t, r_{t^+ \to t+1}) - \rho\,\sigma_\delta \sigma_{\delta'}\). (b) The SMU Cox study found that the composite tracked efficient prices well in March 2020 but converged slowly during fire sales. What does that imply about \(\rho\) in exactly the months when a reversal strategy is most active, and what would you use as the entry price instead? Check: (a) The only noise shared by the two returns is \(+\delta_t\) in \(\tilde r_t\) against \(-\delta'_{t^+}\) in the gap return, so the bias is \(-\operatorname{Cov}(\delta_t, \delta'_{t^+}) = -\rho\,\sigma_\delta\sigma_{\delta'}\). At \(\rho = 0\) it vanishes. At \(\rho = 1\) with equal variances it is the full Roll bias of §7.9 again. (b) Slow convergence means the composite inherits the stale print, so \(\rho\) rises precisely when dispersion and measured reversal premia are largest. Use the first executable institutional-size trade (or a dealer level you could actually have hit) as the entry price, and report the premium under both definitions.

  6. ROBO and the future. Theo’s first draft of the leakage rule read: “Make sure the model doesn’t use future data.” ROBO complied by deleting the label column, which was the only future data in the table. Write the precise rule in at most 120 words. Name the timestamp field, the join rule, the purge condition, the embargo, and one test that fails the build if anyone breaks the rule. Check: A good answer names available_at and requires an as-of join (available_at <= t0) for every feature. It states the purge as “drop training label \(j\) if \([t_{0,j}, t_{1,j}]\) intersects \([T_0, T_1 + \text{embargo}]\),” with the embargo at least \(\max(h, \text{longest lookback})\). It ships the pure-noise AUC test from block 5 as the guard. Bonus credit for forbidding forward-fill across a data-release date, which is one common way the kind of error behind the 2021 corrigendum gets into a pipeline.

Part III: Isolating Idiosyncratic Alpha (IDO), Factors & Trend

Chapters 8–12

Picture a mixing desk. A bond’s return comes in on a dozen tracks at once: a rates track, a carry track, a credit-beta track, a few factor tracks (value, momentum, quality, low-risk, size), a liquidity track, and somewhere underneath, if you are lucky and the issuer is interesting, a track that is only this bond. Everyone who has ever pitched a credit has pointed at the mix and said “listen to that.” Part III teaches you to press mute on every track but one and find out what is actually there.

The first time Theo did it, the solo channel was silent. The bond he loved, the one whose capital structure he could draw from memory, had returned 9 percent over the year, and every basis point of it was duration and carry. The desk motto was taped to his monitor by the following morning: IDO or it didn’t happen.

Chapter 8, Stripping Beta to Isolate Pure IDO, is the mute button. It decomposes a bond’s return with the signs right (\(-D\,\Delta y\), not \(+\)), separates OAS carry from yield carry, and explains the most useful empirical fact in high yield: measured duration is much shorter than analytical duration, and for CCC bonds it turns negative, because spreads and rates move against each other. It covers DTS, the betas you compute when prices are stale (Dimson and Scholes–Williams lag sums), and the hedge matrix across CDX, Treasury futures, HYG and JNK, and equity puts, which is a constrained least-squares problem so ill-conditioned that ridge regularization is a safety feature rather than a style choice. The 2022 rates sell-off is the case study, because it was the year everyone’s duration hedge was wrong in the same direction.

Chapter 9, Factor Investing in Corporate Credit, is the factor tracks: value, momentum, quality, carry, low-risk, size and liquidity, and the “informed investor” factor from Man Group’s 2022 framework. The chapter is about construction more than discovery, because in credit the construction is the alpha: neutralization within rating, sector, and maturity buckets, DTS-neutral versus market-value-neutral portfolios, long-only constraints, liquidity cost scores that eat the paper return, crowding, and the 2019–2026 debate over whether published credit factors replicate.

Chapter 10, Trend-Following & Time-Series Momentum in Credit (TREND), is the track that is itself a trend, and the one readers who came for trends should turn to first. It applies the time-series-momentum framework to CDX, iTraxx, and credit excess returns, studies the equity-to-credit lead–lag that makes cross-asset trend work, combines trend with carry, scales by volatility, and looks hard at the crisis years, 2008, 2020, and 2022, where trend’s drawdown behavior is the entire reason anyone allocates to it. It also asks what trend does in a market where returns jump, which is a polite way of describing the LMT era.

Chapter 11, Defensive Systematic High Yield, follows BlackRock’s framework: default avoidance, downside mitigation, the CCC problem (where most of the index’s defaults and most of its negative convexity live), quality and low-risk tilts, the arithmetic of upside and downside capture, and the capacity question that decides whether any of this scales.

Chapter 12, Multi-Asset Credit Allocation, zooms out to Nuveen’s framework for rotating across high yield, loans, emerging-market debt, preferreds, securitized credit, and private credit: regimes, valuation per unit of default loss and per unit of volatility, risk budgets, and liquidity tiers, so that the allocation can be unwound in the order the market will let you.

The trend that defines this part is that systematic credit has grown a track record. Factor and trend strategies in credit used to be backtests in white papers; they now have live performance through two full drawdowns, and the sourced figures in these chapters let you judge them. Mags remains unconvinced. “Back in my day we had one factor. It was called ‘I know the CFO.’” Then she asks to see the momentum chart again.

Chapter 8: Stripping Beta to Isolate Pure IDO

8.0 Cold Open: Thirty-Seven Cents

At 2:58 p.m. on the Friday before a lender call, Theo’s screen showed two numbers that refused to agree. He was long $40mm of a B3 first-lien secured bond at +620. The 10-year had sold off 18 bp since lunch. The bond was down thirty-seven cents.

“Analytical duration 4.1,” Kaz said, without looking up. “You’re long $16,400 of DV01. ROBO is sizing the hedge now. Two hundred thirty-two TY contracts, short.”

“The bond only lost thirty-seven cents,” Theo said. “Your duration says it should have lost seventy.”

“Then it outperformed. That’s alpha.” Kaz kept typing. “Congratulations.”

Ines rolled her chair over, holding a coffee she had clearly been nursing since the open. “What’s the pot? If rates are selling off because the data says growth is fine, this bond tightens. Short two hundred thirty-two futures against it and your Treasury hedge isn’t a hedge. It’s a second position, with worse liquidity than the first one had at 9 a.m.”

“So I hedge less?”

“So you find out how much this bond actually cares about rates before you sell something to protect yourself from them.”

From across the aisle, without turning around, Mags said: “In 1994 we hedged B paper with the long bond. Lost on both. By phone.”

Theo opened his old 13-week cash flow model, the one on the USB stick, the way other people touch a lucky coin. “This thing has a duration of thirteen weeks and an empirical duration of zero. Nothing in it has ever moved with Treasuries.”

Kaz lit up. “So it’s a CCC bond.”

Nobody laughed, mostly because it was correct.

Theo wrote the question on a sticky note and put it on his monitor: Of the thirty-seven cents this bond moved today, how much was the bond?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to decompose a corporate bond’s return into carry, rates, spread beta, convexity, and residual, with every sign correct; estimate spread-dependent empirical durations by rating and recognize when the estimate is about to betray you; de-stale a beta estimated on bonds that trade twice a week; build, diagnose, and regularize a hedge matrix across CDX HY, Treasury futures, HYG/JNK, and equity puts; and define IDO precisely enough that a coding agent computes the same number you would.

8.1 The Subtraction: Return Decomposition With the Right Signs

Every restructuring banker has built a sources-and-uses table, and every one of them knows the rule: if the columns do not foot, somebody is about to be embarrassed in front of a client. A bond’s daily return is a sources-and-uses table for performance. The uses side is one number, the realized total return. The sources side is a list of things you did not choose (Treasury carry, the curve, the rate move, the market’s spread move, convexity) and one thing you did: the idiosyncratic residual you were paid to find. The desk calls that residual IDO, and the desk motto, “IDO or it didn’t happen,” is a statement about accounting before it is a statement about skill. Until the sources foot, you do not know whether you made money or the Federal Reserve made it for you.

The P&L explain that the risk system emails out every evening is this table. Nobody reads it, which is why this section exists.

Deriving the decomposition

Write the bond’s price as a function of its yield and time, \(P(y,t)\), and split the yield into a Treasury part and a spread part, \(y = y^{\text{TSY}} + s\). For a callable bond read \(y\) as the option-adjusted yield and \(s\) as the OAS. Over a short interval \(\Delta t\) in which the issuer does not default, a second-order Taylor expansion gives

\[ \frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx \frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial P}{\partial t}\,\Delta t + \frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\,\Delta y + \frac{1}{2}\,\frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial y^2}\,(\Delta y)^2 . \]

Define modified duration \(D^{\text{mod}} = -\frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\) and convexity \(C = \frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial y^2}\). Add the coupon accrual to the price change to get total return. At an unchanged yield, price pull plus coupon accrual earns the yield, so the time terms collapse to yield carry \(y\,\Delta t\) plus a roll-down term when the curve is sloped. Now split \(\Delta y = \Delta y^{\text{TSY}} + \Delta s\) and allow the spread sensitivity to differ from the rate sensitivity. For a fixed-rate bullet they are equal; for a floater, a callable, or a bond trading to a call date they are not. The result is

\[ R^{\text{tot}} \approx \underbrace{y\,\Delta t}_{\text{carry}} + \underbrace{\text{roll}}_{\text{curve}} \;-\; D^{\text{mod}}\,\Delta y^{\text{TSY}} \;-\; D^{\text{spr}}\,\Delta s \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}\,C\,(\Delta y)^2 \;+\; \epsilon . \]

Every symbol carries units. \(R^{\text{tot}}\) is a decimal return. \(y\) and \(s\) are decimal annual rates. \(\Delta t\) is in years under the bond’s day count (30/360 for US corporates). \(D^{\text{mod}}\) and \(D^{\text{spr}}\) are in years. \(\Delta y^{\text{TSY}}\) and \(\Delta s\) are decimal changes, so an 18 bp sell-off is \(0.0018\), not \(18\). The residual \(\epsilon\) collects the Taylor remainder, pricing noise, and anything specific to the issuer.

The index convention isolates the credit part by subtracting a portfolio of par Treasuries whose key-rate durations match the bond’s. To the same order, that portfolio returns \(y^{\text{TSY}}\Delta t + \text{roll} - D^{\text{mod}}\Delta y^{\text{TSY}} + \tfrac12 C^{\text{TSY}}(\Delta y^{\text{TSY}})^2\). Subtracting it leaves the excess return:

\[ R^{\text{xs}} \equiv R^{\text{tot}} - \sum_k w_k R^{\text{TSY}}_k \approx s\,\Delta t \;-\; D^{\text{spr}}\,\Delta s \;+\; (\text{convexity cross-terms}) \;+\; \epsilon . \]

The carry is now OAS carry, \(s\,\Delta t\), not yield carry. The rate term is gone by construction, and that is exactly what the index excess return is designed to do. Finally, rewrite the spread term in relative-change form, because (as §8.4 shows) relative spread changes are the quantity that is stable across credits:

\[ -D^{\text{spr}}\,\Delta s \;=\; -\,\underbrace{D^{\text{spr}}\,s}_{\text{DTS}}\,\cdot\,\frac{\Delta s}{s} . \]

That is the whole chapter in one line. The accounting identity hands you \(\Delta s\), the bond’s own spread change. It does not tell you how much of \(\Delta s\) was the market. Stage two of the subtraction is the factor model

\[ R^{\text{xs}}_{i,t} = \sum_{k} \beta_{i,k}\,F_{k,t} + \epsilon_{i,t}, \]

with factor returns \(F_{k,t}\), loadings \(\beta_{i,k}\), and residual \(\epsilon_{i,t}\). IDO is what survives both stages. The decomposition residual is a bookkeeping error term; the factor residual is the asset.

Assumptions and measure. The expansion assumes small moves, no default inside \(\Delta t\), and option-adjusted durations for callables. The decomposition is accounting and needs no probability measure. Two things built on it do. The expected excess return is a \(\mathbb{P}\) object, because it is what you forecast. The OAS is a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-consistent spread, because it is what discounts the bond’s cash flows to its price. OAS includes compensation for expected default loss, so “the bond yields +620 over Treasuries” is not “the bond is expected to beat Treasuries by 620 bp a year.” The gap is the expected loss, and Chapter 5 priced it.

The thirty-seven cents, itemized

Apply the decomposition to Theo’s bond (illustrative inputs): price $95, \(D^{\text{mod}} = 4.1\), \(D^{\text{spr}} = 4.0\), yield 11.1%, one day of 30/360 carry. The 10-year sold off \(\Delta y^{\text{TSY}} = +0.0018\), and the bond’s OAS tightened 9 bp, \(\Delta s = -0.0009\).

Source Formula Return Cents on $95
Carry \(y\,\Delta t = 0.111/360\) +0.031% +3
Rates \(-D^{\text{mod}}\Delta y^{\text{TSY}} = -4.1 \times 0.0018\) −0.738% −70
Spread \(-D^{\text{spr}}\Delta s = -4.0 \times (-0.0009)\) +0.360% +34
Convexity \(\tfrac12 C (\Delta y)^2\), \(C \approx 20\) +0.000% 0
Residual plug −0.043% −4
Total −0.390% −37

Kaz’s “alpha” was the 34 cents of spread tightening. The question for the next three sections is whether those 9 bp of tightening belonged to the bond or to the rate move. If high-yield spreads systematically tighten when yields rise for growth reasons, the 34 cents is beta wearing a disguise, and a hedge of 232 futures would have converted a modestly hedged position into a short rates bet with a spread rider.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor p.298: “Barclays Capital reports excess returns that equal the difference in total return between a bond and a portfolio of hypothetical par Treasury bonds matching the bond’s key rate duration exposures.”

Annotation. This sentence is the industry’s definition of the first subtraction, and it carries two hidden choices. First, the hedge is key-rate matched, not single-duration matched, so a 30-year bond’s excess return is not polluted by 2s10s steepening. Second, the hedge portfolio is hypothetical: par Treasuries at each key rate, rebalanced costlessly. A desk that hedges with actual futures earns the index’s excess return minus the futures-cash basis, roll costs, and the cheapest-to-deliver switch (§8.6). On a 2026 desk the definition matters for a second reason: the excess-return series you download from an index provider is already a hedged P&L under a hedge you did not choose. Any empirical duration you estimate on excess returns is a duration relative to that hedge. Estimate \(D^{\text{emp}}\) on total returns, then subtract.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Man_2022 p.14: “ICE BofAML excess returns taken as total returns less key rate duration matched sovereign return.”

Annotation. Two index families, one convention. That is convenient and slightly dangerous, because it lets people forget that “excess return” is a model output. Asvanunt and Richardson (2017), The Credit Risk Premium, make the point that the measured credit premium is biased if the term component is mis-hedged; the definition you choose leaks into every Sharpe ratio built on it. For a systematic desk the operational rule is to store total returns, Treasury key-rate returns, and the hedge weights separately, and to compute excess returns in your own code. Then, when the index provider restates history, your backtest does not silently change its mind.

Ways This Blows Up. (1) The sign. \(-D\,\Delta y\) has a minus sign. ROBO, given the formula without it, will report that a rate sell-off made the book money, and the P&L explain will foot perfectly because the residual absorbs twice the error. (2) Units. \(D \cdot \Delta y\) needs \(\Delta y\) in decimal. Feed it 18 instead of 0.0018 and a 4-year bond loses 7,200% on a quiet afternoon. Assert \(|\Delta y| < 0.05\) per day as a data-error trap. (3) Yield carry versus OAS carry. Yield carry belongs to total return and OAS carry to excess return. Mixing them double-counts the Treasury leg, roughly 5% a year in 2026, and hands you a mysterious, very stable “alpha.” (4) Callable HY. Much of a high-yield index is callable, and a bond priced to a call date has a spread duration set by the call, not the maturity. Some of what looks like OAS carry is the short call decaying. When the bond crosses the call price, duration-to-worst jumps. Any rolling regression that treats that jump as a rate response will invent a structural break.

8.2 Empirical vs. Analytical Duration: One Formula, Three Regimes

Analytical duration answers a question nobody asked: what happens to the bond’s price if Treasury yields move and nothing else does. On a desk, nothing else moving is the one scenario that never occurs. Empirical duration answers the question Ines asked: when yields move, what tends to happen to this bond, given that its spread tends to move too?

The RSSG reader already knows the limit case. A name in restructuring trades on dollar price, and every bond at the same seniority converges to the same recovery regardless of maturity. Its sensitivity to the 10-year is roughly zero. Empirical duration is the continuum between that limit and par.

The two-factor derivation

Start from the excess-return identity of §8.1, put the Treasury leg back, and keep only first-order terms. Let \(x_i \equiv \Delta s_i / s_i\) be bond \(i\)’s relative spread change. Then

\[ R_i \approx -D_i\,\Delta y - D_i\,s_i\,x_i , \]

where \(\Delta y\) is the Treasury yield change and, for a bullet bond, \(D_i = D^{\text{mod}}_i = D^{\text{spr}}_i\). Decompose the relative spread change into the part linearly predictable from the yield change and a part orthogonal to it:

\[ x_i = \rho_{y,s}\,\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}\,\Delta y + u_i, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}^{\mathbb{P}}(u_i,\Delta y) = 0 . \]

Here \(\rho_{y,s}\) is the correlation between yield changes and relative spread changes, \(\sigma_s\) the volatility of relative spread changes, and \(\sigma_y\) the volatility of yield changes, all measured over the same horizon. The coefficient \(\rho_{y,s}\sigma_s/\sigma_y\) is the population OLS slope of \(x\) on \(\Delta y\). Substituting and taking the conditional expectation under \(\mathbb{P}\):

\[ \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[R_i \mid \Delta y] = -D_i\,\Delta y\left(1 + s_i\,\rho_{y,s}\,\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}\right). \]

Empirical duration is the negative of the slope of this expectation in \(\Delta y\):

\[ D^{\text{emp}}_i = D_i\left(1 + s_i\,\rho_{y,s}\,\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}\right), \qquad H_i \equiv \frac{D^{\text{emp}}_i}{D_i} = 1 + s_i\,\rho_{y,s}\,\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y} . \]

\(H_i\) is the hedge ratio: the fraction of analytical duration you should actually hedge to minimize the variance of a Treasury-hedged position. (We write \(H\) rather than \(h\) because \(h\) is reserved for the hedge-weight vector in §8.6.) Three properties follow by inspection. Because \(s_i\), \(\sigma_s\), and \(\sigma_y\) are non-negative, the sign of \(\rho_{y,s}\) alone decides whether \(H\) is below or above one. The deviation from one scales with the spread level, so the same correlation that shaves 5% off an IG bond’s duration can erase a B bond’s. And nothing stops \(H\) from going negative.

Define the linkage factor \(\ell \equiv \rho_{y,s}\sigma_s/\sigma_y\), so \(H = 1 + \ell s\). Ben Dor’s 1998–2009 sample has \(\sigma_y = 6.4\) bp a day and relative spread volatilities of 1.6% to 2.5% a day. For B-rated bonds, \(\rho = -0.56\) and \(\sigma_s \approx 2.2\%\) give \(\ell \approx -0.56 \times 0.022/0.00064 \approx -19\) per unit of decimal spread. That is a loss of 0.19 of hedge ratio for every 100 bp of spread, so a B bond at 500 bp has \(H \approx 0.03\), and Theo’s bond at 620 bp comes out slightly below zero. Under the 1998–2009 parameters, every one of Kaz’s 232 contracts was a second position. Under the 2026 parameters in the Trend Watch below, most of them were a hedge. That is the problem.

The estimable form. Theory gives the shape; data must give the numbers. With a panel of bond returns, regress

\[ R_{i,t} = \beta\,(-D_{i,t}\,\Delta y_t) + \gamma\,(-D_{i,t}\,s_{i,t}\,\Delta y_t) + \epsilon_{i,t}, \qquad H(s) = \beta + \gamma\,s , \]

with \(\gamma < 0\) expected. The first regressor is the analytical rate exposure; the second is that exposure scaled by spread. If the two-factor model were exact, \(\beta = 1\) and \(\gamma = \ell\). In data, \(\beta < 1\) for HY even at low spreads, which is the puzzle of §8.3.

Assumptions and failure modes. (i) Horizon: daily, weekly, and monthly \(\rho\) differ, and daily HY marks are stale (§8.5); Dynkin p.436 runs the pooled regression on monthly, carry-adjusted returns for exactly this reason. (ii) Extrapolation: \(H(s)\) is linear in \(s\) inside the sample and nowhere else. Ben Dor p.196 tests 2005–2009 spreads that lay outside the fitting range. (iii) The min-variance hedge also hedges your spread view (see the Poker Table below). (iv) In distress, price is pinned to recovery and \(D \to 0\) whatever \(\rho\) is: a second route to zero duration that this formula does not contain. (v) Price level matters: discount bonds respond asymmetrically (§8.3). On measures: \(\rho\) and the \(\sigma\)’s are \(\mathbb{P}\) sample moments, while \(D_i\) is the derivative of a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-consistent price. The gap between \(D\) and \(D^{\text{emp}}\) is comovement, not mispricing. Nobody is wrong; the bond is just never alone.

The canonical numbers, rebuilt

Table 8.1 restates Ben Dor’s estimates (daily data, August 1998 to November 2009) in our notation.

Baa −0.23 0.85 −0.02 0.74 0.67 0.88

Read the table like a credit agreement: the interesting clauses are the ones that do not say what you expected. The two-factor model predicts the ordering well: IG near one, HY near or below zero. The regression intercepts tell a stranger story. Even as spreads go to zero, Ba bonds hedge at 0.41 and Caa at 0.07. A Ba bond at a tight spread is not a distressed instrument, so the recovery route cannot explain why it ignores Treasuries. And the \(R^2\) for high yield is 0.01 to 0.06. The rate component of an HY bond’s return is not merely small; it is barely there.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor p.191: “If this correlation is negative, the empirical duration would be lower than the analytical one and may even end up being negative.”

Annotation. The sentence is conditional, and the condition is the whole game. In Ben Dor’s 1998–2009 sample the correlation was reliably negative, because rates mostly moved on growth news and Fed easing, and spreads moved against them. The book treats the sign as a fact about the sample. A 2026 desk must treat it as a state variable. In 2022 the condition failed: rates rose on inflation and spreads widened with them, so \(\rho > 0\) and \(H > 1\). The formula held. The parameter moved. Any production system that hard-codes \(H\) from a pre-2020 table is a 2022 loss waiting for a calendar.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Dynkin p.437: “When rates fall, bond prices increase. Due to this negative correlation, however, spreads tend to widen, and thus the bond prices do not increase by as much as would have been expected based on analytical duration alone.”

Annotation. The plain-English version, and the one to read aloud to a PM who asks why the hedged book lost money on a rally. Note the asymmetry the sentence implies for convex payoffs. On a rally, a long credit position under-earns its duration and a full Treasury short loses its full duration, so the hedged book bleeds from both sides. The pooled monthly IG regression in the same chapter (Dynkin p.438–439, January 1992 to April 2014, 737,506 bond-months) finds a base hedge ratio of 0.97 that falls by 0.13 per 1% of spread. That is gentler than daily estimates, which is partly the stale-price effect of §8.5 washing out at monthly horizons.

Three regimes

The formula \(H = 1 + s\,\ell\) has one sign switch, so there are three regimes worth naming:

  1. Flight-to-quality or growth-driven rates, \(\rho < 0\). Yields fall when spreads widen. \(H < 1\) for everything and \(H \le 0\) for single-B and below. This is the 1998–2009 world and the March 2023 week (§8.7).
  2. Decoupled, \(\rho \approx 0\). Rates and spreads move on unrelated news. \(H \approx 1\) even for high yield, and analytical duration is the right hedge by accident. FRED data put 2026 year-to-date here (Trend Watch below).
  3. Inflation-driven rates, \(\rho > 0\). Yields rise when spreads widen, because the same inflation news hurts both. \(H > 1\): high yield has more rate sensitivity than its analytical duration. This was 2022.

Poker Table. Ines draws it on a napkin. “Two hands. In the first, you’re long a Ba bond because you think spreads tighten when the economy is strong, which is also when rates rise. You hedge at the empirical ratio, \(H = 0.4\). Rates rise 50 bp, spreads tighten 30 bp, exactly what the correlation predicted, and the hedge and the bond net to zero. You were right, and you got paid nothing. The minimum-variance hedge saw your view in the correlation and hedged it away, because a view is variance. In the second hand you hedge the full analytical duration. Rates rise, the futures pay, spreads tighten, the bond pays. Now you got paid for the view, and you also carried the risk of the view. Pick the hedge that matches the bet you meant to make. If you have a view that spreads tighten when rates rise, the empirical hedge pays you nothing for being right.”

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor p.219: “An empirical hedge, reduced to reflect this known correlation, would exactly offset both of these market effects. Is this what the investor intended?”

Annotation. This is the most important question in the chapter, asked as a rhetorical aside. A hedge ratio is a choice of objective, not a fact. Minimum total variance gives you \(H\). “Zero rate exposure, keep the spread beta” gives you \(H = 1\) plus a separate decision about spread. “Zero exposure to both” gives you a different instrument set altogether. ROBO cannot choose among these. The spec must name the objective, and §8.9 makes that a required field.

Trend Watch: The Correlation That Changed Sides, 2018–2026. What changed. For two decades the stock–bond correlation was negative or near zero (rolling three-year correlations, November 2000 to 2020, per Morningstar’s diversification research as reported in secondary summaries; approx.). It turned positive in 2021 and was roughly 0.58 for full-year 2022 and 2023 (approx.; same source). The rate–spread correlation \(\rho_{y,s}\) is a cousin of that number: when inflation drives rates, it drives both. How big. In 2022 the 10-year rose from 1.52% to 3.88% and the 2-year from 0.73% to 4.41% (FRED, DGS10/DGS2, year-end closes). The Bloomberg US Corporate High Yield index returned about −11.2% and the IG Corporate index about −15.8% (approx.; secondary data summaries). Apollo’s Torsten Slok noted on December 3, 2022 that the HY total-return index was “down 10% so far in 2022” and attributed it mainly to duration. High yield, the asset class with “negative empirical duration,” lost money on rates. What happened next. Our computation on FRED daily data (ICE BofA OAS by rating against DGS10; relative OAS changes; \(H = 1 + \bar s\rho\sigma_s/\sigma_y\); computed 2026-10-17, index level, correlation route only):

Window \(\rho\): HY / BB / B / CCC / IG Implied \(H\): HY / BB / B / CCC / IG
2024 (249 days) −0.34 / −0.39 / −0.29 / −0.22 / −0.38 0.65 / 0.64 / 0.66 / 0.61 / 0.92
2025 (248 days) −0.35 / −0.38 / −0.31 / −0.31 / −0.32 0.42 / 0.47 / 0.42 / 0.14 / 0.90
2026 YTD to Oct 15 (197 days) −0.03 / −0.10 / +0.02 / +0.09 / −0.08 0.97 / 0.90 / 1.03 / 1.19 / 0.98

In 2024–2025 high yield behaved like the textbook: 0.4 to 0.65 of analytical duration, and the rolling 60-day CCC hedge ratio touched −0.78 in the window ending May 23, 2025. In 2026 so far, daily rate and spread moves have been nearly uncorrelated, and HY’s empirical duration is roughly its analytical duration. IG never left the band [0.79, 1.04] on a rolling 60-day basis. What it means for the desk. The hedge ratio is a time series, and its sign has changed twice in five years. Re-estimate monthly, monitor a rolling \(\rho\) daily, and treat a zero crossing as a regime alarm (§8.7). One more data-infrastructure fact: FRED’s ICE BofA OAS pages state that starting in April 2026 the series include only three years of observations, so the free history now begins in October 2023. A desk that wants Ben Dor’s 1998 start date must build its own spread history from TRACE (Appendix B).

8.3 The Discontinuity: Why a CCC Bond Is an Equity Option That Wears a Tie to Work

If the hedge ratio depended only on the spread level, then a Baa bond at 700 bp and a Ba bond at 700 bp would hedge identically. In December 2008 they did not. The Baa bond was a downgraded, frightened, wide investment-grade credit that still behaved like a bond. The Ba bond at the same spread behaved like a stock. Something other than credit risk lives at the IG/HY line, and it is worth a section, because it is the most RSSG-friendly fact in quantitative credit: a market’s quoting convention is a measurable risk factor.

Two routes to zero duration

There are two separate reasons a corporate bond can stop caring about Treasuries, and a desk that conflates them will mis-hedge both.

The correlation route is §8.2: \(H = 1 + \ell s\) falls to zero when the expected spread response to a rate move cancels the rate move. The bond’s cash flows still discount at Treasury-plus-spread. The market simply moves the spread against the Treasury.

The recovery route needs no correlation at all. Take the cleanest possible case under \(\mathbb{Q}\): a perpetual bond paying a continuous coupon \(c\) per unit of par, a constant short rate \(r\), a constant default intensity \(\lambda\), and recovery of face \(R\) paid at default (the RFV convention). Survival to \(t\) has probability \(e^{-\lambda t}\), so

\[ P = \int_0^\infty e^{-(r+\lambda)t}\,\big(c + \lambda R\big)\,dt = \frac{c + \lambda R}{r + \lambda} . \]

The numerator is the bond’s flow of value: coupons while it survives, plus the expected recovery arriving at rate \(\lambda\). Differentiating with \(\lambda\) held fixed gives the bond’s true rate sensitivity:

\[ D^{\text{haz}} \equiv -\frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial P}{\partial r} = \frac{1}{r + \lambda} . \]

The analytical duration on your risk screen is computed from the bond’s yield, as if every cash flow were a promised coupon. For a perpetuity priced at \(P\), the yield is \(y = c/P\) and the yield duration is \(D^{\text{yld}} = 1/y\). The ratio is

\[ H^{\text{rec}} \equiv \frac{D^{\text{haz}}}{D^{\text{yld}}} = \frac{y}{r+\lambda} = \frac{c}{c + \lambda R} . \]

The recovery-route hedge ratio is the share of the bond’s value flow that still looks like a bond. As \(\lambda \to 0\) it goes to one. As \(\lambda \to \infty\) it goes to zero, and the price goes to \(R\) whatever \(r\) is. That is the restructuring desk’s “trades on dollar price” written as a limit. With illustrative CCC inputs, \(c = 9\%\), \(R = 40\%\), and \(\lambda = 21\%\) (roughly a 1,280 bp spread over a 60% loss given default), \(H^{\text{rec}} = 0.09/(0.09 + 0.084) \approx 0.52\). Half the analytical duration of that bond is fiction before anyone has computed a correlation. To first order the two routes multiply, so \(H \approx H^{\text{rec}}\,(1 + \ell s)\), and a CCC book can lose all of its rate sensitivity by either road.

Kaz, reading over Theo’s shoulder, frowned at the derivation. “So the fulcrum security is the one where the hedge ratio pivots through zero?”

“The fulcrum,” said Mags, “is the class that gets the equity after the lawyers are done. Which is why its hedge ratio is zero.” She paused. “You’re accidentally right. That’s the worst way to be right.”

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor p.194: “With hedge ratios near or below zero across most spread levels, high-yield securities more closely resemble equities than bonds.”

Annotation. Hence the chapter title: a CCC bond is an equity option that wears a tie to work. The same page names the recovery route explicitly. Near default, the market tends to quote all bonds of an issuer at the same seniority “marked at the same dollar price, regardless of maturity,” and a price that does not depend on maturity cannot depend on the discount rate. Two departures for 2026. First, “resemble equities” is now an instruction rather than an analogy. The natural hedge for a CCC position is a credit-equity instrument (CDX HY, single-name or index puts; §8.6), not a futures contract. Second, the 2024–2026 FRED data in §8.2 show HY hedge ratios between 0.4 and 1.0 at the index level. “Near or below zero” described a sample in which \(\rho\) was strongly negative. The equity-like recovery behavior of CCCs is structural. The equity-like correlation behavior of the whole HY market is a regime.

The segmentation hypothesis

Now the puzzle. The recovery route explains a CCC bond trading at 45. It does not explain a Ba bond at a tight spread hedging at 0.41 (Table 8.1). Ben Dor runs three tests that rule out the obvious explanations. Excluding bonds priced below 80 does not remove the gap, so distress is not the cause. Comparing Baa bonds during the 2008–2009 crisis with Ba bonds at overlapping spread levels shows Baa still behaving like a bond. Liquidity controls do not close it either.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor p.207: “Baa bonds maintained a hedge ratio of 0.71, even at spreads of 700 bps, whereas high-yield bonds exhibited zero or even negative hedge ratios for the same level of spreads.”

Annotation. This is the overlap test, and it is the cleanest evidence in the chapter that the IG/HY line is a market convention, not a credit fact. Same spread, same macro shock, opposite behavior. The explanation offered (p.203) is sociological: investment-grade bonds are quoted as a spread to a parent Treasury and run against excess-return benchmarks, so an IG trader’s screen literally moves when the 10-year moves. High-yield bonds are quoted in price and run on total return, so an HY trader’s screen moves when the bid moves. For a systematic desk this has a concrete consequence. A bond downgraded from Baa3 to Ba1 changes its rate hedge ratio at the moment it changes investor base, before anything about its cash flows changes. The fallen-angel trade of Chapter 9 inherits a rate-hedge jump you should model, not discover.

Ben Dor also documents a nonlinearity (p.200). When Ba spreads topped 600 bp in 2002, empirical duration fell to about −2. As spreads blew past 1,000 bp in early 2009, the linear model predicted something far more negative, and it never came: durations bottomed not far below zero. The physics is the recovery route. As \(\lambda\) rises, \(H^{\text{rec}} \to 0\) squeezes the whole product toward zero from both sides. A deeply negative empirical duration requires a bond that is still rate-sensitive and strongly anti-correlated, and very distressed bonds are neither. The production consequence: clip extrapolated \(H(s)\) at a floor such as \(-0.5\) (illustrative) rather than trusting a linear fit at spreads the sample never saw.

Desk Myth vs. Desk Reality. Myth: “High yield has negative duration.” Reality: High yield had negative empirical duration when the Fed was the only thing moving rates. In 2022, inflation moved rates, and high yield had a duration of “yes.”

Price level: the discount-bond asymmetry

One more state variable. Dynkin’s Tables 10.2–10.3 split bonds by price. Discount bonds show an empirical hedge ratio of 1.00 when yields fall and 0.72 when they rise; premium bonds show 0.80 and 0.86. Discount bonds respond fully to good rate news and only partially to bad rate news.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Dynkin p.439–440: “discount bonds should follow a highly desirable behavior in which they react more strongly to favorable yield changes and less strongly to unfavorable ones—a positive convexity effect.”

Annotation. Why this is a 2026 problem: the 2020–2021 issuance vintage priced low coupons at par, and after the 2022 rate shock much of it trades at a discount. A discount bond has more call-free runway (no rational issuer calls a 3.75% coupon in a 5% world), so its duration does not shorten when rates fall. That is part of the positive convexity. A premium callable does the opposite, because its duration collapses toward the call date in a rally. An HY book whose discount share has risen therefore has a hedge ratio that depends on the direction of the next move. The regression of §8.2 should carry a price-bucket interaction, or be run separately for rising- and falling-yield days, before its \(H\) goes into a hedge.

Case Study: One Bond, Four Hedge Ratios (Alltel’s 7.875% 30-Year, 2006–2009)

Ben Dor (p.211) follows a single security through a capital-structure round trip: the Alltel 7.875% bond with thirty years to maturity at issue. (The book prints the CUSIP; we describe the bond and do not reprint identifiers.) The path, using Ben Dor’s dates and estimated hedge ratios:

  1. 2006, rated A2, spread about +200 bp. Rolling empirical hedge ratio about 0.75: a long-dated IG bond behaving like a long-dated IG bond.
  2. May 23, 2007, downgraded to Ba2 at about +450 bp, as the company headed into a leveraged buyout by TPG and GS Capital Partners. Hedge ratio falls to about 0.4. Nothing about the coupon or maturity changed. The holder base and the quoting convention did.
  3. November 21, 2007, downgraded to Caa1 as the buyout closed and the bond sat in a heavily levered structure. Hedge ratio falls into negative territory, as low as −0.6.
  4. January 8, 2009, Verizon’s acquisition closes and the bond is re-rated A2. The hedge ratio climbs from about 0.25 back to about 0.95.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor p.211: “When the bond was further downgraded to Caa1 on November 21, 2007, the hedge ratio dropped even further to negative territory (as a low as −0.6).”

Annotation. One security, one indenture, four hedge ratios, from 0.95 to −0.6. A desk that estimated this bond’s empirical duration over 2006–2009 as one number would have been wrong in every sub-period. The systematic lesson is that \(H\) is a function of rating bucket, spread, and price, re-evaluated whenever any of them changes, with the rating transition treated as a jump. The RSSG lesson is better. The 2007 downgrades were the market repricing a change in the capital structure, the LBO debt landing on top of the existing bonds, and the hedge ratio moved with the capital structure, not with the cash flows. Chapter 13 asks whether the same signature appears before a priming transaction. If a bond’s rate beta collapses before the uptier is announced, that is a free early-warning feature for the Priming Risk Score.

How a systematic desk would have traded it: carry a rating-bucket \(H\) table re-estimated monthly; on a downgrade across the IG/HY line, switch the bond’s \(H\) to the new bucket’s value on the day rather than waiting for a trailing window to notice; and size the Treasury hedge for the whole HY book from bucket-level \(H\), never bond-level, because bond-level \(R^2\) is 0.01.

Trend Watch: CCC Decompression, 2024–2026. What changed. The CCC tier has come apart from the rest of high yield. On FRED’s ICE BofA series the CCC-and-lower to BB OAS ratio was 4.0× at the end of 2024 (746 bp / 186 bp), 5.2× at the end of 2025 (885 / 169), and 6.5× on October 15, 2026 (1,278 / 197). The CCC OAS reached 12.82% on October 14, 2026, while the broad HY OAS was 3.23% and IG 0.84% (computed 2026-10-17). The beta of CCC relative spread changes on HY relative spread changes fell from 0.54 (2024) and 0.55 (2025) to 0.45 (2026 year to date). What it means for the desk. CCCs are loading less on the market spread factor and more on something issuer-specific. In this chapter’s vocabulary, more of their return is idiosyncratic, which for a pure-IDO book is opportunity and for a DTS-scaled risk model is a warning: DTS assumes relative spread changes are common across credits, and in the CCC tier that assumption is weakening. We do not attribute causes here; Chapter 11 takes up the CCC problem and Chapter 14 the recoveries behind it.

8.4 DTS: The Unit of Credit Beta

The restructuring banker’s instinct is that leverage is not one number. Six turns of debt at a software company and six turns at a regional grocer are different risks, and the spread already tells you how different. DTS is the same instinct applied to spread risk. Two bonds with identical spread duration are not equally risky if one trades at 80 bp and the other at 800 bp, because spreads do not move in basis points. They move in percent.

The derivation

Ben Dor’s central empirical regularity is that the volatility of spread changes is proportional to the spread level:

\[ \sigma(\Delta s_i) \approx \kappa\, s_i , \]

where \(\kappa\) is a relative spread volatility (for example, per month) that is roughly common across bonds within a market. Combine it with the first-order excess return of §8.1, \(R^{\text{xs}}_i \approx -D^{\text{spr}}_i\,\Delta s_i\):

\[ \sigma\big(R^{\text{xs}}_i\big) \approx D^{\text{spr}}_i\,\sigma(\Delta s_i) \approx \kappa\, D^{\text{spr}}_i\, s_i = \kappa\,\text{DTS}_i . \]

Excess-return volatility is linear in DTS with slope \(\kappa\). Ben Dor estimates the slope at 8.8% per month for investment grade, with an \(R^2\) of 98% (p.51). The arithmetic for a bond with \(D^{\text{spr}} = 6\) and \(s = 1.5\%\): \(\text{DTS} = 6 \times 0.015 = 0.09\), so monthly excess-return volatility is about \(0.088 \times 0.09 = 0.79\%\). At very low spreads the line has a small structural floor (p.57), which is why DTS slightly understates the risk of the tightest bonds.

Now the beta. Suppose relative spread changes share a common market component, \(\Delta s_i/s_i = x_{M} + u_i\), with \(u_i\) idiosyncratic. Then

\[ R^{\text{xs}}_i \approx -\text{DTS}_i\,x_M - \text{DTS}_i\,u_i, \qquad R^{\text{xs}}_M \approx -\text{DTS}_M\,x_M , \]

so bond \(i\)’s beta to the market’s excess return is

\[ \beta_{i,M} = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(R^{\text{xs}}_i, R^{\text{xs}}_M)}{\mathrm{Var}(R^{\text{xs}}_M)} = \frac{\text{DTS}_i}{\text{DTS}_M} . \]

That is the reason for this section’s title. In the DTS world, credit beta is not estimated; it is computed from two numbers on your risk screen. Merton’s model supports the near-linearity: for firms away from default, the spread’s sensitivity to asset value scales roughly with the spread itself (Ben_Dor p.104–105).

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor p.50: “a portfolio with a weighted spread of 200 bps and spread duration of two years is equally risky as a portfolio with a spread of 100 bps and spread duration of four years.”

Annotation. The sentence that ended the reign of spread duration as the risk unit. For an RSSG reader the translation is that a two-year secured term loan at +400 and a four-year unsecured note at +200 carry the same spread risk, which is precisely the comparison a lender group makes when it trades a maturity extension for a rate increase. The 2026 caveat is the CCC Trend Watch above. DTS’s equivalence rests on common relative spread moves, and the tier where relative moves are least common is where most of the IDO lives. Use DTS as the default risk unit, and let the residual covariance (§8.8) catch what it misses.

DTS-neutral pairs, and why they carry nothing

A long–short pair hedged to zero DTS is the workhorse relative-value trade. With long bond \(L\) and short bond \(S\), set the short notional per unit long to

\[ h_S = \frac{\text{DTS}_L}{\text{DTS}_S} = \frac{D^{\text{spr}}_L\,s_L}{D^{\text{spr}}_S\,s_S} . \]

If the two bonds have similar spread durations, \(h_S \approx s_L/s_S\), and the pair’s OAS carry is \(s_L\,\Delta t - h_S\,s_S\,\Delta t \approx 0\). Ben Dor makes the point directly: matching DTS with similar spread durations “means the trades will also be zero-carry trades” (p.228). Read that as a feature, not a footnote. A DTS-neutral pair has stripped market spread beta and the carry that market beta pays you for holding. What it earns, it earns from convergence between the two names. That is IDO by construction, which is why the DTS-neutral pair is the unit test for any relative-value signal (Chapter 9).

Why DTS beats an estimated beta

The obvious objection: why compute beta from DTS when you can estimate it by regression? Because the regression is unstable, not because it is biased.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor p.274: “the average standard deviation of the beta-based hedge ratios (1.4) is more than double that of the DTS-based hedge ratios (0.6).”

Annotation. On average, the estimated beta and the DTS ratio agree. Month to month, the estimated beta wanders more than twice as far. A hedge ratio that wanders forces rebalancing, and rebalancing in corporate bonds costs real bid–ask (Chapter 18). The general principle, which reappears in every shrinkage estimator in this book: when a structural model gives you an unbiased, low-variance answer, an unrestricted regression has to beat it out of sample, not in sample. For the 2026 desk the practical blend is to start from \(\text{DTS}_i/\text{DTS}_M\) and shrink a rolling regression beta toward it, with the shrinkage weight set by out-of-sample hedge error. The DTS ratio is the prior. The data have to earn the deviation.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Man_2022 p.15: “We therefore adjust our statistical factor risk model (SFRM) with Duration Times Spread (DTS) in order to take into account the various issues referenced above.”

Annotation. This is how DTS travels into a modern risk stack. Divide each bond’s excess return by its DTS, estimate the covariance or principal components on the scaled returns, and multiply back. Without the scaling, a statistical factor model spends its first principal component discovering that high-spread bonds are volatile, which you already knew. With it, the components describe how bonds co-move rather than how much. Man’s motivation (p.13) is that bond betas are “less concentrated around the mean than for equities,” so a model that assumes equity-like beta dispersion mis-sizes everything. ROBO’s version of the instruction is short. DTS-scale before any covariance estimate; never estimate a covariance on raw excess returns of bonds whose spreads differ by more than a factor of two.

Ways This Blows Up. (1) Wrong duration. DTS uses spread duration. For a floating-rate loan, rate duration is near zero but spread duration is roughly the time to maturity or the expected refinancing date. Use \(D^{\text{mod}}\) and your loan book shows no credit risk. (2) Negative or tiny OAS. Some very short or very high-quality bonds print negative OAS, which makes DTS negative and relative spread changes explode. Guard with assert oas > 0 before computing \(\Delta s/s\), and fall back to absolute changes with a warning. (3) A regime-dependent slope. \(\kappa\) is not a constant of nature. It rises sharply in crises, and the proportionality itself bends in the CCC tier (Trend Watch above). DTS makes betas comparable across bonds at a point in time. It does not make volatility forecastable across regimes.

Chapter 10: Trend-Following & Time-Series Momentum in Credit

10.0 Cold Open: The Model Has No Amygdala

At 4:02 p.m. on Thursday, 15 October 2026, the desk’s trend book did something it had not done since the spring: it bought protection on CDX HY. The position was not large, but it was large enough that Ines walked over holding her coffee the way she holds a chip she has not yet decided to bet.

“Theo. Why are we long protection? Is the model panicking?”

Theo had been on the desk three weeks, and he had learned to answer a question about a model with a chart before an opinion. “High yield has widened about fifty-five basis points in three weeks. ICE BofA HY OAS was 2.68% on September 22 and it’s 3.23% today. The fast sleeve crossed.”

“The model cannot panic,” Kaz said without looking up. “It has no amygdala. It has a 60-day EWMA.”

“A 60-day EWMA is what an amygdala looks like when a quant writes the spec,” Ines said.

Mags spoke from the end of the row without turning her chair. “It looks like April of last year: a hundred and nineteen basis points in three sessions, and all of it back inside six weeks. It also looks like the summer of 2007, and it looks like nothing at all.” Now she turned. “Back in my day we had trend-following in credit. It was called ‘Sal stopped picking up the phone.’ When your dealer stopped returning calls, you sold whatever you could and asked questions at Christmas.”

“So which one is it?” Theo asked.

“That’s the hand,” Ines said. “What’s the pot, what are the odds, and who at this table knows more than you?”

Theo looked at the position. In his old job a bond at 60 always had momentum, toward a process. It was never heading toward 40 or toward 80, but toward a lender call, a cleansing announcement, a filing, or a deal. Restructuring bankers watch prices move all day, and they never believe the move is the information. Now he sat on a desk with a robot that believed nothing else.

The rest of the chapter answers the question on Theo’s screen: when is a move in credit spreads information about the next move in credit spreads, and how much should you bet on it?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to: build a time-series momentum (TSMOM) signal on credit excess returns without the sign, roll, and quoting errors that break most first attempts; show that volatility targeting in credit is DTS scaling under another name, and explain why that makes trend followers into forced sellers; combine trend with carry and value in a single forecast whose coefficients you estimate, without joining either tribe; use equity returns as a leading credit trend signal and test whether the lead is real or an artifact of stale bond marks; explain trend’s crisis convexity, and its V-shaped failures, from the shape of the payoff; and hand ROBO a specification it can implement without inventing a decade of whipsaw.

10.1 What a Trend Is, in Credit

Start with the instinct the reader already has. Every RSSG banker has run a trend strategy without calling it one. When a client’s bonds fell five points on a weak quarter, the question in the room was never “is this bond cheap?” It was “who is selling, and are they done?” A stop-loss is a trend rule. So is an issuer DTS cap, a “reduce on downgrade” policy, and a risk committee that meets after a bad month. The systematic desk takes that reflex, writes it down, gives it units, and asks the uncomfortable question the committee never asks: does it make money, net of the times it sold the low?

Two words get used interchangeably on credit desks and should not be.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Paleologo_Advanced_Portfolio_Management p.74: ““Momentum” has a different meaning from trend-following, because it is based on relative performance, whereas the latter is based on absolute performance.”

Annotation. This is the one distinction to get right before any code is written. Cross-sectional momentum, which is Chapter 9’s subject, ranks bonds against each other: it buys the issuers that beat the index and sells the ones that lagged, and it can be fully long-short and market-neutral. Time-series momentum, or trend, compares each instrument only with its own past: if CDX HY’s excess return over the last twelve months was positive, you are long risk, whatever happened to anything else. The two have different risk. A cross-sectional book in a 2008-style sell-off can be long the bonds that fell least and still lose money in a short squeeze. A trend book in the same sell-off ends up short the whole market, which is the point and also the danger. Credit makes the distinction sharper than equities do, for two reasons. The cross-section is a few hundred illiquid issuers with stale prints, so cross-sectional momentum lives in cash bonds and their cost structure. The time series can be traded in a handful of liquid indices, so trend lives mostly in CDX and iTraxx. They are different trades in different instruments with different P&L drivers. A 2026 desk keeps them in separate risk buckets and separate reports, and it does not let a good year in one excuse a bad year in the other.

10.1.1 The instruments, and why index CDS is the futures-like leg

Trend-following was born in futures because futures are cheap to trade, cheap to short, standardized, and continuously quoted. Credit has exactly one instrument family that passes all four tests:

Instrument Names Fixed coupon Quoted as Role for trend
CDX.NA.IG 125 100 bp spread Core US IG trend leg
CDX.NA.HY 100 500 bp price Core US HY trend leg
iTraxx Europe (Main) 125 100 bp spread European IG
iTraxx Crossover 75 500 bp spread European HY
Cash index excess return (ICE BofA, Bloomberg) thousands of bonds n/a OAS, excess return Research and benchmarking, not trading
HYG / LQD and peers ETF baskets n/a price Tradable cash proxy, with an ETF basis
Cboe iBoxx futures (IBHY, IBIG); CME credit futures index n/a price Listed route for futures-only CTAs

The on-the-run index CDS is unfunded (no cash changes hands beyond the upfront), standardized (fixed coupons, quarterly IMM payment dates, a new series every 20 March and 20 September), cleared, and quoted by dealers all day. It is born an excess return: there is no Treasury leg to hedge, because selling protection carries no interest-rate duration to first order. Every one of those properties is missing in a cash bond.

Kaz had once heard Ines say “Crossover” on a call and spent twenty minutes drafting what he believed was a cross-default clause. “It’s 75 sub-investment-grade European names, Kaz,” Ines told him. “The only thing it crosses is your P&L in March.”

Sign conventions, which cause more bugs than any model choice. Spread up means price down. “Long risk” means you sold protection and are long credit. Throughout the chapter a weight \(w>0\) is long risk and \(w<0\) is long protection. CDX HY and the Crossover’s price-quoted cousins move the opposite way to their spreads. ROBO will happily build a strategy that is long when spreads tighten and also long when the price rises, if both columns are named level. Name them spread_dec and price_pts.

10.1.2 Trend on returns, not on spread levels: the carry hurdle

The first derivation is short, and it reverses a desk intuition. Let \(s_t\) be the spread in decimal, \(D^{\text{spr}}\) the spread duration, and \(\Delta t\) the accrual year fraction (ACT/360 for CDS premium). To first order, the excess return of a long-risk position over one period is

\[ r^{ex}_{t+1} \approx s_t\,\Delta t - D^{\text{spr}}\,\Delta s_{t+1}. \]

TSMOM signals on the trailing cumulative excess return over \(h\) periods, which we write \(M^{(h)}_t\) (we use \(M\) because \(S\) is already taken by survival probability and the mid):

\[ M^{(h)}_t = \sum_{k=0}^{h-1} r^{ex}_{t-k} \approx \underbrace{\bar s\, h\,\Delta t}_{\text{carry earned}} - \underbrace{D^{\text{spr}}\,(s_t - s_{t-h})}_{\text{MTM}} , \]

where \(\bar s\) is the average spread over the window. The signal turns short only when \(M^{(h)}_t<0\), that is, when

\[ s_t - s_{t-h} > \frac{\bar s\,h\,\Delta t}{D^{\text{spr}}} \equiv \Delta s^{*}_h . \]

This is the carry hurdle. For high yield at \(\bar s = 4.5\%\) with \(D^{\text{spr}} = 4\) and a 12-month window (\(h\,\Delta t = 1\)), \(\Delta s^*_{12} = 0.045/4 = 112.5\) bp (illustrative). HY spreads must widen by more than about 110 bp over a year before a return-based 12-month trend follower goes short. A spread chart that “looks like it’s trending wider” by 60 bp is, on a return basis, a modest uptrend, because the carry paid for the widening. For IG at 1.0% spread and \(D^{\text{spr}}=7\), the hurdle is about 14 bp. That asymmetry matters: the same rule is quick to turn short in IG, where carry is small relative to duration, and slow in HY, where carry is large relative to duration.

Two consequences follow. First, a trend rule built on the 12-month change in OAS is a different strategy from one built on 12-month returns, and the difference is the carry hurdle. Write the one you mean in the spec. Second, high carry makes a trend follower structurally long credit in normal times, which is why, as §10.6 shows, much of credit trend’s return is a credit beta that changes its mind.

Trend Watch: The index CDS market becomes the trend follower’s venue, 2021–2026. What changed: index CDS activity reached records while single-name activity stalled. ISDA’s research note of 29 July 2026 puts total CDS trading at $41.8tn in 2025, against a prior peak of $38.7tn in 2022 and $31.4tn in 2023. Index products were 93.3% of that, a record $39.0tn ($36.4tn in 2022, $28.1tn in 2023), while single-name activity peaked at $3.3tn in 2023 and fell to $2.8tn in 2025. CDX.NA.IG was 43.4% of 2025 index activity, iTraxx Europe 32.4%, CDX.NA.HY 10.4%, and iTraxx Crossover 7.7%. CDX.NA.IG prints 500–900 trades a day, with more than 900 in Q2 2025. In stress the venue gets busier: index activity in Q1 2020 ran 78.1% above its trailing average, and in Q2 2025 it ran 20.9% above while single-name activity fell 20.7%. H1 2026 activity was $27.4tn, up 27.8% year on year (ISDA, CDS Market Dynamics: Five Years of Activity and a Record 2025). Clearing and electronic execution are close to universal: more than 99% of the three benchmark indices cleared, and SEF share was 96.5–98.0% in H1 2025 (ISDA SwapsInfo H1 2025). Clarus reports cleared USD CDX of $3.94tn in March 2026, up 46% year on year. The listed route: Cboe iBoxx credit futures block trades topped $1bn a month for a second month in August 2026, and IBIG block activity overtook IBHY’s for the first time (The DESK, 16 October 2026). What it means for the desk: the instrument trend needs, cheap two-way risk in size during a sell-off, now exists in credit at index level. It does not exist at single-name level, where activity is shrinking. Credit trend is an index strategy, and §10.9 explains why single-name trend has to be a different engine.

10.2 The TSMOM Engine, Adapted

10.2.1 The Moskowitz–Ooi–Pedersen template

Moskowitz, Ooi, and Pedersen (2012), Time Series Momentum, define the strategy the whole industry now benchmarks against. In 58 liquid futures (equity indices, currencies, commodities, and sovereign bonds), the past 12-month excess return predicts the next month’s return, persistence lasts one to twelve months and then partially reverses, and a diversified portfolio “performs best during extreme markets.” Their sample contains no credit instruments. Everything in this chapter is therefore an out-of-sample transplant, and the transplant has rejection risks.

For instrument \(i\) with excess return \(r^{ex}_{i,t}\), the template is

\[ \text{sig}^{(h)}_{i,t} = \operatorname{sign}\!\big(M^{(h)}_{i,t}\big), \qquad w_{i,t} = \frac{\sigma_{\text{tgt}}}{\hat\sigma_{i,t}}\;\text{sig}^{(h)}_{i,t}, \qquad r^{\text{TSMOM}}_{t+1} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_{i,t}\, r^{ex}_{i,t+1}. \]

Here \(h\) is the lookback (12 months in the headline result), \(\hat\sigma_{i,t}\) is the ex ante annualized volatility, and \(\sigma_{\text{tgt}}\) is the volatility target per instrument.
