17.2 The Mark as a Filter: Smoothing, Stale Prices and the Illusion of Low Volatility

17.2.1 Desk framing: you are fitting someone else’s model

Before any algebra, the shelf has already diagnosed the disease, in a chapter written about vendor-priced public bonds.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.334: “Essentially, unwary modelers may inadvertently end up fitting someone else’s model. … Many supposedly profitable trading strategies end up being the result of an inadvertent fitting of a matrix model as reflected in matrix prices reported by a data vendor.”

Annotation. Bohn and Stein were warning about evaluated prices for bonds that rarely trade: the vendor fills the gap with a model, and a researcher who backtests on those prices is backtesting the vendor’s model. A BDC net asset value is the same object with higher stakes. Under ASC 820 most private loans are Level 3 assets, valued by the manager’s valuation committee with a third-party firm reviewing a sample. A backtest on CDLI, or on any series built from BDC marks, is therefore a backtest on fifty valuation committees. On a 2026 desk this cuts in both directions. It means any “low volatility, low correlation” result is suspect until it survives the corrections below. It also means the valuation model itself is an object we can estimate, and once estimated it is a predictable process, which is the root of every trade in §17.9.

The shelf even tells you what the disease looks like on a chart.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.335: “a time series plot that shows stair-stepped trends in price … will likely reflect matrix pricing as new levels for the price are bled into the reported price, creating auto-correlation in the data.”

Annotation. Plot a BDC’s NAV per share next to the leveraged loan index over 2022 and you will see exactly this: flat treads and small risers, with the risers arriving a quarter or two after the index moved. “Bled into the reported price” is the economic content of the smoothing kernel we are about to write down. The desk’s first diagnostic chart for any private vehicle is that overlay, and its first statistic is the autocorrelation of the reported returns. The modern twist is that the stair-step now has a public counterpart. Listed BDC shares, BDC bonds and a small number of daily-priced private vehicles move between the steps, so the kernel can be estimated against observed prices instead of guessed.

Kaz looks at the overlay and says the natural thing. “So the NAV is just a lagged index. Let’s regress it on the index with a few lags and call the sum of coefficients the true beta.” Then, after a pause that everyone on the desk recognizes: “And let’s just assume Gaussian.” This time he is mostly right, and §17.2.2 says why. The part he will regret comes in §17.2.4.

17.2.2 Derivation: the Getmansky–Lo–Makarov smoothing model

Notation. In this chapter \(t\) counts quarters, not years; we convert explicitly when comparing with monthly public data. We write returns as \(x\) rather than \(r\), because this book reserves \(r\) for the short rate and \(R\) for recovery. All expectations are under the physical measure \(\mathbb{P}\): there is no liquid hedge for a single private loan, so nothing here is priced under \(\mathbb{Q}\).

Assumptions. Let \(x_t\) be the true, unobservable quarterly excess return on the loan portfolio, covariance-stationary with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), and serially uncorrelated. Let \(F_t\) be the excess return on a public factor (the leveraged loan index, say), also serially uncorrelated, with \(x_t=\beta F_t+\epsilon_t\), where \(\epsilon_t\) is idiosyncratic and independent of \(F\) at all leads and lags. The reported (marked) return is a finite moving average of true returns:

\[ x^{o}_t=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\theta_k\,x_{t-k},\qquad \theta_k\in[0,1],\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{K}\theta_k=1 . \]

Here \(\theta_0\) is the share of today’s true return that shows up in today’s mark, \(\theta_1\) the share that shows up next quarter, and so on. The unit-sum constraint says the marks eventually catch up: nothing is hidden forever, only delayed. (When the constraint fails, with \(\sum_k\theta_k<1\), the marks never catch up, because the collateral was never there. That is the fraud case, and §17.8 returns to it.)

Mean. By linearity, \(\mathbb{E}[x^o_t]=\sum_k\theta_k\,\mathbb{E}[x_{t-k}]=\mu\sum_k\theta_k=\mu\). Smoothing does not change the average return. This is why the CDLI’s 9.3% can be a perfectly good estimate of the mean while being useless for risk.

Variance. Because the \(x_{t-k}\) are uncorrelated,

\[ \operatorname{Var}(x^o_t)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\theta_k^2\,\sigma^2 . \]

Since \(\theta_k\in[0,1]\) and \(\sum_k\theta_k=1\), we have \(\sum_k\theta_k^2\le\big(\max_k\theta_k\big)\sum_k\theta_k\le1\), with equality only when one \(\theta_k\) equals one. Reported volatility is deflated by the factor \(\sqrt{\sum_k\theta_k^2}\), and the deflation is largest when the weights are spread evenly: with \(K+1\) equal weights it is \(1/\sqrt{K+1}\).

Autocorrelation. For lag \(j\ge1\),

\[ \operatorname{Cov}(x^o_t,x^o_{t-j})=\sum_{k}\sum_{l}\theta_k\theta_l\operatorname{Cov}(x_{t-k},x_{t-j-l}) . \]

The covariance inside the sum is \(\sigma^2\) when \(k=j+l\) and zero otherwise, so only the terms \(k=l+j\) survive:

\[ \operatorname{Cov}(x^o_t,x^o_{t-j})=\sigma^2\sum_{l=0}^{K-j}\theta_l\,\theta_{l+j}, \qquad \rho^{o}_j=\frac{\sum_{l=0}^{K-j}\theta_l\,\theta_{l+j}}{\sum_{k=0}^{K}\theta_k^2}\;\ge 0 . \]

Every autocorrelation of the reported series is non-negative, and it is zero beyond lag \(K\). Positive autocorrelation in a NAV series is therefore mechanical: it would appear even if the true returns were pure noise. Call it what it is. NAV “momentum” in a smoothed series is a property of the measurement, not of information, and a strategy that trades it inside the private wrapper is trading the valuation calendar.

Sharpe ratio. With \(\text{SR}=\mu/\sigma\) the true Sharpe ratio,

\[ \text{SR}^{o}=\frac{\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{\sum_k\theta_k^2}}=\frac{\text{SR}}{\sqrt{\sum_k\theta_k^2}}\;\ge\;\text{SR}. \]

Beta and correlation to public credit. Because \(F\) is serially uncorrelated and independent of \(\epsilon\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(x_{t-k},F_t)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(F)\) when \(k=0\) and zero otherwise. So

\[ \beta^{o}_{0}\equiv\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x^o_t,F_t)}{\operatorname{Var}(F_t)}=\theta_0\,\beta, \qquad \operatorname{Corr}(x^o_t,F_t)=\frac{\theta_0}{\sqrt{\sum_k\theta_k^2}}\,\operatorname{Corr}(x_t,F_t). \]

The contemporaneous beta to public credit is attenuated by exactly \(\theta_0\). The rest of the beta has not disappeared; it is parked at lags \(1,\dots,K\), where \(\operatorname{Cov}(x^o_t,F_{t-k})=\theta_k\beta\operatorname{Var}(F)\). Correlation is attenuated by the smaller factor \(\theta_0/\sqrt{\sum_k\theta_k^2}\), because the denominator’s volatility was deflated too.

Worked check. Take \(\theta=(0.5,0.3,0.2)\). Then \(\sum_k\theta_k^2=0.25+0.09+0.04=0.38\), so reported volatility is \(\sqrt{0.38}=0.616\) of true volatility and the reported Sharpe ratio is inflated by \(1/0.616=1.62\). The autocorrelations are \(\rho^o_1=(0.5\cdot0.3+0.3\cdot0.2)/0.38=0.21/0.38=0.553\) and \(\rho^o_2=(0.5\cdot0.2)/0.38=0.263\). The contemporaneous beta is half the true beta, and the contemporaneous correlation is \(0.5/0.616=0.81\) of the true one.

Those are not exotic numbers. A two-quarter lag in the marks, which any valuation committee can produce without anyone doing anything wrong, turns an asset with the risk of a single-B loan portfolio into one that reports 62% of the volatility, half the beta and 1.6 times the Sharpe ratio. That is how a vendor field ends up saying “N/A”: the honest answer would have been “about 1.6 times what you see, and correlated with things you already own, a quarter later.”

Desk Myth vs. Desk Reality. Myth: Private credit has low volatility and low correlation with public credit, so it diversifies a high-yield book. Reality: It has low measured volatility because \(\sum_k\theta_k^2<1\), and low contemporaneous correlation because \(\theta_0<1\). Sum the lagged betas and the correlation comes back. Cliff Asness has made the uncomfortable version of the point: “What if investors will actually pay a higher price and accept a lower expected return for very illiquid assets?” and “Attractive smoothness of returns may not come for free” (Asness, “The Illiquidity Discount?”, AQR, December 19, 2019). If investors value not seeing the volatility, the smoothing is a product feature, and somebody is paying for it. The desk’s job is to find out who, and to be on the other side when the feature is withdrawn.

17.2.3 Recovering the beta: Dimson sums and the public-leads-private test

Kaz’s instinct is the Dimson (1979) and Scholes–Williams (1977) correction for nonsynchronous trading, invented for thinly traded stocks and exactly right here. Regress reported returns on the current and \(K\) lagged factor returns:

\[ x^o_t=\alpha+\sum_{k=0}^{K}b_k\,F_{t-k}+u_t,\qquad \hat\beta^{\text{agg}}=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\hat b_k . \]

Under the model, \(x^o_t=\sum_k\theta_k(\beta F_{t-k}+\epsilon_{t-k})\), so the population coefficients are \(b_k=\theta_k\beta\), the residual \(u_t=\sum_k\theta_k\epsilon_{t-k}\) is uncorrelated with every regressor, and

\[ \sum_{k=0}^{K}b_k=\beta\sum_{k=0}^{K}\theta_k=\beta,\qquad \hat\theta_k=\frac{\hat b_k}{\sum_l\hat b_l}. \]

One regression gives you both the true beta and an estimate of the kernel. It is also the public-leads-private test: \(b_1,b_2>0\) with respectable \(t\)-statistics is the lead–lag, and its tradable restatement is the one-quarter-ahead forecast

\[ \mathbb{E}_t\big[x^o_{t+1}\big]=\alpha+\sum_{k=1}^{K}b_k\,F_{t+1-k}, \]

which is known at \(t\) because it uses only \(F_t,F_{t-1},\dots\). The next NAV print is partly already in the public data. A desk that knows the index fell 3% this quarter and that \(b_1\approx0.3\) knows the next mark will carry about \(0.9\%\) of that fall, before the valuation committee meets. The residual \(u_t\) is serially correlated (it is an MA(\(K\)) in \(\epsilon\)), so use HAC standard errors with at least \(K\) lags, or the \(t\)-statistics will flatter you too.

Note what the forecast does not say. It does not say you can buy the NAV low and sell it high, because inside a non-traded fund you transact at the smoothed NAV in both directions, subject to a cap. It says that any public instrument whose price is tied to that NAV (a listed BDC’s equity, its bonds, a fund-of-BDCs ETF) will be repriced by a number you can forecast. §17.9 builds the book on that.

17.2.4 Unsmoothing, and why you should do less of it than you want to

The other direction is to invert the filter and recover \(x_t\) from \(x^o_t\). The workhorse is Geltner’s (1991, 1993) appraisal-smoothing model from real estate, which is the GLM model with geometric weights, \(\theta_k=(1-\theta)\theta^k\) for \(k=0,1,2,\dots\) and \(0\le\theta<1\). Those weights sum to one, and the model collapses to a recursion:

\[ x^o_t=(1-\theta)\,x_t+\theta\,x^o_{t-1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat x_t=\frac{x^o_t-\theta\,x^o_{t-1}}{1-\theta}. \]

For the geometric kernel, \(\sum_k\theta_k^2=(1-\theta)^2\sum_k\theta^{2k}=(1-\theta)/(1+\theta)\) and \(\rho^o_j=\theta^j\), so \(\theta\) is just the first-order autocorrelation of reported returns. The variance of the unsmoothed series follows from \(\operatorname{Var}(a-\theta b)=\operatorname{Var}(a)+\theta^2\operatorname{Var}(b)-2\theta\operatorname{Cov}(a,b)\):

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\hat x_t)=\frac{(1+\theta^2)\operatorname{Var}(x^o_t)-2\theta\operatorname{Cov}(x^o_t,x^o_{t-1})}{(1-\theta)^2}. \]

Now the regret. Real marks contain measurement noise \(\eta_t\) (rounding, one-off valuation calls, the quarter a third-party valuer was replaced), so we observe \(x^o_t+\eta_t\). The inversion is linear, so the noise passes through as

\[ \hat x_t-x_t=\frac{\eta_t-\theta\,\eta_{t-1}}{1-\theta},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat x_t-x_t)=\frac{1+\theta^2}{(1-\theta)^2}\,\sigma_\eta^2 . \]

At \(\theta=0.6\) the noise variance is amplified \(8.5\times\); at \(\theta=0.7\), \(16.6\times\); at \(\theta=0.9\), \(181\times\). Unsmoothing a heavily smoothed series does not reveal the truth. It reveals the noise, enlarged. This is the place Kaz’s Gaussian assumption bites: valuation noise is not Gaussian, it is lumpy (a single large write-down on a concentrated position), and the inversion turns a lump into a spike followed by an echo of the opposite sign.

Three more error-prone spots, each of which has embarrassed someone.

  1. Small samples. Twenty to forty quarterly observations are all most vehicles have. With \(n=30\) and \(\rho_1=0.5\), the standard error of \(\hat\rho_1\) is about \(\sqrt{(1-\rho_1^2)/n}=0.16\), so a 90% interval for \(\theta\) runs from roughly 0.24 to 0.76. Report intervals, not points.
  2. Common smoothing. Couts, Gonçalves and Rossi (“Unsmoothing Returns of Illiquid Funds,” Review of Financial Studies 37(7), 2024) show that funds holding similar assets share a common source of spurious autocorrelation, so unsmoothing fund by fund leaves correlated lag in the residuals and understates systematic risk. Estimate \(\theta\) on a cross-holder panel, which for BDCs is natural: many hold the same facilities.
  3. Frequency. A quarterly \(\rho_1\) is not comparable with a monthly one. If you are benchmarking against the shelf’s monthly autocorrelation buckets for public bonds, aggregate first.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Dynkin_Systematic_Investing_in_Credit p.623: “if corporate bond prices are only updated infrequently and are subject to ‘stale’ pricing, their returns are likely to be positively correlated as new information slowly gets priced in.”

Annotation. Dynkin and coauthors use the trailing autocorrelation of excess returns as a liquidity measure for public corporate bonds, sorting bonds into low, middle and high autocorrelation buckets. Taken to its limit, a private loan is the most illiquid bucket with the volume column deleted: its reported returns are positively autocorrelated by construction, because the only “trades” are valuation-committee decisions. The departure for a 2026 desk is the direction of inference. For public bonds the autocorrelation measures illiquidity; for a private vehicle, the autocorrelation is the smoothing kernel, and once estimated it becomes an input to forecasting the next mark rather than a property to diversify away.

Specification for AI Implementation

The Spec You Hand the Robot (vague version). “ROBO, estimate the volatility of private credit.” ROBO computes the standard deviation of quarterly CDLI returns, annualizes it to 2.1% (illustrative), compares it with the Treasury index, and files private credit as safer than Treasuries. It implemented exactly what was asked. The precise version follows.

Engine. mark_gap, the Mark-Gap Monitor. Pure functions, numpy and pandas only, built in four cumulative blocks across this chapter (smoothing in §17.2, marks in §17.3, flows in §17.4, runs in §17.6). Every block ends with seeded sanity checks.

Data schemas (pandas DataFrames; one row per key; money in USD; shares and rates as decimals, never percent strings; dates are quarter-end datetime64):

table key columns (dtype) source
bdc_quarterly (bdc_id, qdate) nav_ps float; price float or NaN (non-traded); net_debt_to_equity float; w_na_cost, w_na_fv float; fv_total, cost_total float; pik_income, total_income float; first_lien_pct float; n_companies int; restated bool 10-Q/10-K, earnings releases
soi (bdc_id, qdate, facility_id) borrower str; ice_id str or None; lien in {1, 2, “unsecured”, “equity”}; spread_bp float; pik_flag bool; par, cost, fv float; maturity date; industry str schedules of investments (Chapter 25 parser)
redemptions (fund_id, qdate) request_pct float; cap_pct float (default 0.05); fill_pct float; nav_total float; mode in {“tender”, “roc_distribution”, “gated”} 8-K, SC TO-I, N-23c-3
public_index qdate ll_excess_ret float (quarterly; state it); hy_excess_ret float; cdx_fin_spread_bp float vendor; Appendix B

Edge cases the robot must handle. Non-calendar fiscal quarters (align to the nearest calendar quarter end and flag it). Restated NAVs (keep both vintages; never overwrite). price NaN for non-traded vehicles (P/NAV is undefined; never fill it with 1.0). w_na_cost == 0 (return NaN, not infinity). The same facility held by several BDCs (join on ice_id when present, otherwise on fuzzy borrower name plus maturity plus spread). Percentages reported as strings such as “2.8%”. The unit-sum constraint on \(\theta\) (clip to \([0,1]\), renormalize, and report whether the clip bound).

Numerical guards. Require at least \(10(K+1)\) observations for a Dimson regression with \(K\) lags. Solve least squares by SVD (lstsq), not normal equations, because lagged factor returns are nearly collinear in calm regimes. Refuse to unsmooth with \(\theta\ge0.9\) (noise amplification above \(100\times\)).

# ---- Chapter 17 reference engine (mark_gap), block 1: the mark as a filter ----
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def simulate_smoothed(n, theta, beta=1.0, sigma_f=0.04, sigma_e=0.02, seed=17):
    """True quarterly excess return x_t = beta*F_t + e_t; reported x_obs_t = sum_k theta_k x_{t-k}.
    Returns (F, x_true, x_obs). The first K entries of x_obs are NaN (kernel not yet full)."""
    theta = np.asarray(theta, dtype=float)
    if theta.ndim != 1 or theta.size == 0 or np.any(theta < 0) or theta.sum() <= 0:
        raise ValueError("theta must be a non-empty vector of non-negative weights")
    theta = theta / theta.sum()                      # unit sum: marks eventually catch up
    K = theta.size - 1
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    F = rng.normal(0.0, sigma_f, n)
    x_true = beta * F + rng.normal(0.0, sigma_e, n)
    x_obs = np.full(n, np.nan)
    for t in range(K, n):
        x_obs[t] = float(np.dot(theta, x_true[t - K:t + 1][::-1]))   # theta_0 multiplies today
    return F, x_true, x_obs


def glm_moments(theta):
    """Closed-form GLM identities for a unit-sum kernel."""
    th = np.asarray(theta, dtype=float)
    th = th / th.sum()
    ss = float(np.dot(th, th))
    K = th.size - 1
    rho = np.array([np.dot(th[:-j], th[j:]) / ss for j in range(1, K + 1)])
    return {"var_ratio": ss, "rho": rho, "sharpe_inflation": 1.0 / np.sqrt(ss), "beta0_ratio": float(th[0])}


def autocorr(x, j):
    """Lag-j sample autocorrelation, ignoring NaNs at the start of the series."""
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    x = x[~np.isnan(x)]
    x = x - x.mean()
    return float(np.dot(x[j:], x[:-j]) / np.dot(x, x))


def dimson_beta(x_obs, F, K):
    """Regress reported returns on current and K lagged factor returns. Returns (b_0..b_K, sum b_k)."""
    x_obs = np.asarray(x_obs, dtype=float)
    F = np.asarray(F, dtype=float)
    T = x_obs.size
    if T - K < 10 * (K + 1):
        raise ValueError("too few observations for K lags")
    rows, y = [], []
    for t in range(K, T):
        if np.isnan(x_obs[t]):
            continue
        rows.append([1.0] + [F[t - k] for k in range(K + 1)])
        y.append(x_obs[t])
    X, y = np.asarray(rows), np.asarray(y)
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
    return coef[1:], float(coef[1:].sum())


def kernel_from_dimson(b):
    """theta_hat_k = b_k / sum(b), clipped to [0, 1] and renormalised. Returns (theta_hat, clip_bound)."""
    b = np.asarray(b, dtype=float)
    s = b.sum()
    if abs(s) < 1e-12:
        raise ValueError("aggregate beta is ~0: the kernel is not identified")
    th = b / s
    clipped = bool(np.any(th < 0.0) or np.any(th > 1.0))
    th = np.clip(th, 0.0, 1.0)
    return th / th.sum(), clipped


def unsmooth_ar1(x_obs, theta):
    """Geltner inversion x_hat_t = (x_obs_t - theta x_obs_{t-1}) / (1 - theta)."""
    if not 0.0 <= theta < 0.9:
        raise ValueError("theta outside [0, 0.9): noise amplification too large")
    x = np.asarray(x_obs, dtype=float)
    out = np.full_like(x, np.nan)
    out[1:] = (x[1:] - theta * x[:-1]) / (1.0 - theta)
    return out


# --- sanity checks, block 1 ---
theta = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)
mom = glm_moments(theta)
assert abs(mom["var_ratio"] - 0.38) < 1e-12
assert np.allclose(mom["rho"], [0.21 / 0.38, 0.10 / 0.38])
assert abs(mom["sharpe_inflation"] - 1.0 / np.sqrt(0.38)) < 1e-12

F, x_true, x_obs = simulate_smoothed(20_000, theta)
var_ratio = np.nanvar(x_obs) / np.var(x_true)
assert abs(var_ratio - 0.38) < 0.02, var_ratio                      # variance deflation
assert abs(autocorr(x_obs, 1) - mom["rho"][0]) < 0.03                 # mechanical momentum, lag 1
assert abs(autocorr(x_obs, 2) - mom["rho"][1]) < 0.03                 # lag 2
b0, agg0 = dimson_beta(x_obs, F, 0)
bK, aggK = dimson_beta(x_obs, F, 2)
assert abs(agg0 - 0.5) < 0.05, agg0                                   # contemporaneous beta = theta_0 * beta
assert abs(aggK - 1.0) < 0.05, aggK                                   # Dimson sum recovers beta
theta_hat, clip_bound = kernel_from_dimson(bK)
assert np.allclose(theta_hat, theta, atol=0.05) and not clip_bound

# Geltner: exact inversion of AR(1) smoothing, then noise amplification (1 + th^2) / (1 - th)^2
th1 = 0.6
x_ar = np.empty_like(x_true)
x_ar[0] = (1.0 - th1) * x_true[0]
for t in range(1, x_true.size):
    x_ar[t] = (1.0 - th1) * x_true[t] + th1 * x_ar[t - 1]
assert np.allclose(unsmooth_ar1(x_ar, th1)[1:], x_true[1:])
eta = np.random.default_rng(171).normal(0.0, 0.001, x_ar.size)
amp = np.var(unsmooth_ar1(x_ar + eta, th1)[1:] - x_true[1:]) / 0.001 ** 2
amp_theory = (1.0 + th1 ** 2) / (1.0 - th1) ** 2                     # = 8.5
assert abs(amp / amp_theory - 1.0) < 0.05, amp
print("block 1 ok: var ratio %.3f, rho1 %.3f, Dimson sum %.3f, noise amp %.1f"
      % (var_ratio, autocorr(x_obs, 1), aggK, amp))

Why each check is there. The variance ratio and the two autocorrelations are the closed-form identities; if the simulation disagrees, the kernel’s time index is reversed (the most common bug: theta[0] multiplying the oldest return). The two Dimson runs show attenuation (\(\theta_0\beta\)) and recovery (\(\sum_k b_k\to\beta\)) in one picture. The Geltner pair shows that the inversion is exact on clean data and that it amplifies noise by the predicted factor on dirty data.

Second-stage spec (text only). estimate_theta_panel(nav_returns_by_fund, F, K) fits a shared MA(\(K\)) kernel across funds by pooled OLS of \(x^o_{i,t}\) on \(F_{t-k}\) with fund fixed effects, following the Couts–Gonçalves–Rossi logic. It returns \(\hat\theta_k=\hat b_k/\sum_l\hat b_l\) with a block bootstrap over quarters (block length 4), and it refuses to report a point estimate when the 90% interval for \(\theta_0\) is wider than 0.4. ROBO will otherwise report \(\hat\theta_0=0.47\) to three decimals from 22 observations, and someone will put it in a pitch book.

Ways This Blows Up. (1) The calm-regime collinearity trap. In a quiet stretch, \(F_t\), \(F_{t-1}\) and \(F_{t-2}\) are tiny and nearly collinear, the individual \(\hat b_k\) swing wildly, and only their sum is stable; never trade a single lag coefficient. (2) Breaks in the kernel. Valuation policy changes when a new third-party valuer is hired or an auditor pushes back, and \(\theta\) shifts with it. A kernel fitted on 2015–2021 will understate the speed of marks after an episode like 2026, when listed prices forced faster recognition. (3) Asymmetric smoothing. Managers mark gains and losses at different speeds (write-downs tend to arrive in lumps, recoveries gradually). A symmetric MA kernel then misreads a single large write-down as low \(\theta\). Fit up-quarters and down-quarters separately before believing either.

17.3 Marking the Unmarked: BDC P/NAV, Implied Markdowns and the Non-Accrual Gap

17.3.1 Desk framing: a listed CLO with the manager holding the pen

The BDC is the one place where a private loan book has a public price attached. Read it as Theo would read a capital structure. At the top sits a secured revolver from banks; bank loans are about 40% of BDC debt, up from about 20% a decade earlier, and the ten largest banks provide 82% of BDC commitments (Haque and Wang, FEDS Note, August 7, 2026). Below that sit unsecured notes, typically investment-grade rated and issued in $300–$400mm clips. At the bottom sits equity, listed for a public BDC and redeemable at NAV, subject to a cap, for a non-traded one. Since the 2018 change that let BDCs run 2:1 debt to equity, sector leverage has risen from about 0.4x to above 1x (Avalos, Doerr and Pinter, BIS Quarterly Review, March 2025).

Two features make it different from the CLOs of Chapter 21. First, the manager both selects and marks the collateral, and the NAV is the sum of those marks. Second, the equity pays a management fee on gross assets and an incentive fee on income. That fee stream is a claim senior to the shareholder in every state of the world, so even a perfectly marked BDC should trade below NAV unless the manager adds value. The listed equity is therefore a price on three things at once: the loans, the fees, and the market’s opinion of the marks. The trick is to separate them.

Kaz, reading the latest 10-Q, wants to know whether a “tender offer” is an offer made gently. In a sense it is: it is the non-traded BDC’s quarterly offer to buy back up to 5% of its shares at NAV, made politely, and suspended without much ceremony when something more important comes up, such as a merger.

17.3.2 Derivation: from a listed price to an implied asset markdown

Notation. In this section \(P\) is the BDC’s share price (not a bond price), NAV is book equity per share at reported marks, \(A\) is total assets at reported fair value and \(E\) is total NAV. We write leverage as \(\ell=(A-E)/E\), net debt over NAV as the companies report it, rather than \(L\), which this book reserves for loss given default. Then \(A=E(1+\ell)\).

Assumptions. (i) The market values the loan book at \(A(1-m)\), where \(m\ge0\) is the implied markdown as a fraction of reported asset value. (ii) The equity also bears a structural fee drag with present value \(\phi E\) (base and incentive fees capitalized at the equity’s required return, net of any value the manager adds). (iii) The debt is money-good. Then market equity is assets at market, minus debt, minus fees:

\[ P\cdot\text{shares}=A(1-m)-(A-E)-\phi E=E-mA-\phi E . \]

Divide by \(E\) and substitute \(A=E(1+\ell)\):

\[ \frac{P}{\text{NAV}}=(1-\phi)-m(1+\ell) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad m=\frac{(1-\phi)-P/\text{NAV}}{1+\ell}. \]

The factor \(1/(1+\ell)\) is the leverage translation: at \(\ell=1.1\), each point of equity discount maps to only \(0.48\) points of asset markdown. A 20% equity discount is not a claim that the loans are worth 80. It is a claim that they are worth about 90.

Numbers. Blue Owl Capital Corporation (OBDC) bought back about $148mm of its own stock in the fourth quarter of 2025 at “86% of price-to-book value,” with net debt to equity of 1.19x (company release, February 18, 2026). With an illustrative fee drag \(\phi=0.05\), \(m=(0.95-0.86)/2.19=4.1\%\) of assets. Octus reported on April 16, 2026 that BDCs traded “at nearly a 20% discount to net asset value, with certain large names approaching a 50% discount.” At \(P/\text{NAV}=0.80\) and an illustrative \(\ell=1.1\), \(m=(0.95-0.80)/2.1=7.1\%\); at \(0.50\), \(m=(0.95-0.50)/2.1=21.4\%\). The second number is the market saying that a book the manager carries at 98–100 is worth about 78. A widely reported tally put the median listed BDC at about 0.74 times forward NAV at the end of March 2026 (Reuters/LSEG; not independently verified for this edition), which maps to \(m\approx10\%\).

Boundary conditions. If \(P/\text{NAV}>1-\phi\), the formula returns \(m<0\). Floor it at zero and attribute the premium to franchise value: net investment income in excess of the dividend, a lower-cost internal management structure, or a growing fee base. Main Street Capital, an internally managed BDC, has historically traded well above NAV, and nobody believes its loans are worth more than par. If the debt is not money-good, relax assumption (iii): equity becomes a call option on \(A(1-m)\) struck at the debt, worth more than its intrinsic value, so a given price is consistent with a larger \(m\). The money-good formula is then a lower bound on the markdown. That Merton-on-a-CLO extension, and the \(\mathbb{Q}\)-measure link to BDC CDS spreads, belongs to Chapter 23. Do not mix a \(\mathbb{Q}\) spread with this \(\mathbb{P}\) markdown without saying so.

17.3.3 Derivation: the non-accrual gap and the implied carrying value of bad loans

BDCs report non-accrual loans as a share of the portfolio at cost and at fair value. That pair of numbers hides a mark. Let \(w^{C}_{\text{NA}}\) and \(w^{FV}_{\text{NA}}\) be the two shares, and \(C\) and \(FV\) the whole portfolio’s cost and fair value. The non-accrual bucket’s cost is \(w^C_{\text{NA}}C\) and its fair value is \(w^{FV}_{\text{NA}}FV\), so its carrying value as a fraction of cost is

\[ \hat R^{\text{mark}}_{\text{NA}}=\frac{w^{FV}_{\text{NA}}\cdot FV}{w^{C}_{\text{NA}}\cdot C}=\frac{w^{FV}_{\text{NA}}}{w^{C}_{\text{NA}}}\cdot\frac{FV}{C}. \]

The superscript is a warning: this is a mark, not a realized recovery. Compare it with Chapter 14’s realized-recovery distributions, not with the manager’s talking points. Alongside it, track the gap series \(g_t=w^C_{\text{NA},t}-w^{FV}_{\text{NA},t}\), the share of cost sitting in loans that are no longer paying and have been written down. A rising \(g_t\) with a falling \(w^{FV}_{\text{NA},t}\) is the signature of new non-accruals arriving already heavily marked down: the headline (fair-value) number improves while the hole gets deeper.

OBDC’s own releases give a clean four-quarter series (company releases; FV/C of 0.98 is approximate and applied uniformly, so the implied marks are illustrative):

Quarter end NAV/share Non-accrual at cost at FV Gap \(g_t\) \(\hat R^{\text{mark}}_{\text{NA}}\) Net D/E
Sep 30, 2025 $14.89 2.7% 1.3% 1.4pp 0.47 1.22x
Dec 31, 2025 $14.81 2.3% 1.1% 1.2pp 0.47 1.19x
Mar 31, 2026 $14.41 2.0% 1.0% 1.0pp 0.49 1.13x
Jun 30, 2026 $14.26 2.8% 0.8% 2.0pp 0.28 1.11x

In the second quarter of 2026 the fair-value non-accrual rate fell to its lowest level in the series while the cost rate jumped, and the implied carrying value of the bad bucket fell from about 49 cents to about 28. On the same day the industry was quoting 70-cent recoveries, Octus estimated private-credit restructuring recoveries at “approximately 50 cents on the dollar,” “well below the 70% previously cited by many managers” (Octus, April 16, 2026). The mark was moving toward the evidence; it just moved at the speed of the kernel.

Octus also put a number on the cross-holder problem. Adjusting for loans held by several BDCs raised sector non-accruals from 1.45% to 2.18% of cost, and it found “pricing gaps of nearly 40 points as measured by fair value divided by par” in widely held stressed loans. Two managers, one loan, forty points apart. One of them is wrong, and the listed price of each BDC is a vote on which.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.208: “all bonds comprising the Corporate and High Yield indexes with a sequence of five or more unchanged quotes in any month are excluded from the eligible population of bonds for that month.”

Annotation. For public index research, a run of unchanged quotes means the price is stale and the observation is discarded. On a schedule of investments the same rule becomes a signal: a facility marked at the same fair value over par for five consecutive quarters, while its public comparables and its co-holders’ marks moved, is a mark that has not been looked at. Those are the candidates for mark convergence, and they cluster in vehicles whose other marks are also slow. The desk departs from Ben Dor in what it does with the flag. It does not drop the observation; it adds it to the vehicle’s stale-mark share, a per-BDC feature in the §17.9 relative-value model.

Case Study: OBDC and OBDC II, November 2025 to August 2026: Same Loans, Three Prices

This is the natural experiment of the cycle, and every number below is from Blue Owl’s own releases unless marked.

The setup (November 5, 2025). Blue Owl proposed to merge OBDC II, a non-traded BDC, into OBDC, its listed sibling. The portfolios overlapped by about 98%. The exchange was NAV for NAV if OBDC traded at or below NAV, which meant OBDC II holders, who could tender at NAV, would receive listed shares worth less than NAV at market. OBDC II suspended its tender offers pending the close. Same loans, same manager, same marks: the only thing the merger changed was the wrapper, and the wrapper was worth a discount.

The unwind (November 19, 2025). Fourteen days later the merger was terminated: “we are no longer pursuing the merger at this point given current market conditions.” OBDC II would reinstate tenders in the first quarter of 2026, subject to board approval; the release noted that “every quarterly tender since inception has been fully satisfied.” It did not mention the share price or the exchange ratio, which were the whole story.

Three prices in one quarter (February 18, 2026). OBDC reported fourth-quarter NAV of $14.81 and buybacks at 86% of book. That is the first price: the listed market, at 0.86 of the marks. The marks themselves are the second price, at roughly 1.00 of book by definition. The third price was a transaction. The same day, three Blue Owl BDCs agreed to sell $1.4 billion of partial interests in loans to 128 companies (97% senior secured, average position about $5mm, internet software and services the largest industry at 13%) to four North American pension and insurance investors. “The investments will be sold at fair value, which is equivalent to 99.7% of par value as of February 12, 2026.” OBDC II’s $600mm share, about 34% of its commitments including unfunded ones, funded a return-of-capital distribution of up to $2.35 per share, about 30% of NAV and “about six times” a planned 5% tender. Its board said it would use quarterly return-of-capital distributions instead of tender offers from then on. (Cooperation agreements signed in this chapter: 0. Return-of-capital distributions substituted for tender offers: 1.)

Reading it with the engine. §17.3.2 turns 0.86 into an implied markdown of about 4% of assets. §17.3.3 turns the June 2026 non-accrual pair into a 28-cent carrying value on the bad bucket. And the $1.4 billion print says that good loans clear at par, which is exactly what adverse selection in a partial-interest sale predicts. A seller who needs liquidity sells the slices a pension fund will buy, the buyer chooses what it is willing to own, and the clearing price on the chosen slices says nothing about the ones left behind. Ines would call it showing your best two cards to prove your hand is strong.

How a systematic desk would have traded it. Into the merger announcement: short OBDC against a diversified basket of listed BDCs, on the view that a NAV-for-NAV exchange with OBDC below NAV transferred value away from OBDC II holders, who would resist it, and that resistance would come out of the listed price; cover on termination. Through the first quarter of 2026: long OBDC unsecured notes against short OBDC equity, because deleveraging from 1.22x to 1.11x and asset sales at par are good for bondholders and neutral at best for equity. Throughout: watch the redemption queues of Blue Owl’s other non-traded vehicles as the leading indicator of further sales (§17.6). Ines replays the hand through markouts: the trade that paid was the one that read the merger terms as a statement about the marks.

# ---- block 2: from listed prices and disclosures to implied marks ----
def implied_markdown(p_nav, lev, fee_drag=0.0):
    """m = ((1 - phi) - P/NAV) / (1 + ell), floored at 0. NaN for a non-traded vehicle."""
    if p_nav is None or np.isnan(p_nav):
        return np.nan
    if lev < 0 or not 0.0 <= fee_drag < 1.0:
        raise ValueError("leverage must be >= 0 and fee_drag in [0, 1)")
    return max(((1.0 - fee_drag) - p_nav) / (1.0 + lev), 0.0)


def implied_nonaccrual_mark(w_fv, w_cost, fv_over_cost=1.0):
    """Carrying value of the non-accrual bucket as a fraction of its cost (a mark, not a recovery)."""
    if w_cost <= 0:
        return np.nan
    return (w_fv / w_cost) * fv_over_cost


def cross_holder_dispersion(soi):
    """Per facility held by >= 2 vehicles: number of holders, mean, std and range of fv/par."""
    df = soi.assign(px=soi["fv"] / soi["par"])
    g = df.groupby("facility_id")["px"]
    out = pd.DataFrame({"n_holders": g.size(), "px_mean": g.mean(),
                        "px_std": g.std(ddof=0), "px_range": g.max() - g.min()})
    return out[out["n_holders"] >= 2]


def stale_mark_flag(px_by_quarter, n_unchanged=5, tol=1e-4):
    """True where a facility's mark has been unchanged (within tol) for n_unchanged consecutive quarters."""
    px = np.asarray(px_by_quarter, dtype=float)
    run, flags = 1, []
    for t in range(px.size):
        run = run + 1 if (t > 0 and abs(px[t] - px[t - 1]) <= tol) else 1
        flags.append(run >= n_unchanged)
    return np.array(flags)


obdc = pd.DataFrame({
    "qdate": pd.to_datetime(["2025-09-30", "2025-12-31", "2026-03-31", "2026-06-30"]),
    "nav_ps": [14.89, 14.81, 14.41, 14.26],
    "w_na_cost": [0.027, 0.023, 0.020, 0.028],
    "w_na_fv": [0.013, 0.011, 0.010, 0.008],
    "net_de": [1.22, 1.19, 1.13, 1.11],
}).set_index("qdate")
obdc["gap_pp"] = 100.0 * (obdc["w_na_cost"] - obdc["w_na_fv"])
obdc["na_mark"] = [implied_nonaccrual_mark(f, c, 0.98) for f, c in zip(obdc["w_na_fv"], obdc["w_na_cost"])]

# --- sanity checks, block 2 ---
assert abs(implied_markdown(0.86, 1.19, 0.05) - 0.0411) < 1e-3      # OBDC Q4 2025 buyback print
assert abs(implied_markdown(0.50, 1.10, 0.05) - 0.2143) < 1e-3      # a name near a 50% discount
assert implied_markdown(1.02, 1.0, 0.05) == 0.0                      # premium name: floor, not negative
assert np.isnan(implied_markdown(np.nan, 0.9))                       # non-traded: undefined, never 1.0
assert np.isnan(implied_nonaccrual_mark(0.0, 0.0))
assert abs(obdc["na_mark"].iloc[-1] - 0.28) < 0.005                  # ~28c on the bad bucket, Jun 2026
assert abs(obdc["gap_pp"].iloc[1] - 1.2) < 1e-9 and abs(obdc["gap_pp"].iloc[-1] - 2.0) < 1e-9

soi_toy = pd.DataFrame({                                             # illustrative holdings
    "facility_id": ["A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "C"],
    "bdc_id": ["X", "Y", "Z", "X", "Y", "Z"],
    "par": [10.0, 25.0, 5.0, 8.0, 12.0, 3.0],
    "fv": [9.8, 14.5, 4.6, 7.92, 11.88, 2.9],
})
disp = cross_holder_dispersion(soi_toy)
assert list(disp.index) == ["A", "B"]                                # C has a single holder
assert abs(disp.loc["A", "px_range"] - 0.40) < 1e-9                  # a 40-point same-loan gap
assert disp.loc["B", "px_range"] < 1e-9
assert stale_mark_flag([0.97, 0.97, 0.97, 0.97, 0.97, 0.95]).tolist() == [False] * 4 + [True, False]
print(obdc[["gap_pp", "na_mark"]].round(3))

Ways This Blows Up. (1) Gross versus net leverage. Use net debt to NAV as reported, and say so; gross leverage overstates \(\ell\) and understates \(m\). (2) Forward versus trailing NAV. Price-to-forward-NAV and price-to-last-reported-NAV differ by a quarter of markdowns, which in 2026 was most of the signal. (3) Buybacks. Repurchases below NAV are accretive: they mechanically raise NAV per share, so \(P/\text{NAV}\) can fall while NAV rises. OBDC’s buyback was, technically, an open market purchase, the most expensive three words in finance, deployed here to make money for the holders who stayed. Adjust NAV per share for the accretion before computing \(m\). (4) Off-balance-sheet claims. Unfunded commitments are not in \(A\) but are a call on liquidity; joint ventures and preferred equity sit between debt and equity and break the two-layer algebra. (5) Fee drag is not a constant. The incentive fee falls away when income approaches the hurdle, so \(\phi\) shrinks exactly in stress; holding it fixed overstates \(m\) in bad quarters.

Part V: Market Microstructure, Portfolio Trading, ETFs & Loans

Chapters 18–22

Equities are a supermarket. Every item has a price tag, there is one checkout, and the queue is visible to everyone. Corporate credit is a bazaar. There are no price tags; every price is a negotiation; the merchant studies your face while you study the rug; and if you ask three stalls for a quote on the same rug, all three now know something about you. Electronification is the slow installation of barcode scanners, one stall at a time. The ETF is a supermarket built next to the bazaar that sells sealed boxes of bazaar goods at a posted price, and the people who open the boxes for a living are called authorized participants. The loan market is the stall at the back where you agree a price today and the rug arrives in three weeks, maybe.

Ines runs this part of the book, because it is a poker room with worse lighting. “In the bazaar the merchant reads your face,” she says. “On the RFQ, the merchant reads your hand history. Be the merchant.”

Chapter 18, OTC Credit Microstructure & the Market Maker’s Equations, is the core derivation of the book’s market-making half. It walks through Harris’s taxonomy of traders, the Roll, Glosten–Milgrom, and Kyle models of the spread, and then the Avellaneda–Stoikov and Guéant–Lehalle–Fernandez-Tapia machinery in full (the HJB equation, the exponential-utility ansatz, the reservation price \(r^{\text{res}}\), the optimal spread) before adapting it to the thing credit actually is: RFQs rather than limit order books, win probabilities that depend on the distance to a composite price, inventory that cannot be unwound at will, and a jump-to-default term that adds \(q\lambda J\) to the reservation price. It decodes TRACE, measures RFQ hit rates, and treats BWIC leakage as the information problem it is.

Chapter 19, Portfolio Trading & Basket Pricing Engines, prices a 150-line portfolio trade in ninety seconds: the sum of fair values, less liquidation costs, less a risk charge on the residual covariance over the unwind horizon, which requires a covariance matrix for bonds that have not traded this month, a factor model and shrinkage to make it invertible, an eviction rule for the lines you refuse, a stress model for liquidity that becomes correlated exactly when you need it not to, and a healthy fear of the mystery box, the basket assembled by someone who knows which lines are the problem.

Chapter 20, Credit ETF Creation/Redemption Arbitrage (HYG, JNK, LQD, BKLN), explains how the sealed boxes get made and unmade: authorized participants, custom baskets, bid-side NAV, the arbitrage bands set by creation and redemption costs, ETF price as the market’s real-time estimate when the bonds themselves are not trading, and March 2020, when the boxes traded at discounts that looked like a malfunction and were in fact the only honest price on the screen.

Chapter 21, Leveraged Loans, CLOs & Loan-Market Microstructure (TREND), is the back stall: settlement that takes weeks, CLO constraints (CCC buckets, overcollateralization and interest-coverage tests) that turn vehicles into forced sellers on a schedule, repricing waves, the halting arrival of loan e-trading, and the loan and CLO ETFs that now sit on top of a market never designed for daily liquidity.

Chapter 22, Market-Structure Regulation & the Forces Reshaping Liquidity (TREND), takes each rule that changed the plumbing (TRACE reporting-time changes, T+1 settlement, the Treasury clearing mandate, Basel III endgame and dealer capital, CDS reporting and clearing) and works through what it did to the economics of a desk.

The trend that defines this part is that the basket became the unit of liquidity. Single bonds still trade one at a time, by negotiation, but an increasing share of risk moves in portfolios and ETF creation units, priced by engines in seconds, and the data exhaust from those trades is the raw material for everything in Part III. Mags, asked about this, says that back in her day you could get a two-way market on a single bond by calling someone who owed you a favor, and that it was worse, and that she misses it.

Chapter 18: OTC Credit Microstructure & the Market Maker’s Equations

11:52 a.m. The RFQ arrived the way bad news always arrives on a credit desk: politely, in a grey box, with a countdown timer. Client sells $8mm Halvorsen Packaging 7.25% Senior Secured Notes due 2029 (a fictional issuer; B2/B), disclosed, five dealers in competition, three minutes to respond. The composite said 91.25.

Kaz’s auto-quoter had already filled in a bid of 90.875. “Avellaneda–Stoikov,” Kaz said, with the calm of someone whose model has never been subpoenaed. “We’re long three million already. Twenty-day realized vol, half-spread from the fitted win curve, rounded to the nearest eighth, because this market is a medieval guild.”

Theo had the indenture open on his second monitor, because he always had a credit document open on his second monitor. “Their lender call is at noon,” he said. “And the indenture lets them buy back notes below par through open market purchases, with no cap. If they announce a discounted repurchase at noon, today’s sellers are the people who were told first.”

“Is an open market purchase like open outcry?” Kaz asked. “Do they have to shout?”

“They have to pay less than you,” Theo said.

“So the seller may know something,” said Ines, without looking up. “What’s the pot, what are the odds, and who at this table knows more than you?”

“The client,” Theo said. “Maybe four of the five dealers. Definitely not the auto-quoter.”

From across the row, Mags did not look up either. “Back in my day we’d just not pick up the phone.”

Ines dragged the bid to 90.25 and sent it. It did not trade; someone covered at 90.50. Twenty minutes later the bond was 86 bid, and the chat windows filled with the noise a market makes when it finds out who the patsy was. On $8mm, the winner had just bought a $360,000 lesson (illustrative).

Kaz stared at the screen. “The model was right about the inventory.”

“The model was right about the part you asked it about,” Ines said. “A quote is four things glued together. You priced one.”

That is the question this chapter answers: what is the right bid, and how much of it is fear, how much greed, how much suspicion, and how much the price of being asked again tomorrow?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to: map Harris’s trader taxonomy onto the credit ecosystem and say who is a forced seller to whom; estimate an effective spread from TRACE prints with Roll’s trick, and know when the estimator is lying; derive Kyle’s \(\lambda\) and estimate it from markouts; derive the Avellaneda–Stoikov (AS) quotes from the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation without skipping steps; solve the Guéant–Lehalle–Fernandez-Tapia (GLFT) inventory-bounded problem as a linear ODE system; extend both to jump-to-default; fit an RFQ win curve and price a hit-ratio target; decode a TRACE file into features; and model a BWIC as a first-price auction with a leaky list. You will also be able to hand all of it to ROBO in a spec that leaves it nothing to guess.

18.1 Harris’s Zoo, Relabeled for Credit

A restructuring banker learns to ask who holds the paper and what are they forced to do. A market maker asks the same question, but at the speed of a timer and about everyone at once. Larry Harris’s Trading and Exchanges (2003), the standard practitioner text on market microstructure, sorts traders by why they trade. Utilitarian traders trade for some reason other than profiting from the trade itself: hedging, investing cash, meeting a redemption, or obeying a regulator. Profit-motivated traders trade because they think the price is wrong or about to move. These include the informed, who know something about value; order anticipators, who know something about other people’s orders; and bluffers, who want you to believe they know something. Between them stand the dealers, who sell immediacy, and the arbitrageurs, who sell convergence. Harris adds four dimensions of liquidity: immediacy (how fast you can trade), width (the cost of a round trip), depth (how much size you can do at that cost), and resiliency (how fast the price recovers after you trade).

Relabeled for the credit ecosystem of Chapter 1, the zoo looks like this.

Harris type Credit population (2026) What they want What they cost the dealer
Utilitarian, uninformed Insurers selling fallen angels for capital reasons; index funds at month-end; CLOs curing CCC buckets; LDI-linked holders meeting margin calls Immediacy at a fair price, predictably timed Little in expectation. This is the dealer’s bread.
Utilitarian, arbitrage ETF authorized participants (Chapter 20); portfolio-trade desks (Chapter 19); CDS–bond basis traders Convergence of a basket to its NAV Basket risk and the mystery-box problem, but rarely issuer-level information
Profit-motivated, mostly uninformed about issuers Systematic factor pods trading momentum, value, and carry baskets (Chapters 9–11) Factor exposure Factor beta, which the dealer can hedge. IDO or it didn’t happen: their markouts are mostly not toxic once you strip the factor.
Profit-motivated, informed Distressed and crossover funds; LMT participants; anyone who has actually read the indenture To trade before the information is in the price The residual markout, which is the whole adverse-selection problem
Order anticipators Anyone who has seen a BWIC list, a leaked run, or a large RFQ shopped to too many dealers (§18.9) To trade ahead of known flow Pre-auction drift, paid by the seller
Dealers Bank dealers; non-bank liquidity providers, about 10% of credit market-making revenue in 2024 (approx.; industry dossier) Spread, and future flow Competition. Non-banks bring a different \(\gamma\) and a different \(k\) (§18.4).

Harris’s four liquidity dimensions turn into the four things an RFQ engine must estimate before it answers anything. Immediacy is the win probability within the timer. Width is the reservation spread plus the markup. Depth is how the reservation price changes with block size, not just with one more lot. Resiliency is the impact decay after a print, which is the spring Paleologo describes for equities (Paleologo p.152–153). In bonds the spring is the dealer’s own inventory, and it relaxes only when the dealer finds the other side. The rest of the chapter derives a model for each.

Desk Myth vs. Desk Reality. Myth: “The bid–ask spread is the dealer’s profit.” Reality: The quoted spread is four charges, and only one of them is profit. Fear is the inventory risk premium, \(\gamma\sigma^2(T-t)\) in §18.4. Greed is the markup a dealer with some pricing power can charge, \(\tfrac{2}{\gamma}\ln(1+\gamma/k)\). Suspicion is the expected adverse markout, \(2\pi\sigma_V\) in Glosten–Milgrom (§18.3). Franchise is a negative charge: the subsidy a dealer pays to keep winning enough RFQs to stay on the client’s list (§18.7). Realized profit is the spread minus the markout. On a toxic RFQ it is negative, which is why “the dealer made the spread” is something only people who have never been a dealer say.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.19: “the bond market is structured around a Request for Quotation (RFQ) process that has hardly changed for decades. Corporate bond bid/ask prices are indicated by dealer runs that are not firm and actionable”

Annotation. Our analysis: the Man authors are right about the protocol and, by 2026, wrong about the responder. The disclosed RFQ is still a sealed-bid auction among a handful of dealers. What changed between 2022 and 2026 is who answers it. Trumid reported 88% of eligible RFQ line items executed with no human touch in September 2025, and Tradeweb’s AiEX handled more than 40% of its institutional trades in 2025 (sources in Trend Watch, §18.7). The runs are still “not firm and actionable”, which is why §18.2 has to recover spreads from prints rather than quotes. The same page also complains about “if filled” trades. That complaint is the reason the modern engine treats fill probability as a modeled variable rather than as noise: in §18.7 the win curve \(P(x)\) is a first-class input to the quote, not an afterthought in the backtest.

18.2 Roll’s Trick: Seeing the Spread When No One Will Show You One

Equities show you a spread. Credit shows you a print, fifteen minutes late, with the size capped and the side sometimes ambiguous, and asks you to infer the spread from it, like a sommelier asked to name the vintage from the cork. Roll (1984), “A Simple Implicit Measure of the Effective Bid-Ask Spread in an Efficient Market” (Journal of Finance 39(4)), found that the spread leaves a fingerprint in the autocovariance of price changes. A trade at the bid tends to be followed by a trade at the ask, so prices bounce, and the bounce is negatively autocorrelated.

18.2.1 Derivation

Let \(m_t\) be the efficient mid, a random walk \(m_t = m_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t\) with \(\varepsilon_t\) i.i.d., mean zero, variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\). Let \(I_t \in \{-1,+1\}\) indicate whether print \(t\) was a customer sell (at the bid) or a customer buy (at the ask). Let \(c = S/2\) be the effective half-spread in price points. The print is

\[ p_t = m_t + c\,I_t . \]

Then \(\Delta p_t = \varepsilon_t + c\,(I_t - I_{t-1})\). Assume first, as Roll did, that \(I_t\) is i.i.d. with \(\mathbb{P}(I_t = 1) = \tfrac12\), independent of \(\varepsilon\). Then \(\text{Var}(I_t) = 1\) and all cross-covariances vanish, so

\[ \text{Cov}(\Delta p_t, \Delta p_{t+1}) = c^2\,\text{Cov}(I_t - I_{t-1},\, I_{t+1} - I_t) = -c^2\,\text{Var}(I_t) = -\frac{S^2}{4}. \]

Solving for the spread gives Roll’s estimator:

\[ \widehat{S}^{\text{Roll}} = 2\sqrt{-\widehat{\text{Cov}}(\Delta p_t, \Delta p_{t+1})}. \]

Bao, Pan & Wang (2011), “The Illiquidity of Corporate Bonds” (Journal of Finance 66(3)), use the same covariance directly as an illiquidity measure, \(\gamma^{\text{BPW}} = -\text{Cov}(\Delta p_t,\Delta p_{t+1})\) computed on TRACE prices. They find bond illiquidity far larger than quoted spreads suggest, and priced in the cross-section. (Their \(\gamma\) is not our risk aversion \(\gamma\), hence the superscript.)

Now break the assumption the way credit breaks it. Large customer orders are split: a $25mm sell goes out as five $5mm RFQs over an afternoon. Model the trade signs as a symmetric two-state Markov chain with lag-one autocorrelation \(\rho \in [0,1)\), so that \(\text{Cov}(I_t, I_{t+j}) = \rho^{|j|}\). Expanding term by term,

\[ \text{Cov}(I_t - I_{t-1},\, I_{t+1} - I_t) = \rho - 1 - \rho^2 + \rho = -(1-\rho)^2, \]

so \(\text{Cov}(\Delta p_t,\Delta p_{t+1}) = -c^2(1-\rho)^2\) and

\[ \widehat{S}^{\text{Roll}} \;\to\; S\,(1-\rho). \]

Order splitting makes Roll underestimate the spread by the factor \((1-\rho)\). Add informed flow that moves the mid in the direction of the trade over several prints, so that the \(\varepsilon_t\) are positively autocorrelated, and the covariance can turn positive. The square root then has no real solution. That is not a numerical accident. It is the estimator telling you that the bounce has been overwhelmed by momentum, which is information in its own right (§18.3). Dynkin’s team makes the same point from the other side when it uses return autocorrelation as an illiquidity proxy: investors split trades, which produces positive autocorrelation, and stale prices do the same (Dynkin p.771).

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Ben_Dor_Quantitative_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.120: “for most bonds the time between a broker-dealer buy and sell transaction for a given CUSIP can be very long, so it is difficult to calculate an accurate bid-ask spread using TRACE.”

Annotation. Our analysis: this is the practical objection to Roll in credit, and it bites harder than it looks. Roll’s algebra assumes the mid barely moves between consecutive prints, so that \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\) is small next to \(c^2\). When a dealer’s round trip spans three days, the mid diffuses between prints and the bounce is buried. The covariance estimate is unbiased in theory and useless in practice, because its standard error scales with \(\text{Var}(\Delta p)\), which is now dominated by \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\). Ben Dor’s team responded by building Liquidity Cost Scores from trader indications rather than prints. The 2026 desk has a third option the 2010 authors lacked: dense electronic RFQ logs, its own and the platforms’, where both sides of the market are observed within seconds. Use Roll on TRACE as a cross-check and a stress indicator, not as your spread.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Dynkin_Systematic_Investing_in_Credit p.702: LCS “measures the cost of an immediate round-trip transaction of a typical institutional size and is expressed as a percentage of a bond price”

Annotation. Our analysis: notice the three qualifiers, immediate, round-trip, and typical institutional size. Roll measures none of them exactly: it measures the average bounce across whatever sizes printed, with no immediacy constraint. For spread-quoted bonds, LCS is the bid–offer spread times spread duration. Ben Dor p.123 then multiplies the indications of non-benchmark bonds by an adjustment factor between 1.50 and 1.83, which is the industry admitting in writing that dealer indications are tighter than dealer markets. The modern desk uses LCS-type composites as the prior and its own RFQ fills as the likelihood.

Trend Watch: the great spread compression, and its stress reversals (2004–2026). What changed: TRACE dissemination was phased in from 2002 to 2005. Edwards, Harris & Piwowar (2007, Journal of Finance 62(3)) and Goldstein, Hotchkiss & Sirri (2007, Review of Financial Studies 20(2)) both find that transparency lowered customer trading costs (magnitudes vary by sample and bond type; see the papers). How big, then: Chen, Lesmond & Wei (2007) estimate bid–ask spreads of about 25 bp for AAA bonds and 180 bp for CCC; Man’s 2022 authors note that spreads are “markedly tighter in the current market” (Man_Quantitative_Credit_Alpha_Early_Mover_2022 p.20). The stress reversal: the same Man page charts a 20-day average HY bid–ask (Bloomberg data, 1 July 2017 to 2 February 2021) that gaps out in February–March 2020 and then normalizes. Kargar et al. (2021, Review of Financial Studies) estimate that at the March 2020 peak, customers’ willingness to pay for immediacy rose by roughly 200 bp per dollar traded, and flow shifted from risky-principal to slower agency trades. 2026: MarketAxess data reported by The DESK (2026-10-01) show the median EUR IG bid–ask falling from 0.0879 to 0.0673 (−23.5%) over the 34 weeks to 2026-08-23. In the March 2026 stress, however, EUR IG bid–ask hit 64% above its January average, and recovery took 4 weeks (EUR IG), 6 (US HY), 8 (US IG), 13 (EUR HY), and 14+ (EM). What it means for the desk: the median spread is a fair-weather number. A cost model calibrated on a calm window, by Roll or anything else, underprices exactly the trades you most need to price. Make the spread estimator regime-conditional, and carry the stress multiplier as a parameter.

Ways This Blows Up. (1) Taking the absolute value. When the sample covariance is positive, someone always writes 2*sqrt(abs(cov)). That reports a spread when the data are reporting momentum. Return NaN and log the sign. (2) Mixing sizes. Odd lots pay more than blocks (Edwards, Harris & Piwowar 2007), and “5MM+” capped prints are a different market from $50k retail prints. Estimate by size bucket. (3) Interdealer double counting. Both dealers report an interdealer trade. Leave both legs in and you manufacture a bounce of exactly zero width between two identical prices, which biases the covariance toward zero (§18.8). (4) Stale prints. Prints days apart measure diffusion, not bounce. Cap the gap between consecutive prints or weight by it.

Specification for AI Implementation (Roll estimator)

The Spec You Hand the Robot. What ROBO built from the vague version (“estimate the bid–ask spread from TRACE”): it averaged (ask print − bid print) over all prints on the same day, on a bond that traded twice a week, and reported a spread of zero for every day with one print. The precise spec: input a time-ordered vector of cleaned prices (points per 100 par) for one bond and one size bucket. Output (spread, autocov) in points. Require at least min_obs price changes. Return NaN when the autocovariance is non-negative, and never take an absolute value. Sanity checks: recover a known spread on simulated Roll data, recover \(S(1-\rho)\) under order splitting, and return NaN under momentum.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats, integrate, signal

RNG = np.random.default_rng(18)

def roll_spread(prices, min_obs=20):
    """Roll (1984) effective spread from consecutive trade prices (points per 100 par).
    Returns (spread_points, autocov). spread is NaN when autocov >= 0 (Roll undefined)."""
    p = np.asarray(prices, dtype=float)
    p = p[np.isfinite(p)]
    if p.size < min_obs + 2:
        return np.nan, np.nan
    dp = np.diff(p)
    c = np.cov(dp[1:], dp[:-1], ddof=1)[0, 1]
    if c >= 0.0:
        return np.nan, c          # momentum or splitting dominates: never take abs()
    return 2.0 * np.sqrt(-c), c

def simulate_roll(n, spread, sigma_mid, rho=0.0, phi_mid=0.0, rng=RNG):
    """p_t = m_t + (spread/2) I_t. I_t: symmetric +/-1 Markov chain with lag-1 autocorr rho.
    Mid increments: AR(1) with coefficient phi_mid (phi_mid > 0 mimics informed drift)."""
    stay = 0.5 * (1.0 + rho)
    flips = rng.random(n) >= stay
    flips[0] = False
    I = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0]) * np.where(np.cumsum(flips) % 2 == 0, 1.0, -1.0)
    eps = rng.normal(0.0, sigma_mid, n)
    dm = signal.lfilter([1.0], [1.0, -phi_mid], eps)
    m = 90.0 + np.cumsum(dm)
    return m + 0.5 * spread * I

# Sanity 1: Roll recovers the spread when signs are i.i.d.
s_hat, _ = roll_spread(simulate_roll(200_000, spread=0.50, sigma_mid=0.05))
assert abs(s_hat - 0.50) < 0.02, s_hat
# Sanity 2: order splitting shrinks the estimate to S(1 - rho)
s_split, _ = roll_spread(simulate_roll(200_000, spread=0.50, sigma_mid=0.05, rho=0.6))
assert abs(s_split - 0.50 * 0.4) < 0.02, s_split
# Sanity 3: informed drift turns the covariance positive -> NaN, not a fake spread
s_mom, c_mom = roll_spread(simulate_roll(50_000, spread=0.10, sigma_mid=0.10, rho=0.6, phi_mid=0.4))
assert np.isnan(s_mom) and c_mom > 0, (s_mom, c_mom)
gamma_bpw = lambda prices: -roll_spread(prices)[1]   # Bao-Pan-Wang illiquidity, points^2

The third check is worth working by hand. With \(S = 0.10\) and \(\rho = 0.6\), the bounce contributes \(-c^2(1-\rho)^2 = -0.0025 \times 0.16 = -0.0004\) to the autocovariance. The mid increments have stationary variance \(0.01/(1-0.16) \approx 0.0119\) and lag-one autocovariance \(0.4 \times 0.0119 \approx 0.0048\). Momentum wins by a factor of twelve, and a well-behaved estimator says so by refusing to answer.

Part VI: Capital Structure Arbitrage & Volatility Surfaces

Chapters 23–24

One patient, four doctors. The equity market, the equity options market, the CDS market, and the bond market each examine the same firm and each issue a diagnosis: a stock price, an implied volatility surface, a CDS spread, a bond price. Merton’s insight was that all four are looking at the same thing, the firm’s asset value \(V_t\) and its volatility \(\sigma_V\), and that their diagnoses must therefore be consistent. Capital structure arbitrage is the bet that when the doctors disagree, they will eventually agree, and that you know which one is right. Its risk is that you are wrong about which doctor, or that the patient contracts a disease none of the doctors had a word for. In May 2005 the patient was General Motors, the credit market said “downgrade,” the equity market said “takeover bid,” and a large number of funds that were long the bonds and short the stock discovered that the doctors can disagree for a very long time.

Kaz is at home in this part, because it is almost entirely math, and uneasy in it, because the math keeps bumping into documents. “A springing lien,” they ask, “is a lien that… springs?” Mags nods. “Usually at you.”

Chapter 23, Cross-Asset Convexity & the Volatility Surface, links the surfaces. It derives \(\sigma_E E = \sigma_V V\, N(d_1)\) and uses it to turn equity volatility into a credit spread, covers the CreditGrades model that commercialized the idea, and follows Carr and Wu in reading deep out-of-the-money puts as credit instruments and the skew as a market price for jump-to-default. It expresses the Greeks in spread terms so a bond trader can use them, treats convertible and capital-structure arbitrage as trades on the same surface, and takes two autopsies: May 2005, when the cross-asset hedge failed in both legs at once, and Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023, when the equity, options, and credit markets priced the same balance sheet at three different speeds.

Chapter 24, Bond-to-CDS Basis & Deliverable Obligation Mechanics, is the CDS doctor’s chart, read closely. It prices the premium and protection legs, defines the risky annuity, handles standard coupons and upfronts, and then works through the several things people mean by “basis” (against Z-spread, against asset swap, against par-equivalent CDS spread), the funding and repo terms that explain most of a negative basis, the cheapest-to-deliver option, and the two-stage auction. The last third is where the chart gets interesting: orphaned CDS when the debt moves and the reference entity does not, the manufactured credit events at Hovnanian and the Windstream fight, the 2019 ISDA narrowly-tailored-credit-event supplement that followed, and what liability management transactions have done to the definition of a credit event.

The trend that defines this part is a migration. Single-name CDS liquidity has thinned and concentrated, index CDS and equity options have become the practical instruments for expressing a view on credit volatility, and the legal boundary of what counts as a credit event has been tested by people who read the definitions more carefully than the drafters did. The quant consequence is that the “arbitrage” in capital structure arbitrage is increasingly a bet on the relative speed of four markets rather than on a true mispricing, and the desk that measures those speeds, with the lead–lag tools from Chapter 10 and the hedge matrices from Chapter 8, is the desk that gets paid. Ines’s summary is shorter. “Four players, one deck, and one of them has read the rules. Figure out which.”

Part VII: Alternative Data, NLP, AI & Systems

Chapters 25–27

A credit agreement is a program. It has variables (“Consolidated EBITDA”), functions (“Permitted Investments”), conditionals (“so long as no Event of Default shall have occurred and be continuing”), recursion (Consolidated EBITDA is defined in terms of Consolidated Net Income, which excludes items defined by reference to Consolidated EBITDA), and a type system that two law firms will argue about for eighteen months. What it does not have is a compiler. For forty years the runtime was a lawyer. Part VII builds the compiler, then builds the machine it runs on.

Theo’s first specification for ROBO in this part read: “compute the capacity of the general Restricted Payments basket.” ROBO returned “$50 million.” The basket was “the greater of $50 million and 100 percent of Consolidated EBITDA,” and Consolidated EBITDA that quarter was negative, so ROBO was, infuriatingly, correct. Theo rewrote the spec. It now has units, a definition graph, a fiscal-quarter lookup, and a test case named after the quarter in question.

Chapter 25, NLP for Credit Agreements, Indentures & PACER Dockets, parses the program. It treats defined terms as nodes in a graph and finds the cycles, segments the document, extracts definitions, normalizes “greater of” baskets into capacity functions of EBITDA, uses language models for extraction with schema validation and mandatory citations back to the page, and feeds the result into the capacity calculator and the Priming Risk Score features of Chapter 13. It then turns to the court docket: EDGAR for the documents, CourtListener and RECAP for the filings, Rule 2019 statements as a time series of who holds what and when the Ad Hoc Group formed, split, or re-formed, claims registers as a map of the unsecured pool, and DIP roll-ups as the first move of the endgame. It uses synthetic agreement text throughout, and it studies how fast each of these signals decays once the market has read the same filing.

Chapter 26, AI Agents & LLMs on the Credit Desk (TREND), is the operating manual for the specifier, which is to say for the reader. It covers the pricing and research tools that language models have made possible, agentic workflows for research and surveillance, evaluation and hallucination controls (a citation that cannot be checked is a hallucination with a footnote), document question-answering with provenance, and the discipline of writing a spec a machine cannot misread: units, boundary conditions, edge cases, deterministic replay, and tests that fail loudly. It tracks adoption on desks from 2023 through 2026, with dates.

Chapter 27, System Construction, Low-Latency Infrastructure & ASICs/FPGAs, is the machine. It is honest about latency economics: a bond RFQ gives you seconds, but the hedge and the quote-pull happen in microseconds, and a desk that is slow to pull its quotes when Treasuries gap is a desk that has donated money to someone faster. It covers the ingestion pipeline, the security master (an LMT exchange creates new identifiers, and a security master that does not know this will price the wrong bond), pricing and risk engines, the OMS and EMS, FIX, FPGA trigger tables that evaluate \(\Delta P = -D\,\Delta y\) per bond against a threshold without asking a CPU, kernel bypass, latency budgets as a queueing problem, and the kill switch, with Knight Capital in 2012 as the reason the kill switch is not optional.

The trend that defines this part is the arrival of language models on the desk and the quiet reassignment of work that followed: reading moved to machines, specifying moved to humans, and the humans who could specify best turned out to be the ones who had read the most documents by hand. Mags observes that back in her day you read the indenture yourself and were wrong in private. Theo observes that ROBO is wrong in public, instantly, and with a stack trace, and that he has come to prefer it.

Chapter 26: AI Agents & LLMs on the Credit Desk

26.0 Cold Open: Section 6.08(b)(xiv)

The summary came back in eleven seconds. That was the first warning sign: nothing true about a restricted payments covenant has ever taken eleven seconds.

Theo had given ROBO the credit agreement for Halyard Holdings, a fictional sponsor-backed widget maker the desk uses as its practice dummy (312 pages, two amendments, and one “technical” amendment that was not), and typed: Summarize the restricted payments covenant. ROBO returned four clean paragraphs: a builder basket, a ratio-based unlimited basket at 5.25x, a general basket at “the greater of $40mm and 30% of Consolidated EBITDA,” and a management-equity basket. Every paragraph had a citation. The general basket cited §6.08(b)(xiv).

Theo opened the PDF. Section 6.08(b) ran from (i) to (xii) and then stopped, with the calm of a document that has said everything it means to say.

“There is no fourteen,” he said.

Kaz leaned over. “It’s within two of the right answer.”

“So is a bluff,” said Ines, without looking up.

“The builder basket is real, though,” Kaz went on. “Who’s the builder? Does the contractor need to be bonded?”

“It builds from retained excess cash flow.”

“So it’s a contractor who only works with your money.” Kaz thought about it. “That’s every contractor.”

Mags spoke from two desks over, in the voice she saves for things that used to be worse. “Back in my day, an associate who made up a section number got fired by phone, and by grudge, before the closing dinner. This thing makes one up in eleven seconds, and nobody gets fired.”

Theo checked the other three paragraphs. They were right: the right numbers, the right sections, the right cross-references to the definition of Available Amount. That made it worse. A summary that is wrong everywhere gets thrown away. A summary that is right three times out of four teaches you to stop checking, and the fourth paragraph is the one that sizes the position.

Ines finally turned around. “What’s the pot, what are the odds, and who at this table knows more than you? Right now, the document does. The robot is just the one talking loudest.”

So here is the question this chapter answers: how do you put a machine that is sometimes wrong, and confident when it is, into a process that may never be wrong silently?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

  • treat a language model as a stochastic reader with measurable power, calibration, and failure modes, and validate it the way Bohn and Stein validate a PD model;
  • write a citation contract that makes every machine claim checkable by code, and measure the three rates (accuracy, validity, support) together with the one that hurts, the “footnoted hallucination”;
  • set an abstention threshold from the desk’s own costs instead of from vibes, and see why benchmark scoring trains models to guess;
  • compute the reliability of an agent chain with an imperfect verifier, and explain why “workflows first, agents last” is arithmetic and not taste;
  • govern an LLM like a vendor model (SR 11-7 lineage, FINRA Notice 24-09, FINRA’s 2026 oversight report) and wire it into the desk like an untrusted data feed;
  • hand ROBO a specification it cannot misread, which turns out to be a skill you already have: you used to call it reading a credit agreement.

26.1 What a Language Model Is, for a Specifier

Strip away the marketing and a language model is one object: a conditional distribution over the next token given everything before it. Write \(x_{1:t}\) for the token sequence so far (the prompt, the retrieved pages, the model’s own output to date) and \(\theta\) for the frozen weights. The model supplies

\[ p_\theta(x_{t+1} = v \mid x_{1:t}), \qquad v \in \mathcal{V}, \]

a probability for every token \(v\) in a vocabulary \(\mathcal{V}\) of order \(10^5\) entries. Generation samples one token, appends it, and repeats. The temperature \(T>0\) reshapes the distribution before sampling,

\[ p_T(v \mid x_{1:t}) = \frac{p_\theta(v \mid x_{1:t})^{1/T}}{\sum_{u \in \mathcal{V}} p_\theta(u \mid x_{1:t})^{1/T}}, \]

so \(T \to 0\) concentrates all mass on the most likely token (greedy decoding) and \(T = 1\) samples from the model as trained. Three consequences matter for anyone who will specify work to one of these.

First, the model produces text that is probable given the text, and “probable” equals “true” only under conditions. When the answer is stated in the context, is salient, and is determinate, the most probable continuation is usually the correct one. When any of those fails, the model still produces the most probable continuation, and the most probable continuation of “the general basket appears in Section 6.08(b)(” is a plausible roman numeral. That is why fabricated citations look right: they are draws from the distribution of real citations. §6.08(b)(xiv) is not a random error. It is a typical one, and that is the bad news.

Second, the model is a reader, not a calculator. Arithmetic done “in its head” is next-token prediction over digits. On a credit desk this rule has no exceptions: the model may locate the “greater of $40mm and 30% of Consolidated EBITDA” clause and extract its parameters into a typed record, but the capacity is computed by deterministic code (§26.12), and so are the waterfall, the leverage ratio, and the make-whole. The model calls tools; it does not impersonate them.

Third, a token is both the unit of cost and the unit of attention. Vendors price per million input and output tokens, and a model’s context window, its working memory, is measured in tokens too. A 300-page credit agreement is roughly 150,000 words, or 200,000 to 260,000 tokens depending on the tokenizer (approx.; one vendor’s pricing page notes that its newer tokenizer produces about 30% more tokens for the same text). “It fits in the context window” is now true of most single documents. Whether the model used what was in the window is a different question.

Reading is not using

Liu et al. (2023), Lost in the Middle (TACL), put the relevant fact for a question at different positions in a long context and measured accuracy. The curve is U-shaped: facts near the start or the end of the context are used, and facts in the middle are used much less, even by models built for long contexts. A credit agreement’s definitions sit at the front, its covenants in the middle, and its signature pages at the end. The U-curve therefore puts the least attention on the part of the document that decides recoveries. Liu and Liu (2026), Reading Is Not Using, sharpen the point for financial documents: as unrelated context grows from 2,000 to 128,000 tokens, a risk disclosure’s influence on the model’s judgment decays to the noise floor, even though the model can still retrieve the disclosure when asked. Retrieval accuracy and decision influence are different measurements, and only the second one moves money.

Desk Myth vs. Desk Reality. Myth: “We gave it the whole agreement, so it considered the whole agreement.” Reality: You gave it the whole agreement the way you give a summer analyst the whole data room. What was actually read depends on position, on salience, and on what was asked. Ask narrow questions against retrieved spans, with the span’s location logged, and measure accuracy by position (§26.12 includes a toy U-curve test).

The stochastic reader, formally

For the rest of the chapter, a reader is a randomized map

\[ \mathcal{R}_\theta : (q, \mathcal{D}, \xi) \mapsto y, \]

from a question \(q\), a document store \(\mathcal{D}\), and the sampling randomness \(\xi\) (temperature, seed, and, as §26.9 shows, the inference server’s batch composition) to an output \(y\). The desk cares about the physical-measure probability \(\Pr^{\mathbb{P}}\big(A(y) = 1 \mid q, \mathcal{D}\big)\) that the output is correct, about how that probability varies with the question type, the position of the evidence, and the document length, and about whether the reader knows it. One convention, stated once: every probability in this chapter is a \(\mathbb{P}\) quantity, an error rate, an agreement rate, or a cost. No LLM output is ever a \(\mathbb{Q}\) object. Spreads, hazard rates, and implied vols enter the chapter only as inputs to, or outputs of, the deterministic pricers that the reader feeds.

This framing has a payoff that the rest of the chapter collects. A reader with a measurable hit rate, a measurable calibration curve, and measurable failure modes is a model, and credit has a mature discipline for validating models of exactly this type: binary outcomes, rare costly errors, and a regulator who wants documentation.

[SOURCE EXTRACTION] Bohn_Stein_Active_Credit_Portfolio_Management p.394: “Diagnosability: In conjunction with transparency, the ability to drill into a model’s behavior is an important aspect of validation.
